title: learned
text:
Dhrona’s nightly batch never changes the files Ramabana briefs from. It commits each candidate it keeps on its own pending/<id> branch of the learned folder’s git repository. The briefing and skill discovery read only the folder’s files, which are its HEAD, so a pending candidate has no effect until a person accepts it. --no-learned leaves out the folder whatever it holds.
pending lists what waits, diff shows one candidate’s change, accept moves it onto HEAD, and reject drops it. Each of diff, accept and reject returns a dict with ok and id, and error when ok is False, so a host such as Leela can show the result as it is. They take the lock a Dhrona batch holds, and refuse while a batch runs. accept also refuses a candidate that would take AGENTS.md past LEARNED_MAX, the 2,000 characters Dhrona allows one candidate, since accepted rounds add up.
compact asks Dhrona for a shorter AGENTS.md when accepted lessons crowd it. Dhrona’s editor model merges and shortens the paragraphs Dhrona proposed, keeps every paragraph a person wrote byte for byte, and commits the result as one more pending candidate, which diff, accept and reject act on like any other. compact(folder, id) also folds in pending candidate id, the case accept refuses for size: the refusal returns length and names /learned compact ID, and accepting that compaction accepts the candidate with it. compact returns {ok, id, before, after}, where before and after are the file’s length in characters, or {ok: False, error}. It needs the dhrona extra, and says so when Dhrona is missing. It runs one model turn, so it takes as long as that turn.

reject

    folder, id
):
Drop pending candidate id; {ok, id}.

):

    folder, id

Move pending candidate id onto HEAD, which the next briefing reads, then the other candidates onto it: {ok, id, commit, moved, stale}.

Each candidate waiting for review, oldest first, as {id, at, subject, files, stale}; at is when it was proposed, in epoch seconds, and stale why it cannot be accepted or None.

Move each pending candidate proposed on an older HEAD onto HEAD where it picks cleanly; returns (moved, stale) ids.

<cfg>/learned, whether or not a session runs with it.

    cfg:str='~/.config/ramabana', on:bool=True

Turn learning on or off in this machine’s config.toml, its comments kept; cfg’s settings.json is never written. Raises ValueError for a config.toml that is not TOML.

enabled
def enabled(
    cfg:str='~/.config/ramabana'
):
Whether learning is on: learning in this machine’s config.toml, which a value only <cfg>/settings.json holds moves into the first time it is read. On unless set off.


A candidate is accepted in a throwaway worktree first, so a conflict never leaves markers in the files a running session briefs from. HEAD moves only when the pick is clean. After it moves, restack moves every other candidate proposed on an older HEAD onto the new one where it picks cleanly, and accept returns those ids as moved. A candidate that no longer picks cleanly, for example one that edits a line a compaction rewrote, is listed as stale, and pending gives the reason in its stale field, so a host can show it beside the candidate. Ids sort by when Dhrona proposed them, which moving does not change. A candidate whose change HEAD already holds is accepted with commit None. The commit keeps Dhrona as its author, and its commit time is the moment of acceptance, which is where Dhrona’s 30-day expiry clock starts.

import os, json, time
def git(d, *a): return subprocess.run(['git', '-C', str(d), *a], check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()
def propose(folder, files, id):
    "What Dhrona's `keep` does: a commit on `pending/<id>` off HEAD, the folder's files untouched."
    wt = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'wt'
    git(folder, 'worktree', 'add', '-q', '-b', PENDING + id, str(wt), 'HEAD')
    for rel, text in files.items(): (wt/rel).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); (wt/rel).write_text(text)
    git(wt, 'add', '-A'); git(wt, '-c', 'user.name=Dhrona', '-c', 'user.email=d@x', 'commit', '-qm', f'Lesson from a replay: {id}')
    git(folder, 'worktree', 'remove', '--force', str(wt))

    f = Path(d)/'learned'; f.mkdir()
    (f/'AGENTS.md').write_text('A rule a person wrote.\n')

    a, b, c = '20261019-010101-aaaaaa', '20261019-020202-bbbbbb', '20261019-030303-cccccc'
    propose(f, {'skills/sizes/SKILL.md': '---\nname: sizes\ndescription: x\n---\nuse ls\n'}, a)
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': 'Something else entirely.\n'}, b)
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': 'A third view.\n'}, c)
    test_eq([(p['id'], p['files']) for p in pending(f)], [(a, ['skills/sizes/SKILL.md']), (b, ['AGENTS.md']), (c, ['AGENTS.md'])])
    test_eq((f/'AGENTS.md').read_text(), 'A rule a person wrote.\n')   # nothing pending reaches the briefing
    assert not (f/'skills').exists()
    assert '+use ls' in diff(f, a)['diff']
    r = accept(f, a)
    test_eq(r['moved'], [b, c])                            # the others now sit on the new HEAD
    assert r['ok'] and r['commit'] and (f/'skills'/'sizes'/'SKILL.md').exists() and a not in [p['id'] for p in pending(f)]
    test_eq(git(f, 'log', '-1', '--format=%an'), 'Dhrona')
    test_eq(accept(f, b)['ok'], True)
    test_eq([p['stale'] for p in pending(f)], [STALE])     # `c` rewrites the line `b` changed
    head, text = git(f, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD'), (f/'AGENTS.md').read_text()
    r = accept(f, c)                                       # it rewrote the line `b` changed
    assert not r['ok'] and 'no longer applies' in r['error'], r
    test_eq((git(f, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD'), (f/'AGENTS.md').read_text()), (head, text))   # HEAD and the files are as they were
    assert '<<<<' not in text and git(f, 'status', '--porcelain') == ''
    test_eq(reject(f, c), dict(ok=True, id=c))
    test_eq(pending(f), [])
    test_eq(accept(f, c)['ok'], False)                     # gone
    test_eq(accept(f, '--force')['ok'], False)             # not an id, never an option
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': 'Hand edit pending.\n'}, a)
    (f/'AGENTS.md').write_text('an uncommitted edit\n')
    assert 'uncommitted' in accept(f, a)['error']
    git(f, 'checkout', '-q', '--', '.')
    with _locked(f) as held:                                # a batch holds it
        assert held and 'batch is running' in accept(f, a)['error'] and 'batch is running' in reject(f, a)['error']
    test_eq(len(git(f, 'worktree', 'list').splitlines()), 1)   # no worktree left behind
    test_eq(pending(Path(d)/'none'), [])
    git(f, 'checkout', '-q', '--', '.'); reject(f, a)
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': 'A rule a person wrote.\n' + 'x' * LEARNED_MAX}, a)   # past Dhrona's limit
    head, r = git(f, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD'), accept(f, a)
    assert not r['ok'] and 'past the 2,000' in r['error'] and r['length'] > LEARNED_MAX and git(f, 'rev-parse', 'HEAD') == head, r
    assert a in learned_command(f) and 'past the 2,000' in learned_command(f, f'accept {a}')
    test_eq(learned_command(f, f'reject {a}'), f'rejected {a}')
    test_eq(learned_command(f), 'nothing is pending')
    assert 'say /learned' in learned_command(f, 'frobnicate')

    git(f, 'init', '-q'); git(f, 'add', '-A'); git(f, '-c', 'user.name=t', '-c', 'user.email=t@x', 'commit', '-qm', 'first')
    a, big, x, y = '20261019-010101-aaaaaa', '20261019-020202-bbbbbb', '20261019-030303-cccccc', '20261019-040404-dddddd'
    lessons = 'A rule a person wrote.\n\n' + 'Read sizes with ls -l. ' * 40 + '\n'
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': lessons}, a); accept(f, a)
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': lessons + '\n' + 'Run pytest -q before a commit. ' * 40 + '\n'}, big)
    propose(f, {'skills/rg/SKILL.md': '---\nname: rg\ndescription: x\n---\nuse rg\n'}, x)
    propose(f, {'AGENTS.md': lessons.replace('Read sizes', 'Read file sizes', 1)}, y)
    r = accept(f, big)
    assert not r['ok'] and r['length'] > LEARNED_MAX and f'/learned compact {big}' in r['error'], r

    assert r['ok'] and r['before'] > LEARNED_MAX >= r['after'], r
    assert 'nothing is pending' in compact(f, '20990101-000000-abcdef')['error']
    r = accept(f, r['id'])                                  # the compaction carries `big` with it
    assert r['ok'] and (f/'AGENTS.md').read_text() == 'A rule a person wrote.\n\nRead sizes with ls -l.\n\nRun pytest -q before a commit.\n', r
    test_eq((r['moved'], r['stale']), ([x], [y]))           # `x` moved onto the compacted file; `y` edits a line it rewrote
    test_eq([(p['id'], p['stale']) for p in pending(f)], [(x, None), (y, STALE)])
    assert f'{y}  AGENTS.md' in learned_command(f) and '(stale: it no longer applies' in learned_command(f)

    assert accept(f, x)['ok'] and accept(f, y)['error'] == STALE

learned_command is the text form a terminal shows. /learned in a session and ramabana-learned from a shell both use it: with no argument it lists what is pending, diff ID, accept ID and reject ID act on one, and compact proposes a shorter AGENTS.md.
Learning is one setting per machine, learning in config.toml (see setup), and it is on unless set off. set_enabled(cfg, False), /learned off in a session, or ramabana-learned off from a shell turn it off for every session on this machine, whatever its config folder. Off leaves the learned AGENTS.md and learned skills out of the briefing, drops the briefing’s rule to record lessons, keeps remember to plain notes, has Agent.lessons() return none, writes no start.json, and makes Dhrona’s nightly schedule return “learning is off” without touching the learned folder. Lessons already kept stay where they are, unread. The review queue still works, so a person can clear it. Agent(learned=False), the CLI’s --no-learned, turns learning off for one session only.
Ramabana 0.2.44 kept the switch in each config folder’s settings.json. When config.toml does not set learning, enabled(cfg) reads it from <cfg>/settings.json and writes it into config.toml, so a choice made there survives; the settings.json an embedding app shares is never written. A config.toml that is not valid TOML is never rewritten: set_enabled raises ValueError saying so, and /learned on returns that message:

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    os.environ['RAMABANA_CONFIG'] = str(toml := Path(d)/'config.toml')
    try:
        assert enabled(d)
        test_eq(learned_command(learned_folder(d), 'off'), 'learning is off')
        test_eq((enabled(d), (Path(d)/SETTINGS).exists()), (False, False))
        assert '\nlearning = false\n' in toml.read_text()
        test_eq(set_enabled(d, True), True)
        toml.unlink(); (Path(d)/SETTINGS).write_text(json.dumps({'editor': {'tabSize': 2}, 'learning': 'off'}))
        test_eq(enabled(d), False)   # 0.2.44's setting moves to config.toml, and settings.json is left as it was
        assert 'learning = false' in toml.read_text() and json.loads((Path(d)/SETTINGS).read_text())['learning'] == 'off'
        toml.write_text('learning = [')
        assert 'not valid TOML' in learned_command(learned_folder(d), 'on') and toml.read_text() == 'learning = ['
    finally: os.environ.pop('RAMABANA_CONFIG')

title: runtime
text:
A local engine such as LiteRT is a C++ library loaded into the Python process. It prints its messages straight to file descriptors 1 and 2, the process’s standard output and standard error, so they never pass through Python’s print or logging. When a turn fails, for example because the prompt was longer than the model’s window, the only explanation is often one of those lines. This section captures the descriptors during a model call and keeps the lines that explain a failure.
interesting picks those lines out of captured text. It drops the engine’s routine startup messages, keeps lines that mention an error, a failure, an exceeded limit or running out of memory, and returns the last limit of them.


source


def interesting(
    text, limit:int=4
):
The lines of captured output a person should see: complaints, not chatter.


Engines have no log level to filter on, so interesting matches words. In this log three lines are startup chatter and one says why the call failed:

log = '''Created TensorFlow Lite XNNPACK delegate for CPU.
Loading model from /models/gemma-e4b
I0000 00:00:1730000000.000000 metal delegate ready
ERROR: input tokens 21014 exceeds max_num_tokens 16384
'''
interesting(log)

Repeated lines collapse into one, and only the most recent limit lines are kept. An engine that fails on every step of a tool loop prints the same error many times, and the user needs to see it once.

test_eq(interesting('ERROR: oom\nERROR: oom\nERROR: oom'), ['ERROR: oom'])
interesting('\n'.join(f'error {i}' for i in range(10)), limit=2)

captured is a context manager that records what is written to descriptors 1 and 2 inside its with block. It copies the output rather than hiding it: the bytes still reach the terminal, and the last 8,000 bytes of each descriptor (MAX_KEEP) are kept in cap.text. cap.problems runs interesting over that text.
Only one captured block is active at a time across threads, because two threads redirecting the same descriptor would restore each other’s copies and leave the real descriptor detached. A thread that cannot take the lock within half a second runs its block without capture. Setting RAMABANA_NO_NATIVE_CAPTURE=1 turns capture off.


source


def captured(
    fds:tuple=(1, 2), enabled:NoneType=None
):
Copy what is written to descriptors 1 and 2 into text, while the output still reaches the terminal.




source


def capture(
    fn, *a, **kw
):
Call fn and return (result, problems); an exception carries them out too.


capture(fn, *args) is the form to use around a single call. It calls fn inside captured and returns a pair: the result, and the problem lines the engine printed. A call can succeed and still print a warning worth showing, as here, where the engine truncated its input:

def _engine_call():
    os.write(2, b'Created TensorFlow Lite XNNPACK delegate for CPU.\n')
    os.write(2, b'WARNING: input exceeds max_num_tokens 16384, truncating\n')
    return 'a short reply'

capture(_engine_call)

When fn raises, capture attaches the problem lines to the exception as native_output and raises it again. Native failures often arrive as an exception with an empty message, and this keeps the real explanation with it:

def _engine_dies():
    os.write(2, b'ERROR: failed to allocate 4.00 GiB for KV cache\n')
    raise RuntimeError('')
try: capture(_engine_dies)
except RuntimeError as e: err = e
err.native_output

title: runtime
text:
Sizing a conversation
These functions decide when a conversation has grown too big for its model. Each limit is a fraction of the context window rather than a fixed number of tokens, so the same code works for a 4k-token local model and a 200k-token hosted one. A fixed reserve would not: with 16k tokens held back from a 4k window, every turn would be due for compaction, and the agent would compact a two-message conversation forever.
estimate_tokens counts the tokens in a text. threshold gives the token count at which compaction becomes due, and should_compact compares a count with it. halvings returns a budget followed by its halves, for retrying a request whose size was only estimated.


source

should_compact
def should_compact(
    used, ctx, reserve:NoneType=None
):
Whether used tokens against a ctx window has crossed the line.




source

threshold
def threshold(
    ctx, reserve:NoneType=None
):
The token count at which a conversation should be compacted, or None when there is no window. reserve is config.toml’s window.reserve, else RESERVE.




source

halvings
def halvings(
    budget, tries:int=3, floor:int=256
):
A budget and its halvings, to retry a prompt whose fit was only estimated.




source

estimate_tokens
def estimate_tokens(
    text, count:NoneType=None
):
Tokens in text: exact via count when a tokenizer is at hand, CHARS_PER_TOKEN otherwise.


estimate_tokens uses the model’s own tokenizer when you pass one as count, and otherwise divides the length of the text by CHARS_PER_TOKEN (3.25). The estimate is rough, and close enough for budgeting.

estimate_tokens('the exporter writes one module per notebook'), estimate_tokens('', ), estimate_tokens('x' * 400)

threshold(ctx) holds back a reserve below the window: the full RESERVE of 16,384 tokens for a large window, and at most a quarter of the window for a smaller one. Without the quarter-window cap, a 4k model would be due for compaction before its first turn.

threshold(200_000), threshold(32_768), threshold(4096)


test_eq(threshold(4096), 3072)
test_eq(threshold(0), None)
should_compact(3000, 4096), should_compact(3072, 4096)

title: runtime
text:
Reading a conversation
A backend stores its conversation as a list of message dictionaries in urai’s format, which is the same for every model. Each message has a role (user, assistant or tool) and content. An assistant message that calls tools also carries tool_calls, and the result of each call comes back as a tool message. Compaction reads this list directly, using urai’s resp_text for a message’s text and tool_rows for its tool calls.
The examples below use this four-message conversation: a request, a tool call, the tool’s result, and the reply.

hist = [
    {'role': 'user', 'content': 'the exporter duplicates cells, please fix it'},
    {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'Reading the exporter.',
     'tool_calls': [{'function': {'name': 'view_file', 'arguments': {'path': 'nbdev/maker.py'}}}]},
    {'role': 'tool', 'content': 'def _make_exists(self, cells):\n    with self.fname.open("a") as f: ...'},
    {'role': 'assistant', 'content': 'It appends, so a second export duplicates every named cell.'},
]
[(m.get('role', '?'), resp_text(m)[:40], [name for name, _ in tool_rows(m)]) for m in hist]

serialise writes a list of messages as the text a summarizing model reads. Each message goes in a <message> tag, with its tool calls named in a <tool-calls> tag, and each text is clipped to mx characters (2,000 by default). Tool results make up most of a conversation’s length and little of its meaning, so clipping them costs little.


source

split_previous
def split_previous(
    msgs
):
Split off a leading summary: (previous_summary_or_None, remaining_msgs).




source

serialise
def serialise(
    msgs, mx:int=2000
):
Messages as the tagged block the summarizer reads, each text clipped to mx.



print(serialise(hist))

Once a conversation has been compacted, its first message is a user message that starts with SUMMARY_PREFIX and holds the summary. split_previous separates that summary from the messages after it. The next compaction can then update the existing summary with the new messages, instead of summarising the old summary as if it were ordinary conversation.

prev, rest = split_previous([{'role': 'user', 'content': SUMMARY_PREFIX + '## Goal\nfix the exporter'}] + hist)
prev, len(rest)


test_eq(split_previous(hist), (None, hist))
split_previous([])

summarise_prompt builds the request sent to the summarizing model. With no earlier summary it asks for a new one in a fixed format: goal, constraints, progress, key decisions, next steps and critical context. When split_previous finds an earlier summary, it asks for that summary to be updated with the new messages instead. extra adds a line saying what the summary should focus on.
The summary is usually written by a cheaper model with a smaller window, so max_tokens caps the size of the request. When the whole request does not fit, the earlier summary is cut to a quarter of the budget, and the messages after it fill what is left, cut from the end. The instructions come last and are kept whole while the budget can hold them.


source

fold_summary
def fold_summary(
    msgs, summariser, extra:str='', max_tokens:NoneType=None, count:NoneType=None
):
Summarise msgs in runs that each fit max_tokens, every summary updated with the next run; ’’ when a step answers nothing.




source

transcript_runs
def transcript_runs(
    msgs, budget, count:NoneType=None
):
msgs in consecutive runs whose transcript fits budget tokens; a message that alone is larger makes a run of its own.




source

summarise_prompt
def summarise_prompt(
    msgs, extra:str='', max_tokens:NoneType=None, count:NoneType=None
):
The bounded prompt handed to the summarizer, choosing fresh or update instructions.


With no budget the request holds the whole conversation, one <message> per message, followed by the format instructions:

p = summarise_prompt(hist)
test_eq(p.count('<message'), len(hist))
estimate_tokens(p)

With a budget, the request always fits. When the budget is too small to hold the instructions as well, they are cut too, as at 120 and 30 tokens below. A request with cut instructions still gets an answer, while a request over the limit would be refused by the engine.

[estimate_tokens(summarise_prompt(hist, max_tokens=n)) for n in (2000, 400, 120, 30)]


for n in (2000, 400, 120, 30): assert estimate_tokens(summarise_prompt(hist, max_tokens=n)) <= n
summarise_prompt(hist, max_tokens=30)

Summarising needs a second model call, and sometimes no summarizing model is available or its summary cannot be trusted. Surgical compaction needs no model. surgical_history rewrites old messages as short lines, one per request, reply, tool call and tool result, each cut to a token budget for its role. What was asked, what was called, what came back and what was concluded all survive, at a fraction of the size.
truncate_middle does the cutting. It keeps the start and end of a text and replaces the middle with …, because paths, error messages and diffs carry most of their meaning at the ends. Cut to 12 tokens, this long name keeps its file and its last function:


source

truncate_middle
def truncate_middle(
    text, budget, count:NoneType=None, mark:str=' … '
):
Keep both ends of text inside a token budget.




source

surgical_history
def surgical_history(
    msgs, policy:NoneType=None, count:NoneType=None
):
Render old history as a compact, readable DSL while preserving tool evidence.



truncate_middle('nbs/01_runtime.ipynb::Compactor.compact::summarise_prompt', 12)

Each role has its own marker: § for the user, » for the assistant’s text, ▶ for a tool call and > for its result. The lines of a tool result are joined with ¶.

print(surgical_history(hist))

SURGICAL_POLICY sets the budgets: 2,000 tokens for a user message, 150 for the assistant’s text, 60 for a tool call and 35 for a result. The user’s own words are kept nearly whole, and tool results are cut hardest. policy overrides any of them:

print(surgical_history(hist, policy={'result': 8, 'assistant': 20}))

title: runtime
text:
Reorienting the model
After compaction the model sees a summary where its conversation used to be, and it can draw wrong conclusions from that. reorient writes the reminder placed after the summary. It says whether the Python kernel survived, so that the model neither rebuilds variables that still exist nor uses ones that are gone. It tells the model that skill text it read earlier is no longer in context and has to be read again with read_skill, naming the skills when skills is given. It also tells the model not to answer a finished request a second time: if the latest request is complete, the model replies in one line and waits. REORIENT is the reminder with the default arguments.


source

reorient
def reorient(
    kernel_alive:bool=True, skills:tuple=()
):
The system reminder placed after a compacted or otherwise rewritten conversation.



print(reorient(skills=('nbdev', 'fossick')))

When the kernel restarted, the reminder says the namespace is empty. Getting this wrong would send the model looking for variables that no longer exist, or rebuilding ones that do.

test_eq('do not re-import anything' in reorient(kernel_alive=False), False)
print(reorient(kernel_alive=False)[:180])


assert 'inspect_python' in reorient() and 'list_vars' not in reorient()

title: runtime
text:
Notices on the way in
Before a prompt reaches the model, prompt_notices checks it with a few string tests and returns notices: short instructions that tell the model how to treat the prompt. They follow the UserPromptSubmit hook in Answer.AI’s aai-coding prompts, and each one answers a mistake models often make.

A prompt ending in ? is a question. The model answers it and stops, without starting the work it implies (Q_NOTICE).
A prompt containing “please read”, “read the” or “have a look at” asks the model to read the target in full before answering (READ_NOTICE).
A bare approval such as “go”, “ok” or “do it” approves only what the user explicitly agreed to, not everything the model proposed earlier (APPROVAL_NOTICE).
A prompt starting with “BTW” is a side request. The model answers it and then goes back to the task it was on (BTW_NOTICE).
A prompt starting with a verb such as fix, add, run or rename, or ending in as NAME, asks for action. The model does the work and checks it before replying (ACTION_NOTICE).

Three one-character prompts are shortcuts and get only their own notice: . continues the agreed task, ; asks for the last answer in simpler words, and , asks what the user needs to answer next.


source

notices_block
def notices_block(
    prompt
):
The notices for prompt as one reminder to append to it, or ''.




source

prompt_notices
def prompt_notices(
    prompt
):
Notices a submitted prompt earns, from aai-coding’s UserPromptSubmit hook.


A question gets Q_NOTICE and nothing else. A bare “go” gets APPROVAL_NOTICE:

test_eq(prompt_notices('can you fix the exporter?'), [Q_NOTICE])
prompt_notices('go')

A prompt can earn several notices. Here an imperative gets one, a side request that asks for a read gets two, and “thanks” gets none:

[len(prompt_notices(p)) for p in ('fix the exporter', 'BTW please read nbs/01_runtime.ipynb', 'thanks')]

notices_block is the function the agent calls. It wraps the notices in one <system-reminder> block, ready to append to the prompt, or returns '' when there are none.

print(notices_block('ok'))


test_eq(notices_block('thanks'), '')
notices_block('thanks')

title: runtime
section: Fitting a notebook into the prompt
text:
Fitting a notebook into the prompt
A prompt can carry the user’s open notebook inside a <notebook> tag, one <cell> per cell. Each cell has a compact attribute that the user sets: keep, auto or discard. compact_notebook_context leaves the prompt alone when it fits. When it does not, it removes discard cells, then auto cells, each in notebook order, until the prompt fits. It never removes a keep cell. A <context-compacted> tag records how many cells were left out.
fits is a function that says whether a prompt fits. The agent passes the backend’s fits, so the decision is made against the real window of the model in use.


source

compact_notebook_context
def compact_notebook_context(
    prompt, fits
):
Reduce a tagged notebook only when prompt does not fit. A keep cell is never removed.


A notebook of three cells, one with each setting, and a question about it. When everything fits, the prompt comes back unchanged:

nb = '''<notebook path=analysis.ipynb>
<cell id=1 compact="discard">print(load_everything())  # 900 lines of output</cell>
<cell id=2 compact="auto">df = read_csv('sales.csv')</cell>
<cell id=3 compact="keep">model.fit(df)  # the cell the question is about</cell>
</notebook>

why did the fit fail?'''
print(compact_notebook_context(nb, fits=lambda s: True))

With a lower limit the discard cell goes first, and <context-compacted> records it:

out = compact_notebook_context(nb, fits=lambda s: len(s) < 270)
print(out)

A lower limit still removes the auto cell as well. The keep cell stays, even though the result is still over the limit, because the user chose to keep it.

tight = compact_notebook_context(nb, fits=lambda s: len(s) < 150)
test_eq('compact="keep"' in tight, True)
test_eq('load_everything' in tight, False)
print(tight)

title: runtime
text:
The compactor
Compactor decides when a backend’s conversation is due for compaction, and carries it out. It keeps the most recent messages as they are and replaces everything older with a summary, followed by the reorient reminder. The summary comes from a second model call, made through the summariser(prompt, sp) function you pass to compact. With strategy='surgical' it uses surgical_history instead and calls no model.
due(backend) says whether the backend has crossed its threshold. compact returns the summary, or '' when it did nothing, and note says what happened either way. on_compact, when given, is called with each new summary. If the summarizer fails or returns nothing, the conversation is left alone. When you give the summarizer’s window as summary_ctx, no request is larger than it: fold_summary splits a history too large for one request into runs that each fit (transcript_runs), summarises the first, and updates that summary with each run after it, so a history of any length compacts. A failed or empty call is retried at half and then a quarter of that size.
Compaction lives in its own class rather than in a rishi callback because it needs a second model call and then replaces the first model’s history, and a callback does not do both.


source

Compactor
def Compactor(
    reserve:NoneType=None, # None reads config.toml's `window.reserve`, else `RESERVE`, each time
    keep_recent:NoneType=None, # None reads `window.keep_recent`, else `KEEP_RECENT`
    auto:bool=True, # compact on crossing the threshold
    kernel_alive:bool=True, # what the reorientation note may promise
    on_compact:NoneType=None, # called with each new checkpoint
    strategy:str='summary', # 'summary' or deterministic 'surgical'
):
Decide when to compact, and do it.


budget(ctx) is how many tokens of recent conversation survive compaction: KEEP_RECENT (20,000), capped at half of what the window holds besides the system prompt and tools (overhead). Without the cap, a 4k model would count its whole conversation as recent, find nothing older to summarise, and report everything is recent; nothing to compact until the engine refused the turn. compact also keeps at most about half of the conversation, and the part it keeps always starts at a user message.

c = Compactor()
c.budget(200_000), c.budget(32_768), c.budget(4096)


test_eq(c.budget(4096), 2048)
test_eq(c.note, 'not compacted')
c.strategy

Compacting needs a running backend and a summarizer. testing defines doubles for both and runs a compaction end to end.

title: runtime
text:
Answers, without the thinking
Reasoning models think before they answer. Some runtimes return the thinking in a separate channel, and others leave it in the reply, wrapped in <think>...</think>. The agent’s one-shot jobs read the reply as data, such as a label, a summary or a completion to insert, so the thinking has to come off first. A classifier that returned the model’s reasoning would return no label at all.
answer_only removes the thinking from a finished reply, using urai’s split_think.


source

answer_only
def answer_only(
    text
):
A one-shot reply with the model’s thinking removed, however the runtime left it.


In the simple case the thinking is wrapped in a pair of tags:

answer_only('<think>7 times 6. Six sevens are 42.</think>\n\n42')

Some chat templates open the <think> block in the prompt itself, so the reply starts inside the thinking and only the closing tag appears. answer_only handles that too. A reply that opens a block and never closes it, because it hit the output cap, has no answer and gives ''. A reply with no tags comes back as it is.

answer_only('Six sevens are 42. They asked for only the number.\n</think>\n\n42')


test_eq(answer_only('<think>cut off at the cap and never closed'), '')
test_eq(answer_only('thinking, and then the cap hit\n'), 'thinking, and then the cap hit')
test_eq(answer_only('42'), '42')
answer_only('<think>a</think>yes')

A model whose template opens the thinking block does so at every step of a turn: after each tool call, the next reply begins inside a new thought. prefills_think tells whether a model’s template does this, by rendering a one-message prompt and looking for an unclosed <think>. For such a model RishiBackend passes the stream through a ThinkFilter, which drops text until it sees </think>, lets the rest through, and starts dropping again after each tool call. Use answer_only on a finished reply and ThinkFilter on a stream. The filter also counts the characters of thinking (thought) and of answer (answer), so the backend can report a turn that spent all its output thinking. One-shot jobs avoid the problem by asking the model not to think.


source

ThinkFilter
def ThinkFilter():
Drop a template-opened thinking block out of a raw chunk stream. A tool call re-arms it.




source

prefills_think
def prefills_think(
    chat
):
Whether this model’s chat template opens a <think> block and leaves the model to close it.


The closing tag can be split across chunks, and the filter still finds it. The answer comes through whole:

def chunks(*texts): return [{'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': t}]} for t in texts]
def texts(chunks): return ''.join(resp_text(c) for c in chunks)
f = ThinkFilter()
texts(f(chunks('Six sevens', ' are 42.\n</th', 'ink>\n\n', '42')))


test_eq(texts(ThinkFilter()(chunks('deliberating', '</think>', 'yes'))), 'yes')

tool = {'content': [{'type': 'tool_call', 'name': 'search_code', 'arguments': {}}]}
out = list(ThinkFilter()(chunks('think 1', '</think>', 'calling ') + [tool] + chunks('think 2', '</think>', 'done')))
test_eq(texts(out), 'calling done')
test_eq(out[1], tool)

f = ThinkFilter()
test_eq(texts(f(chunks('cut off at the cap'))), '')
test_eq((f.thinking, f.thought, f.answer), (True, 18, 0))

f = ThinkFilter()
test_eq(texts(f(chunks('deliberating', '</think>\n\n'))), '')
test_eq((f.thinking, f.answer), (False, 0))

title: runtime
text:
Usage
Usage holds the token counts and cost of a turn: tokens in and out, cached tokens, tokens written to the cache, reasoning tokens, the cost in dollars, and the number of turns. Two Usage values add up, so a session’s total is sum of its turns, and subtracting an earlier running total from a later one gives what was used in between. Its repr is the one-line summary shown in the terminal’s status bar.


source

Usage
def Usage(
    model:str='', input:int=0, output:int=0, total:int=0, cached:int=0, cache_write:int=0, reasoning:int=0,
    cost:float=0.0, turns:int=0
)->None:
Token counts and cost for a turn or a session; values add up.



a = Usage(model='anthropic/claude-sonnet-5', input=12_000, output=800, total=12_800, cached=9_000, cost=0.041, turns=1); a

The sum takes the model name from the right-hand value, so a session that switched models reports the model it uses now:

b = Usage(model='openai/gpt-5.6-terra', input=3_000, output=200, total=3_200, cost=0.008, turns=1)
sum([a, b], None)


test_eq((a + None).total, a.total)
test_eq(sum([a, b], None).turns, 2)
a.dict()['cached']

title: runtime
text:
Backend
Backend is the contract the agent uses to talk to a model. One backend holds one conversation. It starts the model on first use, sends a message with send or streams the reply with stream, asks one-shot questions with oneshot, counts tokens, and replaces or restores the conversation’s history. Subclasses supply the engine-specific methods whose names start with an underscore. RishiBackend, further down, is the one the agent uses.
send, stream and oneshot do not raise when the model fails. A model that cannot start, a stream that breaks and an empty reply all become text: note holds the latest status, problems keeps the last 20 problem lines, and turn_error says why the last turn failed. A caller can always show the user what the backend returned.
The examples below run the base class itself, which has no engine, to show these rules.


source

fit_content
def fit_content(
    c, room, save, how:str='', count:NoneType=None, tail:int=0
):
Message content c within room tokens: the newest pictures that fit stay and the rest are saved and named, then text past the room becomes an excerpt. The last tail characters of the last text part are always kept.




source

excerpt
def excerpt(
    text, room, save, how:str='', count:NoneType=None, tail:int=0
):
text cut to its head and its end within room tokens, the last tail characters always kept; the whole goes to save(data, suffix) and the note names the file.




source

omitted
def omitted(
    n, path, how:str=''
):
The note an excerpt carries where n characters were cut: where the whole is, and how to read it.




source

trim_hist
def trim_hist(
    hist, need, count:NoneType=None, keep:int=2, save:NoneType=None, how:str=''
):
Free about need tokens from hist in place, the oldest tool results first and then the oldest pictures; the last keep messages stay whole. With save, a trimmed result is kept in a file its note names. Returns what was freed.




source

msg_tokens
def msg_tokens(
    m, count:NoneType=None
):
One history message’s tokens: its text, its tool calls’ arguments, and IMG_TOKENS a picture.




source

img_tokens
def img_tokens():




source

margin
def margin():




source

Backend
def Backend(
    spec, sp:str='', tools:tuple=(), approve:NoneType=None, tool_max_len:NoneType=None, shared:bool=False, **kw
):
The contract a model engine meets: start, send or stream a turn, count tokens, and replace history.


The base class has no engine, so start fails. It returns None and records the NotImplementedError in note instead of raising it:

b = Backend(resolve('gemma-e4b'))
b.start(), b.note

send on a backend that could not start returns the same note, and the failure is in problems. A caller that never checks for errors still shows the user something true:

test_eq(b.send('hello'), b.note)
b.problems

pending_tokens(msg) estimates what a message will add to the conversation. Each image or audio part counts as img_tokens(), config.toml’s window.image_tokens or IMG_TOKENS (1,600), so a 120 KB image is not counted as the tokens of its bytes:

test_eq(b.pending_tokens([bytes(120_000), 'what is this?']),
        b.pending_tokens('what is this?') + IMG_TOKENS)

problem adds a line to problems. It skips a line identical to the one before it and keeps the latest 20:

for _ in range(30): b.problem('ERROR: oom')
len(b.problems), b.problems[-1]

Before the model has started there is no tokenizer, so count_tokens falls back to estimate_tokens. used_tokens is the size of the conversation so far, and pct_full is that size as a share of the window:

b.count_tokens('a prompt of some length'), b.used_tokens, round(b.pct_full, 3)

fits(msg) says whether the conversation plus msg still fits in the window, keeping back a quarter of the window for the reply, but no less than 128 and no more than 1,024 tokens. This is the fits that compact_notebook_context receives. The gemma-e4b spec used here has a 16,384-token window, and a spec with no window (ctx=0) fits anything:

big = 'x' * 200_000
b.fits('a short prompt'), b.fits(big)


test_eq(Backend(ModelSpec('unbounded', 'remote', 'v/m', ctx=0)).fits(big), True)
b.spec.ctx

fits charges the pending message margin() more than its estimate, config.toml’s window.margin or EST_MARGIN (1.15), because a count from characters runs short on code and escapes. A hosted chat’s token_count is what its last step reported, so after replace_hist or restore_hist, used_tokens gives window_tokens, an estimate of the briefing, the tool schemas and every message, until the chat reports again. Without that, a compaction left the old count in place, fits still failed, and each retry compacted again. A hosted chat that has not reported a step yet counts window_tokens too, and one not started yet counts the conversation it will restore, so the first turn after a resume is measured before it goes out.
trim(need) frees tokens from the oldest tool results first, then the oldest pictures, and leaves the newest two messages whole. With spill set, a trimmed result is written whole to a file first, and its note names the file and says how to read it (how). shrink_recent(need) cuts the newest two messages a person or a tool wrote, largest first, which trim never touches. fit_content(content, room, save) does the cutting: pictures past what fits are saved and named, the newest kept, and text past the room becomes excerpt, its head and its end around a note such as …[52,000 characters omitted; full text at <path>; read it in pieces with view_file(path, start=N)]. Nothing is lost: the whole is in the file:

from urai import mk_msgs
t = trim_hist(h := mk_msgs(['look at this', 'done']) + [{'role': 'tool', 'tool_call_id': 'c', 'content': 'r' * 9000}] + mk_msgs(['and now', 'ok']), 100)
test_eq(h[2]['content'], TRIMMED)
assert t > 100 and h[-1]['content'] == 'ok'


saved = []
def save(data, suffix): saved.append(data); return Path(f'/tmp/full{len(saved)}{suffix}')
cut = fit_content('head ' + 'x' * 20_000 + ' end', 200, save, 'read it in pieces with view_file(path, start=N)')
assert cut.startswith('head') and cut.endswith(' end') and 'full text at /tmp/full1.txt' in cut and saved[0].endswith(b' end')
pics = fit_content([b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n1', b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n2', b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n3', 'which?'], 2 * IMG_TOKENS, save)
test_eq(pics[0], b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n3')   # the newest picture stays
assert 'which?' in pics and '2 of the 3 pictures' in pics[-1]
print(cut[:60] + ' ... ' + cut[-160:])

oneshot(prompt) asks one question in a throwaway conversation and returns the answer with any thinking removed. It cuts the prompt to fit the window, keeping its end, and returns if_busy (by default '') while another call is using the backend. This subclass stands in for a model that leaves its thinking in the reply:

class Thinker(Backend):
    def _start(self): return self
    def _oneshot(self, prompt, sp, max_tokens): return 'They want one label.\n</think>\n\nsuccess'

test_eq(Thinker(resolve('gemma-e4b')).oneshot('the tests pass'), 'success')
Thinker(resolve('gemma-e4b')).oneshot('the tests pass')

The history methods behave differently: replace_hist, restore_hist and revise_last_assistant raise when no model is running, because there is no conversation to change. replace_hist(summary, keep) is what Compactor calls. snapshot_hist and restore_hist save and restore a conversation, for branching. resume_hist hands a saved conversation to a backend that has not started yet, and applies it when the model starts.

test_fail(lambda: b.replace_hist('summary'), contains='not running')
test_fail(lambda: b.restore_hist([]), contains='not running')
test_fail(lambda: b.revise_last_assistant('...'), contains='not running')

title: runtime
text:
RishiBackend
RishiBackend is the only implementation of Backend, because rishi runs every model, local or hosted. It turns a ModelSpec (a model’s name, runtime, id and window, from core) into a rishi Chat, converts rishi’s usage into Usage, and handles what differs between runtimes:

A LiteRT model gets its window as the engine’s token ceiling, max_num_tokens, and a llama.cpp or ollama model gets it as n_ctx.
A Claude model is asked for high reasoning effort (CLAUDE_EFFORT) unless RAMABANA_EFFORT names another level.
On MLX, one-shot questions run in a separate conversation on the same engine, so a completion never sees earlier completions.
A local model’s window is set from the window it was trained for, capped by Ramabana’s limit for that model, and narrowed again if the engine reports a smaller one.
When a hosted service refuses the tool schemas, the backend moves that model to the tags channel, where the schemas travel in the system prompt and calls come back as <tool_call> blocks in the text, and retries once.
When a reply on the tags channel describes a tool call instead of making one, the backend sends one reminder (TAG_REMINDER) asking the model to make the call.

rishi adds two callbacks to a chat by default: a reminder on every message, and a sliding window that forgets old messages without summarising them. RishiBackend removes both (ROUTINE_CBS), because Compactor does that job. LiteRT runs the tool loop inside the engine, so the text a model writes before a tool call never reaches Ramabana. QUIET_RUNTIMES lists such runtimes, and narrates is False for them.
LiteRT models run on the GPU by default. rishi asks for the GPU, and falls back to the CPU with a warning when the build has no GPU support. RAMABANA_LITERT_BACKEND=cpu pins a model to the CPU, and gpu asks for the GPU explicitly. A backend= argument, or eng_kw={'backend': ...}, takes precedence over the variable. RISHI_LITERT_GPU=0 stops rishi asking for the GPU at all.


source

make_backend
def make_backend(
    spec, **kw
):




source

getattr
def __getattr__(
    name
):




source

RishiBackend
def RishiBackend(
    *a, max_steps:int=40, **kw
):
The Backend that runs every model, local or hosted, through rishi’s Chat.




source

use_chat
def use_chat(
    f
):
Build model conversations with f for the duration, instead of rishi’s Chat.


use_chat(f) makes backends build their conversations with f instead of rishi’s Chat, for the duration of a with block. testing uses it to put in urai’s CachedChat, which replays a real model’s recorded answers with no weights and no network. Here f is a stub chat that answers from a script, so nothing is downloaded:

from ramabana.core import ModelSpec

built = []
class StubChat:
    def __init__(self, model, **kw): built.append((model, kw)); self.hist = []
    def oneshot(self, prompt, sp='', think=None, max_tokens=None): return 'replayed'
    def close(self): pass

with use_chat(StubChat):
    be = make_backend(ModelSpec('stub', 'remote', 'openai/gpt-x', 8000))
    assert be.start() is not None
    test_eq(built[0][0], 'openai/gpt-x')
    test_eq(be.oneshot('a cheap job'), 'replayed')
    test_eq(be._usage().total, 0)
test_eq(_MK_CHAT, None)

Ramabana does not set LiteRT’s constrained decoding, since rishi turns it on itself when there are tools. A conv_kw you pass goes through unchanged:

def _a_tool(query: str) -> str:
    "A tool."
    return ''
kw = make_backend(resolve('gemma-e4b'), tools=[_a_tool])._runtime_kw()
assert 'enable_constrained_decoding' not in kw.get('conv_kw', {})

title: runtime
text:
Runs
A run is one piece of model work that can be cancelled: the turn the user started (kind='root'), or a sub-agent that the turn delegated to (kind='child', made with child). Runs form a tree. Cancelling a run cancels everything under it, and the tool calls of the whole tree count against one budget, through draw.
A run starts pending, becomes running with start, and ends completed, failed, cancelled, detached or terminated. cancel asks the backend to stop and waits up to grace seconds. A run whose backend does not stop in time is detached: the caller treats it as over and ignores anything the model sends later. terminate closes the backend outright.
A run also keeps what the user should see while it works. status is the last line the model wrote before its latest tool call. notes keeps up to 100 such messages for the now pane, the live view beside the terminal (pane), and write appends a line to the run’s transcript file when it has one. tell queues a message from the user for a running sub-agent, and drain_inbox hands the queued messages over. air returns a reminder to tell the user where the work stands once 8 tool calls in a row have gone by with less than 100 characters said before them. repeated counts identical calls with identical results in a row, so the agent can tell a model that it is looping.

A run whose backend stops when asked ends cancelled. A run whose backend cannot stop ends detached once its grace period runs out:

import threading, time

class _Blocking:
    def __init__(self, stoppable=True): self.stoppable, self.released = stoppable, threading.Event()
    def cancel(self):
        if self.stoppable: self.released.set()

r = Run('run_cancelled', grace=.05)
r.start(_Blocking())
threading.Thread(target=lambda: (r.backend.released.wait(), r.finish()), daemon=True).start()
test_eq(r.cancel().state, 'cancelled')

r = Run('run_detached', grace=.01)
r.start(_Blocking(False))
test_eq(r.cancel().state, 'detached')

Once its run is cancelled, a backend’s stream stops yielding, drops what the model sends later, and does not retry:

class _CancelStream(Backend):
    def __init__(self):
        from ramabana.core import ModelSpec
        super().__init__(ModelSpec('cancel-test', 'fake', 'fake/cancel', ctx=1000))
        self.first, self.release, self.calls, self.recoveries = threading.Event(), threading.Event(), 0, 0
    def _start(self): return self
    def _stream(self, msg, **kw):
        self.calls += 1
        yield 'first'
        self.first.set(); self.release.wait()
        yield 'late'
    def cancel(self): self.release.set(); return True
    def _usage(self): return Usage()
    def _recover(self, e): self.recoveries += 1; return True

be, run, chunks = _CancelStream(), Run('run_late', grace=.05), []
run.start(be)
t = threading.Thread(target=lambda: chunks.extend(be.stream('x', run=run)), daemon=True)
t.start(); assert be.first.wait(.2)
run.cancel(); t.join(.2)
test_eq(chunks, ['first'])
test_eq((be.calls, be.recoveries), (1, 0))

test_eq(r.state, 'terminated')

title: setup
text: This module holds what has to happen before a session starts. The terminal session runs best inside tmux, a terminal multiplexer that divides one window into panes. tmux gives Ramabana a split for the now pane, the live view of the turn described in pane, and with its extended keys setting on it delivers shift+enter to the program as a key of its own, which the session uses to queue a message for the next turn. So the first run starts Ramabana inside a tmux server of its own, offers to install tmux when it is missing, and ramabana --doctor reports what it found. The module also decides whether the code index needs rebuilding.

Extras and scripts
Every console script that the package installs starts in this module, so it imports only fastcore and the standard library, and never ramabana.core. That keeps a script quick to start and lets it check for its dependencies before it imports them.
installed(mod) says whether a module would import, without importing it. need(extra) checks the modules an extra provides, as listed in EXTRAS, and returns the install command for the ones missing, or '' when all are there. Looking up one of those names on this module returns that main, or, when its extra is missing, a stand-in that prints the install command and exits with status 2. ramabana.core re-exports installed, need, EXTRAS and SCRIPTS.

title: setup
text:
The config
Each session gets a tmux server of its own, started as tmux -L ramabana-<id> with the config file <cfg>/tmux.conf. A new server reads the current config and inherits the current environment, so a second session never picks up the first one’s API keys or virtual environment. That server never reads ~/.tmux.conf, and your own tmux setup is left as it was.
Extended keys are a tmux setting that passes key combinations such as shift+enter through to the program in the pane, instead of folding them into plain enter. tmux_conf(version) returns the config for a given tmux version, adding only the lines that version understands: extended-keys arrived in tmux 3.2 and extended-keys-format csi-u in 3.5, and an older tmux prints an error for each line it does not know. tmux_version reads the version from the output of tmux -V. The config claims true colour (RGB) only when $COLORTERM says the terminal draws it. The cell below prints the config for tmux 3.5.

def tmux_conf(
    version
):
TMUX_CONF with the lines tmux version understands.

    s

The (major, minor) in tmux -V output such as tmux 3.5a, or None.

title: setup
text:
The relaunch
Setup collects everything about the tmux that Ramabana runs in: the config, the relaunch into it, the install offer and --doctor.
Setup.launch runs before an interactive session starts. Outside tmux it replaces the current process with tmux new-session on a new server, running the same command line in the same folder. Quitting Ramabana then ends that tmux session and returns you to your shell. launch does nothing for a one-shot prompt, for --json, when stdin or stdout is not a terminal, and when --tmux off or $RAMABANA_TMUX=off says to stay out of tmux. It also needs tmux 3.0 or later. The relaunched process has $RAMABANA_WRAPPED set, so it never relaunches a second time. Inside tmux, --pane auto then opens the now pane.
The server is set to destroy-unattached, which ends the session when you detach or close the window, so Ramabana never keeps running where nobody can see it. The history is saved, and --resume latest reopens it. The command runs under sh with a short wrapper, HOLD, that waits for enter after a non-zero exit, so an error stays on screen instead of vanishing with the tmux session.
Inside a tmux server of your own, launch turns extended-keys on for that server when it is off. The change lasts until the server exits, and only programs that ask for extended keys receive them.
Every effect on the outside world goes through an argument of Setup: which, system, run, execvpe, ask and isatty, plus environ, argv and cwd. The examples pass fakes for all of them, so they run without tmux and change nothing.


source

Setup
def Setup(
    cfg:str='~/.config/ramabana', # holds `tmux.conf` and `setup.json`
    environ:NoneType=None, # default `os.environ`
    argv:NoneType=None, # the command line to rerun; default `sys.argv`
    cwd:NoneType=None, # where the session starts; default the current folder
    which:function=which, system:function=system, run:function=run, execvpe:function=execvpe, ask:function=_no_stdin,
    isatty:NoneType=None, # whether stdin and stdout are terminals
):
The tmux ramabana runs in: its config, the relaunch into it, the install offer, and --doctor.


The example builds a fake machine, Box, that has tmux 3.5 on PATH and records each command run, each question asked and the execvpe it would make. launch reruns the command line on a new tmux server, starting in /work, with $RAMABANA_WRAPPED set and the original options at the end:

from types import SimpleNamespace
import tempfile

class Box:
    "Programs on PATH, the commands run, the prompts shown and the exec made."
    def __init__(self, have=('tmux',), version='tmux 3.5a', system='Darwin', answer='', ext='on'):
        self.have, self.version, self.system, self.answer, self.ext = set(have), version, system, answer, ext
        self.calls, self.asked, self.execd = [], [], None
    def which(self, name): return f'/bin/{name}' if name in self.have else None
    def run(self, cmd, **kw):
        self.calls.append(list(cmd))
        if 'install' in cmd: self.have.add('tmux')
        return SimpleNamespace(returncode=0, stdout={'-V': self.version, 'show': self.ext}.get(cmd[1], ''))
    def ask(self, q): return self.asked.append(q) or self.answer
    def execvpe(self, *a): self.execd = a

def mk(box, **kw):
    return Setup(tempfile.mkdtemp(), environ=kw.pop('environ', {'PATH': '/bin'}), argv=['-c', '--pane', 'on'], cwd='/work',
                 which=box.which, system=lambda: box.system, run=box.run, execvpe=box.execvpe, ask=box.ask, isatty=lambda: True)

box = Box()
mk(box).launch()
exe, argv, env = box.execd
test_eq((exe, env['RAMABANA_WRAPPED'], argv[argv.index('-c'):][:2], argv[-2:]), ('/bin/tmux', '1', ['-c', '/work'], ['--pane', 'on']))

The ramabana script, run_cli, makes the tmux decision before it imports the CLI. Importing the CLI takes about 0.4 seconds, so deciding first means the process outside tmux hands over to tmux quickly. launch_args(argv) reads just enough of the command line to know the session is interactive, without the full option parser, and returns the cfg and tmux values launch needs, or None to leave the decision to the CLI’s main. A prompt, --json, --doctor, an option refusal rejects, or any option it is unsure of returns None.
refusal holds the checks main makes before it starts anything, such as --pii without --vault, and returns the reason or ''. Running it here means a bad option is refused in your terminal, not on tmux’s hold screen. bare_resume gives a bare --resume the value PICK_SESSION, which lists this folder’s sessions to choose from. When run_cli has already called launch, it sets LAUNCHED so that main does not call it again.

title: setup
text:
config.toml
~/.config/ramabana/config.toml holds this machine’s settings: one file, edited by hand, that every Ramabana on the machine reads. A session started with another --cfg, and an app that embeds Ramabana with a config folder of its own, read the same file and never write into their own folder for it. $RAMABANA_CONFIG names another file; the tests use it.
A value can come from four places, and the first that has one wins:



Source
Example




a command-line flag
--model gpt-5.4


an env var
$RAMABANA_MODEL, or $LEELA_MODEL inside Leela


config.toml
[jobs] turn = "gpt-5.4"


the built-in default
claude-opus-5-5



KEYS lists every key: its type, the env var and the flag that beat it, what it sets, and the values it may take. The tables are [jobs], the model each job runs on; [window], the numbers the window guard works with; [compaction]; [runtime], what a model is started with; and [cli], the defaults of the terminal session’s flags that take a value. [jobs] image is the OpenAI-compatible model generate_image draws with. [azure] holds Azure OpenAI’s endpoint, which $AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT beats, read as named with no prefix (Key.plain), and the api_key_env that names the env var holding its key. A key an earlier release read, such as azure.deployments, is reported with what to do instead (RETIRED_KEYS). A [model."NAME"] table corrects the numbers fastllm’s table gives one model: max_input_tokens, max_output_tokens and supports_images. Given model_id, the same table defines a model of that name, with runtime, base_url, api_key_env, api_name, vendor_name and ctx; core registers it.
load_config reads the file again only when it changes. An entry it cannot use takes its default and gives one warning, which Agent.problems and ramabana config show repeat: a key nobody knows, with the nearest one it might mean; a value of the wrong type or outside its choices; a file that is not TOML. Nothing raises.

title: setup
text:
Installing tmux
When tmux is missing, offer_install asks once whether to run the command that installs it, and shows the command: brew install tmux on macOS, sudo apt-get install -y tmux or sudo dnf install -y tmux on Linux. installer picks the command from what is on PATH. The command runs attached to the terminal, so sudo can ask for a password.
The answer is stored in <cfg>/setup.json. A no is never asked again, and neither is a yes whose install worked. Ctrl+c at the prompt, or an install that failed or was interrupted, stores nothing, so the next run asks again. ramabana --doctor asks even after an earlier no. Without tmux, the session starts in the current terminal and prints one line on how to get the now pane.
The first example says yes on a Mac with Homebrew, and the session relaunches in the tmux it installed. The second says no on Linux, and a second launch does not ask again:

title: setup
section: Whether the code index needs to run
text:
Whether the code index needs to run
The search_code tool searches a code index that kosha builds over the installed packages and the open folders. Rebuilding it, called a sync, takes time, so the session skips it when nothing it reads has changed.
index_gate(cfg, roots) decides this without importing kosha. It takes a fingerprint, index_state, of what a sync would read: the installed distributions that importlib.metadata finds, with their modification times (pkg_state), and for each folder its git HEAD and a digest of git status with the modification times of the paths it names (root_state). Outside git, a folder’s fingerprint is the newest modification time among its entries. It returns the fingerprint and a reason to run kosha, or '' to skip it. The reason is '' when the fingerprint matches the one the last good sync saved in <cfg>/kosha-state.json and each folder’s .kosha/code.db and kosha’s package database, kosha_env_db(), exist. Otherwise index_changes says what changed, such as packages changed: +foo 1.2.
After a good sync the session calls save_index to store the new fingerprint. Either way log_index appends one line to <cfg>/kosha.log, and --doctor shows the last line through last_index. The example walks a fresh folder through a first sync, a missing index, an unchanged state and a new package:

title: monitor
text: This module covers two kinds of work that happen outside the turn you are typing in. A folder review reads the changes someone else made to a watched folder and reports on them at the start of your next turn. The beat, at the end of the page, runs scheduled work on a timer even when no session is open.

title: monitor
text:
Folder reviews
Say a colleague, a script or another agent is editing files in a folder you care about, and you want the agent to look over each change. You ask it to watch the folder with instructions such as “check each change for correctness”. From then on, whenever files under that folder change, a reviewer reads the diff, follows the instructions, and its report is waiting for you in the next turn.
A watch is that standing request. The model opens one with shalya’s watch tool, as watch(target, kind='folder', instructions=..., pattern=...), where pattern is a list of globs that limits which files count. The tool stores the watch as a row in the vault, beside the page, search and reminder watches, so list_watches and cancel_watch see it too. Monitors is the side that does the reviewing. Monitors.sync copies the vault’s folder rows into this session, and Monitors.check calls it first, so a watch the model opens is picked up on the next check. A host without a vault offers the model no way to open a folder watch, but code can still open one with Monitors.add.
A new watch records the folder as it stands as its baseline, and only changes after that are reviewed. The reviewer gets the watch’s instructions and the changes, and nothing from the conversation that created the watch, so the instructions have to say everything. add refuses a watch without them.
Each completed review goes into a queue, and the agent adds the queued reviews to the next prompt it sends, through review_notice. The review is also noted to the user and filed in memory under one key per watch, so a newer review of the same folder replaces the older one. The agent runs Monitors.check in a background thread between turns.

title: monitor
text:
Change detection
snapshot records the text of every readable file under the watched folder that matches the pattern, and changed compares two snapshots and returns the files added, edited or removed. A file larger than SNAP_MAX_BYTES is recorded by its size alone, so a change to it shows as a changed size with no diff. report turns the changes into a short list of files with their added and removed line counts, followed by the unified diffs, clipped to REVIEW_MAX_CHARS, and summarise gives the one-line count such as 1 added, 1 edited.
A watch’s settle window, 20 seconds by default, is the least time between two reviews of one folder. Changes that arrive inside the window wait and go into the next review together, which keeps a burst of saves from producing a burst of reviews. check(force=True) looks anyway.

title: monitor
text:
Reviewer
The reviewer is a read-only sub-agent: a second agent with the session’s read tools and none that write, briefed with REVIEW_SP, and limited to REVIEW_MAX_STEPS steps. It cannot edit the watched folder, so it describes any fix instead of making it. Without a model to run it on, the change is recorded with status unreviewed. The baseline moves forward after every attempt, including a failed one, so a change is never reviewed twice.

Monitors.sync
def sync():
Mirror the host’s folder watches: add new vault rows, drop removed ones.



from ramabana.testing import FakeBackend, MemHost, SPEC

The example watches a two-file project held in memory by MemHost, with FakeBackend standing in for the reviewer’s model; it answers every question with sub answer. Nothing has changed right after add, so the first check returns nothing. After one file is edited, the check returns one record holding the summary, the review and the diff.

h = MemHost({'/proj/a.py': 'def a(): return 1\n', '/proj/notes.md': 'hello\n'})
m = Monitors(h, get_backend=lambda: FakeBackend(SPEC))
w = m.add('/proj', 'Review each change for correctness.')
test_eq(len(w.snap), 2)
test_eq(m.check(), [])

h.write('/proj/a.py', 'def a(): return 2\n')
rec, = m.check()
test_eq((rec['status'], rec['files'], rec['summary']), ('ok', 1, '1 edited'))
test_eq(rec['review'], 'sub answer')
assert '-def a(): return 1' in rec['changes'] and '+def a(): return 2' in rec['changes']

A file added inside the settle window waits, so the plain check returns nothing and force=True reviews it. A removed file shows as removed. Each check also queued its record, and drain hands them all over once, which is what the agent does before its next turn.

h.write('/proj/b.py', 'def b(): pass\n')
test_eq(m.check(), [])
rec, = m.check(force=True)
test_eq((rec['summary'], rec['status']), ('1 added', 'ok'))

del h.files['/proj/notes.md']
test_eq(m.check(force=True)[0]['summary'], '1 removed')


test_eq(len(m.drain()), 3)
test_eq(m.drain(), [])
test_eq(review_notice([]), '')

test_eq(_globs('*.py, *.ipynb'), ['*.py', '*.ipynb'])
test_eq(summarise({'a': ('', 'x'), 'b': ('x', 'y')}), '1 added, 1 edited')
test_fail(lambda: m.add('/proj', '  '), contains='needs instructions')

check(block=False) returns None at once when another check is already running, instead of waiting for it. The agent’s background thread uses the blocking form.

h.write('/proj/a.py', 'def a(): return 3\n')
m.checking.acquire()
try: test_eq(m.check(block=False), None)
finally: m.checking.release()
test_eq(m.check(force=True)[0]['summary'], '1 edited')

The same flow through the model’s tools. VaultLike is a stand-in for a vault host, which stores watches as rows and keeps notes in memory. The watch tool opens a folder watch, the next check picks it up through sync and takes its baseline, an edit produces a review filed under the key folder-review:w1, and cancel_watch makes the watch disappear from Monitors on the next check.

from ramabana.tools import MemoryHost, WatchHost, watch_tools

class VaultLike(MemHost, MemoryHost, WatchHost):
    "A host whose watches table is a list and whose memory is the notes it was handed."
    def __init__(self, files): super().__init__(files); self.rows, self.notes = [], []
    def watch(self, target, action='remind', every='1d', note=None, **params):
        w = dict(id=f'w{len(self.rows)+1}', kind=action, target=target, every=86400, note=note, runs=0, last_status='', **params)
        self.rows.append(w); return w
    def watches(self, due_only=False): return list(self.rows)
    def unwatch(self, wid): self.rows = [r for r in self.rows if r['id'] != wid]; return True
    def poll(self): return {'checked': 0, 'ran': 0, 'results': []}
    def remember(self, text, title=None, tags=(), key=''): self.notes.append((title, key, text)); return dict(doc_id='d1', title=title)
    def memory_search(self, query, limit=8): return []
    def memory_tree(self, document=''): return []
    def memory_read(self, node_id): return {}
    def memory_forget(self, doc_id): return False
    watch_actions = ('url', 'remind', 'web', 'folder')

vh = VaultLike({'/proj/a.py': 'one\n'})
vm = Monitors(vh, get_backend=lambda: FakeBackend(SPEC))
wt = {t.__name__: t for t in watch_tools(vh)}
print(wt['watch']('/proj', kind='folder', instructions='Review each change.'))
test_eq(vm.check(force=True), [])
test_eq([w.id for w in vm.all()], ['w1'])
vh.write('/proj/a.py', 'two\n')
rec, = vm.check(force=True)
test_eq((rec['watch_id'], rec['review']), ('w1', 'sub answer'))
test_eq(vh.notes[-1][:2], ('folder review: proj: 1 edited', 'folder-review:w1'))
test_eq(wt['cancel_watch']('w1'), 'cancelled w1')
test_eq(vm.check(), [])
test_eq(vm.all(), [])

watching folder /proj as w1, every 1d

title: monitor
text:
The beat
Some work should run on a timer whether or not anyone has a session open: a nightly job that learns from the day’s sessions, say. Ramabana hands the timing to pobblebonk, a small scheduler that installs one job with the operating system’s own scheduler (cron, launchd or the Windows task scheduler) and keeps its schedules, the work they fired, and the notes that work left in a SQLite database.
A schedule is a name, an interval, and a callback that runs when the schedule fires. A beat is one pass over the schedules that runs every one that has come due. A note is a short title and body that a callback leaves for whoever reads next. Several readers can share one database, and each reader sees each note once.
This module holds Ramabana’s end of that arrangement. on_tick(name) registers the callback for a schedule from Python. pob opens the shared database, or returns None when pobblebonk is not installed. beat_notes takes the notes a reader has not seen yet, and beat_notice wraps them in a <beat> block, which the agent adds to its next prompt. Each session reads under its own reader name, so every open session sees every note. The packages that define recurring work own their schedules. Ramabana only runs them.

):

Register the callback a fire of schedule name runs.


tick is the ramabana-tick command. Run plainly, it registers the callbacks, runs one beat, prints how many schedules ran of those that fired, and exits. With no schedules registered it does nothing and still exits successfully. --install hands ramabana-tick --quiet to pobblebonk to run every --every seconds, and --uninstall removes it. beat_command builds that command line, quoting the path for the platform’s shell, and heartbeat returns pobblebonk’s scheduler module or None.
launchd and cron start a job on /usr/bin:/bin, which holds neither claude in ~/.local/bin nor Homebrew’s git-lfs. Off Windows, beat_command therefore runs the beat through /usr/bin/env with the PATH of the shell that installed it, and --install prints that PATH. Only PATH is carried: a key exported in a shell profile does not reach the beat. A tool installed in a new folder after --install is found once ramabana-tick --install runs again. Task Scheduler on Windows gives a job the user’s environment, so the Windows command is unchanged.
An installed package registers a callback through a ramabana.ticks entry point (TICK_GROUP). The entry point’s name is the schedule’s name and its value is the callback. The beat imports the package only when that schedule fires, so a slow or broken package costs nothing until then. A package that fails to import fails that one fire, and pobblebonk retries it or leaves a note. An on_tick callback with the same name replaces the entry point’s. Dhrona registers its nightly job this way:
[project.entry-points."ramabana.ticks"]
dhrona = "dhrona.improve:nightly"

beat_notes(beat)

['watches: 2 of 5 fired', 'nightly']


Once a reader has drained the notes, it gets nothing more, while another reader still sees all of them. beat_notes returns an empty list when there is no database, or when reading it fails, so a locked database never stops a turn.

test_eq(beat_notes(beat), [])
test_eq(beat_notes(beat, reader='another'), ['watches: 2 of 5 fired', 'nightly'])
test_eq(beat_notes(None), [])

class _Broken:
    def drain(self, reader, limit=20): raise RuntimeError('the database is locked')
test_eq(beat_notes(_Broken()), [])
