text:
This page is one of the five skills that ship with Ramabana. A skill is a piece of markdown that the agent reads when a task calls for it, so that the guidance costs nothing in turns that do not need it. The system prompt lists every skill the session found with a one-line description, the read_skill tool returns one in full, and /skill theory prints it in a terminal session.
The skill’s text is this module’s docstring. nbdev builds it from the description line above and the exported markdown cell below, and pyproject.toml registers the module under the pyskills entry point as theory, so any agent built on shalya can find it once Ramabana is installed. To change what the agent reads, edit the exported cell.
The agent reads this skill when the user asks about the Theory of a piece of software, in Peter Naur’s sense of the word.
Read this when the user says the Theory of something, or asks to discuss, find, or capture a Theory. “Theory” is Peter Naur’s programming-as-theory-building, in the sense this team uses the word.

title: Theory
text:
The Theory
The sense is Naur’s, from his 1985 paper Programming as Theory Building. A program is not its source code and not its documentation. It is the theory held in its builders’ minds. They understand how the code maps onto the world, why it took the shape it did, and how to extend it sensibly.
Consequences Naur draws:

A developer has to hold the Theory in mind, which means expressing it in its most minimal form. There is always time for details later. When discussing the Theory, conciseness is king. That does not mean excluding important details, and it does not mean giving the developer the illusion of control. It means iterating until the core that is true is found, and anchoring into that.
The Theory cannot be fully written down. Documentation captures artifacts of the Theory, not the Theory itself, which is why “just read the docs” never fully onboards anyone.
A program whose theory-holders have all left is dead, even if it still runs. Reviving it is closer to rebuilding than to reading.
Modification quality depends on the Theory, not the code. Someone holding the Theory makes changes that fit the program’s nature. Someone without it makes patches that gradually corrode the design.

title: Theory
text:
Using it
Working in an unfamiliar codebase, find the Theory first and read the code through it. Ask what facts or constraints drove it, how the design follows from them, and which alternatives the builders rejected and why. search_code finds the pattern. The Theory says why it is the pattern.
Reviewing a change, ask what Theory the change assumes and whether that matches the Theory of the codebase. A patch can be locally correct and still violate the Theory. Line-by-line review never sees that.
When the user says “the Theory of X”, they assume this vocabulary. Do not re-explain Naur. Discussing a Theory means talking it through in conversation. Do not turn it into a process, a checklist, or markdown files unless the user asks for a written artifact.
Stating or discussing a Theory, follow the write_prose skill closely. A Theory lives in minds, and its statement has to be plain enough to hold there.

title: Write prose
text:
This page is one of the five skills that ship with Ramabana. A skill is a piece of markdown that the agent reads when a task calls for it, so that the guidance costs nothing in turns that do not need it. The system prompt lists every skill the session found with a one-line description, the read_skill tool returns one in full, and /skill write_prose prints it in a terminal session.
The skill’s text is this module’s docstring. nbdev builds it from the description line above and the exported markdown cell below, and pyproject.toml registers the module under the pyskills entry point as write_prose, so any agent built on shalya can find it once Ramabana is installed. To change what the agent reads, edit the exported cell.
The agent reads this skill before it writes prose with an author’s voice, such as a blog post or release notes. Its companion write_docs covers reference prose.
Read this before writing narrative prose: blog posts, essays, announcements, talks, release notes with a voice, and anything else where the author is present on the page. For reference prose – docstrings, comments, READMEs, API docs, changelogs, PR descriptions, commit messages, messages to a colleague – read write_docs instead. The same slop is banned there; the register is voiceless. The standard here is The Economist’s.
Here is a passage from The Economist:
Each sentence sets out to say one thing, says it, and stops. It is plain English. It carries no byline and needs none. Plainness does the work. It is not selling anything. It lets the reader work out the takeaways.
Write like that.
Here is a horrendous rewrite, as sloppy as possible:
Do NOT write like that.
The numbers below refer to the [bracketed] markers in both passages. Where a number appears in each, the pair is the sloppy and the plain version of the same thing. Entries 17, 18, 25 and 26 are tells at scales the one-paragraph sample cannot show.
Tells 9 and 19 are two faces of one device linguists call agent defocusing: grammar that pushes the true actor out of the subject seat. The passive is the third face. The positive rule is Williams’s characters-and-actions principle: make the doer the subject and the deed the verb. A tool subject with a mechanical verb (“the parser rejects malformed input”) is not defocusing. The tool really is that event’s actor, though its verb still has to pass tell 21. The tell fires when a person’s deed is narrated with the person missing. Tell 21 is the neighbour rather than another face. There, no person exists, and the verb rather than the subject seat is what goes wrong.
Tells 1, 2, 11, 13 and 24, along with tell 5’s noting fillers, are all metadiscourse: text about the text rather than about the subject. Openers advertise the piece, labels advertise the fact, pivots advertise excitement, closers advertise closure, preambles advertise importance. Signposting earns its place at document scale, in a table of contents or an abstract, the same boundary tell 14 draws for summaries.

title: Write prose
text:
Banned words
Statistically overrepresented in LLM output. Replace or delete on sight.

Kill on sight: delve, utilize, leverage (verb), facilitate, elucidate, embark, endeavor, encompass, multifaceted, tapestry, “a testament to”, paradigm, synergy, holistic, catalyze, juxtapose, nuanced (as filler), realm, landscape (metaphorical), myriad, plethora, minted (metaphorical), and -bearing compounds such as load-bearing and text-bearing. Also shape/shaped as loose jargon for structure or influence (“same shape”, “the shape of the API”, “your tests shaped ours”); it is fine as a geometric term or for array dimensions, and for influence say what actually happened: adapted, copied, informed. Also land/landed/lands as metaphor (“the fix landed”, “a note lands in the output”); things do not land, so say merged, committed, pushed, released, appears.
Suspicious in clusters, so remove most of them: robust, comprehensive, seamless, cutting-edge, innovative, streamline, empower, foster, enhance, elevate, optimize, pivotal, intricate, profound, resonate, underscore, harness, navigate (metaphorical), cultivate, bolster, cornerstone, game-changer, invariant (usually “rule” or “guarantee”; keep it only where nothing plainer is accurate).
Replacements are almost always simpler words: utilize -> use, leverage -> use, facilitate -> help, robust -> strong, comprehensive -> complete, seamless -> smooth, empower -> let, foster -> encourage, enhance -> improve, optimize -> improve.

The lists are examples of one rule: always reach for the simplest, most normal, least jargony word that is still correct.
Much of the clarity core above is codified in ASD-STE100: one idea per sentence, active voice with the doer as subject, one meaning per term, and plain words over inflated ones. Borrow the discipline, not the sound. STE is voiceless and choppy by design, built for non-native mechanics under time pressure, and it would fail the standard the Economist passage sets. That sound is correct in reference prose, which write_docs covers.
Never hard-wrap prose. Write each paragraph as one continuous line and let the display soft-wrap it. Manual line breaks mid-paragraph make text painful to reflow, edit and copy.
In technical prose, put code symbols in backticks: function names, parameters, file paths, module and package names, and literal syntax.

title: Write prose
text:
What good prose sounds like
Good writing has a voice. You read it and someone is there. They have opinions. They are occasionally wrong. They will make a joke in the middle of a technical explanation and it works.
The sentences are not all the same length. Most are short. An occasional longer one earns its length by carrying a single connected thought too big to split. That variation is what keeps a reader moving. LLMs cannot do it unprompted: every sentence comes out the same mid-length, the same mid-energy.
Say what you mean. “This is broken”, not “there may be some areas for potential improvement”. Say “use”, not “utilize”. If a different topic could be swapped in and the paragraph still read fine, nothing has been said yet. Get specific. Not “improves developer productivity” but “saves me twenty minutes every deploy”.
To have a draft checked, send these rules and the draft to a subagent with delegate_search. Name the audience, so tells 20 and 23 can be judged. Ask for flagged spans rather than a rewrite. Only do this when the user asks for a prose check.

The agent reads this skill before it writes, reviews or refactors code. When the skill is present, the system prompt tells it to.
Read this before writing, reviewing, refactoring, or assessing code. These are Answer.AI’s coding standards adapted to Ramabana’s tools and nbdev workflow.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Improve shared tooling
A finished task helps once. A better tool helps every later task, every later session and every agent, and ergonomics count as much as capability. Most code you have read was written by people who put up with tool friction rather than fix it. The workaround is your default. Here the tools are ours and one edit away. When repository-owned tooling grates, fix it or say so. Never quietly work around it, and do not expand the current task without the user’s agreement.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Read before writing
Use search_code before writing non-trivial code: the answer or the established pattern is usually already in the repository or an installed package. Read the exact source before editing it. Use grep for exhaustive literal audits such as call sites and renames. Match the surrounding design unless the request is specifically to change it.

title: Coding patterns
section: Every construct must earn its place
text:
Every construct must earn its place
Readers assume everything present is necessary. Seeing str(x) on something already a str, they stop and wonder what it guards against. When the answer is nothing, they paid for a mystery with no payoff. The same goes for defensive copies, speculative exception handling, redundant coercions, unused parameters, abstractions and compatibility branches. Know why a construct is needed before adding it, and leave it out when you cannot say. The cost doubles in nbdev projects, where the examples are the documentation.
Knowing why you need a construct does not mean waiting for someone to ask for it. A user who finds a gap concludes the library cannot do it and moves on. Judge a library feature by whether the design calls for it and users would expect it.
Comments state constraints the code cannot express. Never write one to say where a change came from, what the next line does, or why the change is correct. That comment addresses the reviewer, not the next reader. It becomes noise the moment the change is merged. Add type hints, docstrings and abstractions only where they improve the public contract or the surrounding code consistently uses them. Prefer concise readable code over verbose enterprise boilerplate.
Make the requested change and no unrelated cleanup. Never discard edits already in the working tree.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Prefer the fastcore ecosystem
When choosing dependencies, first check whether fastcore or another existing project dependency already provides the capability. Do not add a dependency where the repository already has an adequate primitive, and do not hand-roll what a dependency already does.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Plain commands are the contract
The bare invocation is the contract: pytest -q, nbdev-export. Project configuration exists precisely so the plain command does the right thing, and then every invocation is short, identical and instantly readable. Use the command the repository documents in its README, pyproject.toml or Makefile.
A flag, redirect or pipe states that this one call has a requirement the defaults do not cover. Used that way it carries information. The reader stops, asks why, and finds an answer. Sprinkled defensively on every call, decorations destroy that signal. Every command looks exceptional so none is, and the one deliberate flag is indistinguishable from habit. Transcripts compound the damage, since each decorated call teaches later calls to decorate too.

Wanting the same flag on every run means a missing configuration line. Promote it and go back to the bare command: pytest --timeout 300 on every run becomes timeout = 300 under [tool.pytest.ini_options].
Do not check-then-apply when applying is the goal. Apply formatters when formatting is the goal, and reserve check-only modes for final verification and CI.
Run commands and read their complete output. Never pipe diagnostics through head, tail or any filter that hides failures. The truncation is decided before the output exists. It hides the surprises worth seeing. Never merge stderr into stdout with 2>&1. Separated, a crash is unmissable.
Where output genuinely cannot come back inline, redirect stdout and stderr to separate files and read both.
A real one-off requirement gets its flag once, with the reason stated alongside, and disappears again on the next call.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Preserve docments and delegation
Docments are trailing parameter comments used as API documentation, and they are the house signature style here. Never remove them while refactoring. For a signature with docments or many parameters, keep the opening parenthesis on the definition line, put one parameter on each indented line, and put the closing ): alone at definition indentation.
Where **kwargs passes through to a known callable with useful named parameters, use @delegates(callee) and name the collector kwargs, which is what delegates requires. Do not use @delegates where the callee itself exposes only **kwargs.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Raw strings by default
Write any non-trivial string literal as a raw string: regexes, prompt and skill text, code or markup inside strings, paths with escapes, and anything multi-line. In a plain string a stray backslash-n or backslash-d either errors or silently corrupts. Each miss costs a round trip to diagnose and another to fix. The r costs nothing when no escapes are present. Make it the default rather than the exception.
The exception is a skill body, which is an exported markdown cell and reaches the module as a plain docstring that nbdev writes without the r. Spell escapes out in words there rather than showing them literally.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Tests earn their place
All code costs something to write, maintain and read. Tests cost most. Every test has to keep passing forever, is read by every future contributor, and has to be revised whenever the behaviour it pins changes. Never write a test as a reflex, and do not aim anywhere near full coverage. A test earns its place only when one of three things is true.

It documents an idea. In nbdev notebooks the examples are the documentation.
The logic is intricate enough that you had to think carefully to get it right: edge cases, parsing, arithmetic, tricky conditionals, the places a future change could silently break it.
The code assumes something about an external system, such as a file format, an API’s response shape or another tool’s behaviour, that could change one day and that we want to hear about when it does. These have to exercise the real thing, because a mock merely restates our assumption.

Wiring and orchestration get no tests: re-exports, delegations, one-line glue, and functions that only sequence calls to other tools. A test there asserts that Python works and pins down internals we may want to change. The strong tell is a test that needs recording fakes or mock collaborators to reach the code, which tests a transcript of the implementation rather than logic. Extract the logic into a small pure function and test that, or do not test at all.
For a behaviour change, work red-green: write the test first, run it to see it fail, make the change, run it again to see it pass. A regression test has to fail for the reported bug before the fix and pass after it. In notebooks there are no separate test cells. The red-green check applies to the assertion you actually added or revised.

Prefer as few tests as possible. One test that walks through many checks is more readable and faster than many small ones.
A check worth keeping goes in a test file or a notebook cell, never left as an ad-hoc command. In a notebook the checks made while exploring often are the narrative. They stay as example cells.
Assert the logic, not incidentals. Check what the behaviour guarantees, never byte-exact renderings, exact reprs or field order. A test comparing a whole output string locks in formatting decisions that were never the point. Never use a test to lock in behaviour unless that exact behaviour is part of the contract.
Do not run slow or network-touching suites until finishing a session, or after a change likely to affect them. Run the fast checks while you work; a final verification still runs every slow check the change could affect.

In nbdev projects the notebook is source, documentation, examples and tests at once. Edit the source notebook rather than the generated Python, preserve docments and explanatory structure, export with the project’s nbdev command, and run the documented tests.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Configuration and versioning
Read from standard locations rather than duplicating configuration: project settings from pyproject.toml under the package’s own table, release notes from .github/release.yml. Infer what can be inferred, such as the package name from [project].name. Bundle data files inside the package and read them with importlib.resources.
Version bumps belong to a release, never to a change. Bump immediately after releasing. The tree then always carries the next release’s version. A downstream pin is different. It belongs to the change that creates the dependency. When a change makes one package consume another’s new behaviour, stamp the consumer’s pin in the same session. A pin deferred to release time is a forgotten pin.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Handoffs, events, and honest state

Treat acceptance of background work as a lifecycle boundary. Register ownership atomically, under the same lock as competing starts and shutdown. Wake both sides on timeout, rejection and shutdown. A worker that registers after a rejection stops and emits no accepted-work event.
Make replay or terminal completion an explicit state, not a guess from the latest event. A later bookkeeping event must not erase a terminal sequence. Reset it only when the next unit of work is accepted. Keep application errors separate from transport errors, so an application failure does not trigger connection recovery.
When you move work or response ownership between layers, audit the old producer, every consumer, and both the success and failure paths. Keep every response field callers read. Find and update all callers and tests that expect the old contract.
Keep the plan truthful. Mark done steps done, keep one step active, and leave the rest pending. A [done] note inside a pending step does not complete it.

title: Coding patterns
text:
Ramabana workflow
Use Ramabana’s native tools rather than instructions written for another harness:

search_code finds repository and installed-package behaviour.
view_file or the notebook cell tools read the exact source before editing.
replace_text or edit_cell make narrow, auditable changes (edit_file when the exhash group is on).
edits is a list of {"oldText", "newText"} objects and commands a list of lists: send them as structured values, not as a JSON string. A refused edit means nothing changed: fix the payload rather than resending it.
inspect_python reads live state without mutation. run_python performs requested transformations in new bindings.
run_shell verifies edits with the repository’s own commands.
read_skill loads specialized workflows before using them. Read write_docs for the prose that ships with code, write_prose for narrative writing, and theory for the design a codebase is derived from.

Writing the code does not complete the task. Run the relevant tests or checks, read the result, fix failures, and report exactly what you verified. Never claim a file changed or a check passed without tool evidence from the current session. Before reporting a behaviour change, have an independent subagent review the exact changed files and tests, and check its findings against the real diff and test output.

title: pyrepl
text:
A kernel reports what a cell produced as a stream of messages: text printed to stdout, a result value, a rich display, an error. A notebook stores the same things as a list of dicts in nbformat, the notebook file format. ExecOutcome holds the result of one request in that shape: whether it succeeded, its outputs, its execution count and its error, if any. The terminal, the session log that log_cell writes, and the tests all read the same list.
output_text flattens such a list to plain text, which is what tests, logs and a plain terminal need. The cell below shows each kind of output.


source


def output_text(
    outputs
):
Flatten notebook outputs for tests, logs and plain terminal fallbacks.




source


def ExecOutcome(
    ok:bool=True, outputs:list=<factory>, execution_count:int | None=None, error:str | None=None
)->None:
One kernel request in nbformat’s output shape.



outs = [{'output_type': 'stream', 'text': 'hello\n'},
        {'output_type': 'execute_result', 'data': {'text/plain': '42'}},
        {'output_type': 'error', 'ename': 'ValueError', 'evalue': 'bad', 'traceback': []}]
test_eq(output_text(outs), 'hello\n42\nValueError: bad')
test_eq(output_text([{'output_type': 'stream', 'text': ['a', 'b']}]), 'ab')
test_eq(output_text([{'output_type': 'error', 'ename': 'E', 'evalue': 'v',
                      'traceback': ['line one', 'line two']}]), 'line one\nline two')
test_eq(output_text([]), '')

title: pyrepl
text:
The kernel
Kernel starts and drives a private ipykernel, the standard Python kernel for Jupyter. start launches it in cwd, waits until it is ready, and runs a bootstrap cell that starts Dhrishti inside it. Dhrishti serves the kernel’s namespace from a background thread. The bootstrap prints the server’s port behind a marker, and start reads the marker to set base, the server’s address. The session is registered under the name <project>-pyrepl-<pid>, so another terminal can find it.
execute runs one cell and returns an ExecOutcome. It passes each output to on_output as it arrives, so the terminal can show it at once. complete asks the kernel for tab completions at a cursor position, interrupt stops the running cell, and shutdown stops the kernel, forcing it when it does not stop within timeout. A Kernel that is not running answers execute with an error and complete with no matches, as the second cell shows.


source

Kernel
def Kernel(
    cwd:str='.'
):
A private ipykernel with Dhrishti serving its live namespace.



kernel = await Kernel('.').start()
r = await kernel.execute('a = 6 * 7\na')
test_eq((r.ok, output_text(r.outputs)), (True, '42'))
assert kernel.base.startswith('http://127.0.0.1:')


dead = Kernel('.')
r = await dead.execute('1 + 1')
test_eq((r.ok, r.error), (False, 'kernel is not running'))

r = await kernel.execute('1/0')
test_eq(r.ok, False)
assert 'ZeroDivisionError' in r.error and 'ZeroDivisionError' in output_text(r.outputs)

r = await kernel.execute("for i in range(3): print(i)")
test_eq(len([o for o in r.outputs if o['output_type'] == 'stream']), 1)
test_eq(output_text(r.outputs), '0\n1\n2')

await kernel.execute('import json')
matches, start = await kernel.complete('json.du', 7)
test_eq((sorted(matches), start), (['dump', 'dumps'], 5))

test_eq(await dead.complete('json.du', 7), ([], 7))

title: pyrepl
text:
The host
The agent needs a host whose Python tools reach this kernel. Its file, search and web tools stay the ordinary ones. Dhrishti is the piece that changes: it sends the agent’s run_python, inspect_python and variable listing over HTTP to the agent half of the Dhrishti API. Every call it makes goes to /agent/api/..., which needs no token, and none of these paths reads the owner token that opens /api/exec, /api/set and /api/promote. So no tool call can change the owner’s namespace. The only code here that reads the owner token is promote, which runs when the person types /promote.
log_cell keeps the whole session in one notebook, the session log that Dhrishti keeps. The person’s cells go in as code cells with their real outputs, and each agent turn goes in as markdown cells for the prompt and the answer, in the order they happened.


source

DhrishtiHost
def DhrishtiHost(
    roots, # the folders the agent is confined to; each must exist
    base, *, ns:NoneType=None, # live namespace; fresh dict when None
    approvals:NoneType=None, # write approval handler
    note:NoneType=None, # status callback
    web:bool=True, # use fossick when installed
    index:bool=True, # start a Kosha sync for every open root
    graph:bool=False, # build Kosha's call graph during sync
    rerank:bool=True, # rerank Kosha hits with flashrank
    rerank_model:NoneType=None, # flashrank model; None uses its default
    memory:NoneType=None, # memory, ask and watch backend
    apis:NoneType=None, # API specification backend
    kernel:NoneType=None, # live kernel; None runs in process
    read_outside:bool=False, # let read-only tools name any path on this machine
    deny:tuple=('*/.ssh/*', '*/.aws/*', '*/.gnupg/*', '*/.config/gcloud/*', '*/.netrc', '*/.git-credentials', '*/.codex/auth.json', '*/.claude/.credentials.json', '*/.env', '*/.env.*', '*/id_rsa*', '*/id_ed25519*', '*.pem', '*.key', '*.p12'), # what `read_outside` still refuses to open
    read_roots:tuple=(), # folders the read tools search and no write may touch
    tmux:NoneType=None, # None detects `$TMUX`; False off; True on; or this host's own pane (target or `Pane`)
    read_guard:NoneType=None, # `(ReadCheck) -> None | str | Refusal`: what the read tools may send
    model_local:NoneType=None, # `() -> (local, model)` for the turn's model
):
A LocalHost that starts on a Dhrishti overlay, for callers that build one directly.




source

use_kernel
def use_kernel(
    host, base
):
Point host’s Python at a Dhrishti overlay in place, keeping every other tool group.




source

Dhrishti
def Dhrishti(
    base
):
The agent half of a Dhrishti session, in the shape of a kernel a LocalHost can hold.


Dhrishti is everything a LocalHost needs from a kernel: the calls run, inspect, list_vars, log_cell and describe, and the two facts scopes and kind. run always uses the overlay, whatever scope the model asks for, and inspect accepts only the isolated and overlay scopes. The cells below run code in the overlay and read it back.

from shalya.host import LocalHost


k = Dhrishti(kernel.base)
k.scopes, k.kind, k.run('from_the_kernel = 1')


test_eq(k.scopes, ('isolated', 'overlay'))
test_eq(k.kind, 'ipykernel')
test_eq(k.run('from_the_kernel = 1'), '(ok)')
test_eq(k.inspect('from_the_kernel + 1', 'overlay'), '2')
assert 'from_the_kernel' in k.list_vars()
assert 'only honours' in k.inspect('1+1', scope='nonsense')
test_eq(k.base, kernel.base)

There are two ways to give a host this kernel. use_kernel(host, base) takes the host a session already has and points its Python at the Dhrishti session at base, in place. Every other tool group stays as it was, so a host with a vault keeps its memory tools. The terminal calls it when you switch to Python mode or attach to a session, and so does mk_agent(python=URL). DhrishtiHost(roots, base) builds a new LocalHost that starts on a Dhrishti session, for code that creates its host directly.
The first cell below compares the tool names of a host with memory before and after use_kernel, and nothing is added or lost. After that, a DhrishtiHost shows the overlay at work: the agent’s owner = None leaves the person’s owner as it was. The cells after it check log_cell, a session that has no log, and describe, which keeps falsy values such as 0 and ''.

from shalya.tools import tools_for


class Store:
    def tree(self, document=''): return []
    def search(self, query, limit=8): return []
    def read(self, node_id): return {}
    def topics(self, limit=12): return []
    def forget(self, doc_id): return False
    def remember(self, text, title=None, tags=()): return {'doc_id': 'd1', 'title': 'x'}
    def ask(self, q, ref=None, instruction='', **kw): return {'answer': '', 'cited': []}
    def watch(self, target, **kw): return {'id': 'w1'}
    def watches(self, due_only=False): return []
    def unwatch(self, watch_id): return False
    def poll(self): return {'ran': 0, 'checked': 0, 'results': []}

vaulted = LocalHost(['.'], index=False, web=False, memory=Store())
before = {t.__name__ for t in tools_for(vaulted)}
use_kernel(vaulted, kernel.base)
after = {t.__name__ for t in tools_for(vaulted)}
len(before), sorted(before - after), sorted(after - before)


test_eq(before - after, set())
test_eq(after - before, set())
assert 'memory_read' in after and 'run_python' in after
test_eq(vaulted.scopes, ('isolated', 'overlay'))
test_eq(vaulted.kernel_kind, 'ipykernel')
test_eq(vaulted.run_python('after_the_swap = 2'), '(ok)')
assert 'after_the_swap' in vaulted.list_vars()
test_eq(use_kernel(vaulted, kernel.base), vaulted)


host = DhrishtiHost(['.'], kernel.base, web=False, index=False)
await kernel.execute("owner = {'kept': 1}")

test_eq(host.run_python('mine = len(owner)'), '(ok)')
assert 'mine' in host.list_vars() and 'owner' in host.list_vars()

host.run_python('owner = None')
r = await kernel.execute('owner')
test_eq(output_text(r.outputs), "{'kept': 1}")

assert 'Error' in DhrishtiHost(['.'], 'http://127.0.0.1:1', web=False, index=False).run_python('1')


from fastcore.nbio import read_nb


r = await kernel.execute('logged = 1')
host.log_cell('logged = 1', r.outputs)
host.log_cell('**user**\n\nwhat is logged?', cell_type='markdown')
nb = read_nb(host.agent_log)
test_eq([c.cell_type for c in nb.cells[-2:]], ['code', 'markdown'])
test_eq(nb.cells[-2].outputs, r.outputs)


_real_api = _api
_api = lambda base, path, params=None, timeout=60: {'log': None}
try: nolog = DhrishtiHost(['.'], kernel.base, web=False, index=False)
finally: _api = _real_api
dead_host = DhrishtiHost(['.'], 'http://127.0.0.1:1', web=False, index=False)
test_eq((nolog.agent_log, dead_host.agent_log), (None, None))
test_eq([h.log_cell('x = 1', []) for h in (nolog, dead_host)], [None, None])


_real_api = _api
def _fake_rows_api(base, path, params=None, timeout=60):
    return {'groups': [{'nodes': [
        {'name': 'zero_val', 'type': 'int', 'value': 0},
        {'name': 'blank_val', 'type': 'str', 'value': ''},
        {'name': 'missing_val', 'type': 'NoneType', 'value': None},
    ]}]}
_api = _fake_rows_api
try: described = host.describe()
finally: _api = _real_api
test_eq(described['zero_val'], '0')
test_eq(described['blank_val'], '')
test_eq(described['missing_val'], 'NoneType')


Completion, with the namespace described
Tab completion at the Python prompt draws on two sources. The kernel supplies the candidates. Its completer is IPython’s, with jedi behind it, so it knows imports, attribute chains, dictionary keys and file paths. Dhrishti has no completion endpoint, and its view of the namespace covers only top-level names, so it would complete worse.
Dhrishti supplies the descriptions instead. annotate adds the type and shape Dhrishti reports to each candidate that names a live variable, so the menu shows df -> DataFrame [1200×8] rather than df. Reading descriptions needs no token, so they come from the agent half of the API. They are optional: if the lookup is slow or fails, the menu shows the bare names, never an empty list.


source

annotate
def annotate(
    matches, described
):
Candidate names with their type and shape where the session knows one.



test_eq(annotate(['df', 'dfs'], {'df': 'DataFrame [3×2]'}), ['df -> DataFrame [3×2]', 'dfs'])
test_eq(annotate(['x'], {}), ['x'])
test_eq(annotate([], {'x': 'int'}), [])
test_eq(annotate(['df.copy'], {'df': 'DataFrame [3×2]'}), ['df.copy'])

title: pyrepl
section: Attaching to a session someone else owns
text:
Attaching to a session someone else owns
Sometimes the kernel already exists. Leela, for example, runs a Python session with its own Dhrishti server, and you want a Ramabana agent beside it rather than a second kernel. ramabana --attach NAME starts no kernel. It finds the running server and points the agent’s host at it. The other program keeps the person’s prompt, so in this case there is no Python mode, and Ramabana is only the agent.
find_session(attach) turns a name into the server’s address. A URL passes straight through. Otherwise it reads Dhrishti’s registry of live sessions and tries, in order, an exact session name, a name of the form <attach>-pyrepl-<pid>, and the name of the folder the session runs in. When two sessions match it raises with both rather than pick one, and when none matches it names the sessions that are running. sessions() lists the live sessions, which is what /kernels and ramabana --kernels print.
find_session only reads the registry and never calls Dhrishti’s serve_in_kernel again. Called on a session that is already serving, serve_in_kernel returns the right port but also repoints that session’s logs and resets its agent mode, so a readonly session would come back restricted.
Promotion is not available here. The agent’s work shows in the shared session notebook and over the API that the owning program already watches, and the person promotes from that program, which holds the token.


source

sessions
def sessions():
Every live Dhrishti session: what to pass to --attach, and where it is.




source

find_session
def find_session(
    attach
):
Base URL of the live Dhrishti session named attach, or attach if it is a URL.



test_eq(find_session('http://127.0.0.1:9999'), 'http://127.0.0.1:9999')
test_fail(lambda: find_session('no-such-session-anywhere'), contains='no live dhrishti session')

The real registry is shared by every Dhrishti session on this machine, so the next cell replaces dhrishti.serving.active with a fixed list for each check and runs the real resolution code against it. It covers a match by full name and by project name, a refusal when two sessions share a name, a project name that must not match a longer one that starts the same way, and a match by folder name.

from unittest.mock import patch

def _entry(name, port, cwd='/x/proj'):
    return {'name': name, 'port': port, 'pid': port, 'cwd': cwd, 'base': f'http://127.0.0.1:{port}', 'started': 0}

one = [_entry('proj-pyrepl-111', 9001, '/home/proj')]
dupe_name = [_entry('proj-pyrepl-111', 9001, '/home/a'), _entry('proj-pyrepl-111', 9002, '/home/b')]
by_cwd = [_entry('some-other-name-222', 9003, '/home/leela')]

with patch('dhrishti.serving.active', lambda: one):
    test_eq(find_session('proj-pyrepl-111'), 'http://127.0.0.1:9001')
    test_eq(find_session('proj'), 'http://127.0.0.1:9001')

with patch('dhrishti.serving.active', lambda: dupe_name):
    try:
        find_session('proj-pyrepl-111')
        assert False, 'expected a refusal'
    except RuntimeError as e:
        msg = str(e)
        assert 'matches more than one' in msg
        assert '/home/a' in msg and '/home/b' in msg
        assert '9001' in msg and '9002' in msg

cross_project = [_entry('ramabana-pyrepl-1', 9004, '/home/ramabana'),
                 _entry('ramabana-extra-pyrepl-2', 9005, '/home/ramabana-extra')]

with patch('dhrishti.serving.active', lambda: cross_project):
    test_eq(find_session('ramabana'), 'http://127.0.0.1:9004')

with patch('dhrishti.serving.active', lambda: by_cwd):
    test_eq(find_session('leela'), 'http://127.0.0.1:9003')
    test_fail(lambda: find_session('eela'), contains='no live dhrishti session')

test_eq(find_session('http://127.0.0.1:9999'), 'http://127.0.0.1:9999')


Colour
hl colours a line of Python for the terminal with rich’s syntax highlighter, which uses pygments. Both are already installed for the transcript. It returns a rich Text whose .plain is exactly the source, or uncoloured Text when pygments cannot read it. Colour changes only what is drawn. log_cell, the session notebook and /copy keep the plain source, because text with colour codes in it cannot be pasted back as code.


source

hl
def hl(
    src
):
src as highlighted Text with .plain == src, or plain Text if pygments cannot lex it.



t = hl('x = 1  # note')
test_eq(t.plain, 'x = 1  # note')
assert t.spans
test_eq(hl('').plain, '')

title: pyrepl
section: The prompt, against a live kernel
text:
The prompt, against a live kernel
The prompt is the terminal’s cli.Ui, and Python mode is one of its modes. The cells below drive it from here because this notebook has the live kernel. They draw the terminal on an emulated screen, EmuTty, and use fake_agent in place of a model. Agent mode is unchanged: the same blocks, folding, approvals, slash commands and status bar. Python mode changes what a typed line means, from a prompt for the model to code for the kernel.
The cells check switching modes with /agent and /python (or /py), /help and /vars in Python mode, prompt history, how each kind of kernel output is shown, a turn that reaches the model and is written to the session notebook, attaching an image in agent mode, and that an @ inside Python code is never taken for an attachment.

from ramabana.testing import fake_agent
from ramabana.cli import CompletionMenu, Ui, run_turn
from teleprint.compositor import Compositor
from teleprint.keys import Key
from teleprint.testing import EmuTty        # not `pyghostty.EmuTty`; see nbs/05_cli.ipynb


tty = EmuTty(80, 40)   # tall enough for /help: `term.text()` has no scrollback
comp = Compositor(tty)
comp._register_signals = lambda: None    # nbdev runs this async cell on a worker thread
await comp.start()
agent, be = fake_agent(host=host, replies=['`owner` is a dict with one key.'])
ui = Ui(comp, agent)
ui.kernel = kernel          # `enter_python` adopts it rather than start a second
await ui.enter_python()
comp.on_key = ui.on_key
ui.paint()
test_eq(ui.mode, 'python')
assert 'python' in ui.status().plain


ui.buf.insert('/agent'); test_eq(ui.submit(), None)
test_eq(ui.mode, 'agent')
assert ui.prompt().plain.startswith('▌')
ui.buf.insert('/py'); await ui.submit()
test_eq(ui.mode, 'python')

ui.buf.insert('/help'); ui.submit()
assert 'python' in tty.term.text()

ui.buf.insert('/vars'); test_eq(ui.submit(), None)
assert 'owner' in ui.transcript.block_text(list(comp.blocks.values())[-1])

ui.buf.clear()
ui.buf.insert('/detach nothing.png')
ui.complete = CompletionMenu(ui.buf, ['/detach'], start=0, show=8)
test_eq(ui.submit(), None)
test_eq((ui.complete, ui.buf.text), (None, ''))
test_eq(ui.history[-1], '/detach nothing.png')

ui.buf.insert('recalled_py = 1')
await ui.submit()
test_eq(ui.history[-1], 'recalled_py = 1')
ui.recall(-1)
test_eq(ui.buf.text, 'recalled_py = 1')
ui.buf.clear()


ui.on_output({'output_type': 'stream', 'name': 'stdout', 'text': 'printed\n'})
ui.on_output({'output_type': 'execute_result', 'data': {'text/plain': '42'}})
ui.on_output({'output_type': 'error', 'ename': 'ValueError', 'evalue': 'bad', 'traceback': []})
kinds = [b.tag for b in comp.blocks.values()][-3:]
test_eq(kinds, ['note', 'reply', 'error'])


await ui.run_code('from_the_prompt = 99')
r = await kernel.execute('from_the_prompt')
test_eq(output_text(r.outputs), '99')
ui.mode = 'agent'
await run_turn(ui, 'what is in owner?')
assert be.sent, 'the turn reached the backend'
test_eq([c.cell_type for c in read_nb(host.agent_log).cells[-2:]], ['markdown', 'markdown'])
ui.mode = 'python'

_real_host = agent.host
try:
    for h in (nolog, dead_host):
        agent.host = h
        await ui.run_code('logless = 1')
        test_eq(ui.turn, None)
finally: agent.host = _real_host
test_eq(output_text((await kernel.execute('logless')).outputs), '1')

_real_log = host.log_cell
host.log_cell = lambda *a, **kw: 1/0
try: await ui.run_code('wedge_check = 1')
except ZeroDivisionError: pass
finally: host.log_cell = _real_log
test_eq(ui.turn, None)


from dataclasses import replace


pics = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(pics / 'shot.png').write_bytes(b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n' + b'0' * 64)
shot = pics / 'shot.png'

ui.mode = 'agent'
be.spec = replace(be.spec, ctx=128_000)
ui.buf.insert(f'/attach {shot}'); ui.submit()
assert 'shot.png' in ui.attach_row().plain
ui.buf.insert('what is in the picture?')
await ui.submit()
assert isinstance(be.sent[-1], list) and shot.read_bytes() in be.sent[-1]
test_eq(ui.attachments, [])
ui.mode = 'python'


leak = pics / '@leak.png'
leak.write_bytes(b'\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n' + b'0' * 64)

ui.mode = 'python'
ui.buf.insert("py_matmul = type('M', (), {'__matmul__': lambda self, o: 42})() @ 1")
await ui.submit()
r = await kernel.execute('py_matmul')
test_eq(output_text(r.outputs), '42')
test_eq(ui.attachments, [])

ui.buf.insert(f'py_leak = 5  # not an attachment: @{leak}')
await ui.submit()
r = await kernel.execute('py_leak')
test_eq(output_text(r.outputs), '5')
test_eq(ui.attachments, [])


Typing more than one line
Ui submits a line when you press enter. That suits a sentence and fails for a block of code, because for i in range(3): is not a program yet. code_state(src) uses the standard library’s codeop.compile_command to say whether the text is complete, incomplete, or invalid, meaning it can never compile. On enter, an incomplete buffer gets a new line under a continuation prompt, a complete one runs, and an invalid one is reported at the prompt without a trip to the kernel. An empty line submits what is pending, as at every Python prompt, and pasted text that compiles runs as one cell.
The first cell below lists the cases. The ones after it type a loop line by line, enter a broken line, and paste two statements.


source

code_state
def code_state(
    src
):
Whether src is a finished statement, an unfinished one, or one that cannot compile.



test_eq(code_state('x = 1'), 'complete')
test_eq(code_state('for i in range(3):'), 'incomplete')
test_eq(code_state('x = ('), 'incomplete')
test_eq(code_state('x = )'), 'invalid')
test_eq(code_state(''), 'complete')
test_eq(code_state('for i in range(3):\n    print(i)'), 'incomplete')
test_eq(code_state('for i in range(3):\n    print(i)\n'), 'complete')

test_eq(code_state('x = 1\ny = 2\n'), 'complete')
test_eq(code_state('import os\nprint(os.getcwd())'), 'complete')
test_eq(code_state('import os\nfor i in range(2):\n    print(i)'), 'complete')

test_eq(code_state('x = 1\ny = )'), 'invalid')
assert 'unmatched' in _syntax_note('x = 1\ny = )')
assert 'multiple statements' not in _syntax_note('x = 1\ny = )')
test_eq(code_state('x = 1\ny = ('), 'incomplete')


await kernel.execute('multiline_ran = []')
ui.buf.clear()
ui.buf.insert('for i in range(3):')
ui.on_key(Key('enter'))
test_eq(ui.buf.text, 'for i in range(3):\n')
assert ui.turn is None
assert ui.CONT.strip() in tty.term.text()

ui.buf.insert('    multiline_ran.append(i)')
rows, (row, line_no, col) = ui.tail()
test_eq(row, len(rows) - 1)
test_eq(line_no, 1)
test_eq(col, Text(ui.CONT + '    multiline_ran.append(i)').cell_len)
assert ui.CONT in ui.prompt().plain
assert ui.prompt().spans

ui.on_key(Key('enter'))
test_eq(ui.buf.text, 'for i in range(3):\n    multiline_ran.append(i)\n')
out = ui.on_key(Key('enter'))
test_eq(ui.buf.text, '')
await out
r = await kernel.execute('multiline_ran')
test_eq(output_text(r.outputs), '[0, 1, 2]')
test_eq(read_nb(host.agent_log).cells[-1].source, 'for i in range(3):\n    multiline_ran.append(i)\n')


ui.buf.clear()
ui.buf.insert('x = )')
ui.on_key(Key('enter'))
assert 'invalid' in tty.term.text() and ui.turn is None
ui.buf.clear()

ui.mode = 'agent'
ui.buf.insert('for the record:')
out = ui.on_key(Key('enter'))
test_eq(ui.buf.text, '')
if out is not None: await out
ui.mode = 'python'


ui.buf.clear()
ui.paste('pasted_a = 3\npasted_b = pasted_a * 2')
test_eq(code_state(ui.buf.text), 'complete')
out = ui.on_key(Key('enter'))
test_eq(ui.buf.text, '')
if out is not None: await out
r = await kernel.execute('pasted_b')
test_eq(output_text(r.outputs), '6')


ui.buf.clear(); ui.buf.insert('df2 = df.copy()')
assert ui.prompt().spans
blk = ui.say(hl('df2 = df.copy()'), 'user', source='df2 = df.copy()')
test_eq(ui.transcript.block_text(blk), 'df2 = df.copy()')
ui.buf.clear()



Getting back out of Python mode
A line that starts with / is a command. It goes to submit without being compiled, because as Python /agent is invalid and Python mode would have no way out. Tab after /mod completes the command name, as it does in agent mode.

def _line(u, s):
    for ch in s: u.on_key(Key(ch, char=ch))
    return u.on_key(Key('enter'))

test_eq(code_state('/agent'), 'invalid')
test_eq(_line(ui, '/agent'), None)
test_eq((ui.mode, ui.buf.text), ('agent', ''))
await _line(ui, '/python')
test_eq((ui.mode, ui.buf.text), ('python', ''))
test_eq(_line(ui, '/help'), None)
test_eq(ui.buf.text, '')
assert 'python' in tty.term.text()
test_eq(_line(ui, '/quit'), 'quit')

ui.buf.clear(); ui.buf.insert('/mod')
test_eq(ui.on_key(Key('tab')), None)
test_eq(ui.buf.text, '/model')
assert ui.complete is not None
ui.complete = None; ui.buf.clear()

_line(ui, 'for i in range(3):')
test_eq(ui.buf.text, 'for i in range(3):\n')
ui.buf.clear()

The main prompt leaves mouse selection to the terminal, so you can select and copy text as usual. enter_transcript turns mouse handling on only while the transcript view is open.


Tab, against the live kernel
complete_python asks the kernel for completions at the cursor. One match completes the buffer in place. Several matches fill in their common prefix and open a menu, each entry described by annotate. The descriptions are fetched off the event loop’s thread, and typing while they are on their way closes the menu without waiting for them, as the last two cells check.

await kernel.execute('completing = {"a": 1}')
ui.buf.clear(); ui.buf.insert('complet')
ui.buf.cursor = len(ui.buf.text)
await ui.complete_python()
test_eq(ui.buf.text, 'completing')
ui.buf.clear()

await kernel.execute('twovals_a = 1\ntwovals_b = 2')
ui.buf.clear(); ui.buf.insert('twovals_'); ui.buf.cursor = len('twovals_')
await ui.complete_python()
assert ui.complete is not None, 'several matches arm the menu'
test_eq(sorted(ui.complete.matches), ['twovals_a', 'twovals_b'])
assert all('->' in d for d in ui.desc), ui.desc

ui.buf.clear(); ui.buf.insert('twoval'); ui.buf.cursor = len('twoval')
await ui.complete_python()
test_eq((ui.buf.text, ui.buf.cursor), ('twovals_', 8))
test_eq(len(ui.complete.matches), 2)
ui.buf.clear()


loop_thread = threading.current_thread()
seen_thread = {}
_real_describe = host.describe
def _watched_describe():
    seen_thread['t'] = threading.current_thread()
    return _real_describe()
host.describe = _watched_describe
try:
    await kernel.execute('threadcheck_a = 1\nthreadcheck_b = 2')
    ui.buf.clear(); ui.buf.insert('threadcheck_'); ui.buf.cursor = len('threadcheck_')
    await ui.complete_python()
finally:
    host.describe = _real_describe
assert seen_thread.get('t') is not None and seen_thread['t'] is not loop_thread
assert all('->' in d for d in ui.desc), ui.desc
ui.buf.clear()


release = threading.Event()
def _blocked_describe():
    release.wait(5)
    return {'twovals_a': 'int', 'twovals_b': 'int'}
_real_describe = host.describe
host.describe = _blocked_describe
ui.complete, ui.desc = None, []
try:
    await kernel.execute('twovals_a = 1\ntwovals_b = 2')
    ui.buf.clear(); ui.buf.insert('twovals_'); ui.buf.cursor = len('twovals_')
    task = asyncio.ensure_future(ui.complete_python())
    for _ in range(500):
        if ui.complete is not None: break
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
    assert ui.complete is not None and ui.desc == []
    ui.on_key(Key('x', char='x'))
    test_eq(ui.buf.text, 'twovals_x')
    test_eq(ui.complete, None)
    release.set()
    await task
finally:
    host.describe = _real_describe
    release.set()
test_eq((ui.complete, ui.desc), (None, []))
test_eq(ui.buf.text, 'twovals_x')
ui.buf.clear()

title: pyrepl
text:
/promote
Values the agent makes live in its overlay. /promote NAME moves one into the owner’s namespace, where it becomes an ordinary variable at your prompt. Promotion is the owner’s act: it is a slash command the person types and never a tool, so the model can ask for it in words but cannot do it. promote(base, name) reads the session’s owner token and calls Dhrishti’s /api/promote. It works only on a kernel this session started. An attached session’s token belongs to the program that started it, and the terminal says so. The test checks that the command runs off the event loop’s thread and that /promote alone prints its usage.


source

promote
def promote(
    base, name
):
Move the agent-layer variable name into the owner namespace of a kernel this session started.



test_eq(promote('', 'x'), 'no kernel of our own; promote from the surface that started the session')


import ramabana.pyrepl as _pyr


seen = {}
def _fake_promote(base, name):
    seen.update(base=base, name=name, thread=threading.current_thread())
    return f'promoted {name}'
_real_promote, _pyr.promote = _pyr.promote, _fake_promote
try:
    ui.buf.insert('/promote answer_42')
    await ui.submit()
finally: _pyr.promote = _real_promote
test_eq((seen['base'], seen['name']), (kernel.base, 'answer_42'))
assert seen['thread'] is not threading.current_thread()
assert 'promoted answer_42' in tty.term.text()
test_eq(ui.buf.text, '')

ui.buf.insert('/promote')
test_eq(ui.submit(), None)
assert 'usage: /promote' in tty.term.text()


Attaching to the live session
The kernel this notebook started is itself a live Dhrishti session, so attaching can be tested against a real server. find_session finds it by its registry name, <project>-pyrepl-<pid>, as Kernel._bootstrap sets it. The process id keeps the name apart from any session left over from an earlier run. The cell after it checks that shutdown forces a kernel that does not stop when asked, and the last one shuts this notebook’s kernel down.

from dhrishti.serving import active


own = next((e for e in active() if e.get('base') == kernel.base), None)
assert own, 'the kernel above is serving'
test_eq(find_session(own['name']), kernel.base)

attached = DhrishtiHost(['.'], find_session(own['name']), web=False, index=False)
test_eq(attached.kernel_kind, 'ipykernel')
assert 'owner' in attached.list_vars()


class _StuckKm:
    has_kernel = True
    def __init__(self): self.forced = None
    async def shutdown_kernel(self, now=False):
        self.forced = now
        if not now: await asyncio.sleep(30)

stuck, km = Kernel('.'), _StuckKm()
stuck.km, stuck.kc = km, None
await stuck.shutdown(timeout=0.05)
test_eq(km.forced, True)
test_eq(stuck.km, None)
assert stuck.base is None

class _GoodKm(_StuckKm):
    async def shutdown_kernel(self, now=False): self.forced = now
good = _GoodKm(); ok = Kernel('.'); ok.km, ok.kc = good, None
await ok.shutdown(timeout=5)
test_eq(good.forced, False)


await kernel.shutdown()
test_eq(kernel.alive, False)

title: pyrepl
section: The agent at the Python prompt
text:
The agent at the Python prompt
--agent-proxy, or /agent_proxy inside a session, makes the session’s agent reachable from Python as ramabana_agent, so code at the prompt can read the agent’s token use or attach a chat callback. ramabana_agents holds every agent bound in that namespace, by label.
AgentBridge runs in the Ramabana process. It serves one HTTP path, /agent, on the loopback address, and answers only requests that carry its random token. It offers a fixed set of operations. usage, turn_usage and chat_usage return token counts and cost for the session, the last turn and the turn’s chat. callbacks lists the chat callbacks that are known and attached, and attach_callback(name) attaches one, on the session’s own thread through dispatch. Anything else is refused. agent_proxy_code writes the source of a small AgentProxy class that calls the bridge, and inject_agent_proxy runs that source in the agent’s overlay with run_python. The terminal also runs it in the kernel itself, so the person’s code sees the proxy too.

title: pane
text:
While a turn runs, the chat shows the answer as it streams and one line per tool call. It does not show, at a glance, which step the turn is on, how far the plan has got, what each sub-agent is doing, or which files have changed so far. The now pane shows all of that in a narrow column beside the chat. It is called the now pane because it shows only the present: what is running at this moment and what this turn has done.
The pane runs as a separate program, ramabana-pane, in a tmux split. tmux is a terminal multiplexer: it divides one terminal window into panes, each running its own program. Because the pane is a separate process, the terminal session hands it information through a file. Several times a second the session writes a snapshot, a JSON file called now.json in the session’s run folder, and the pane reads that file and draws it. This page covers the three parts in order: taking a snapshot, laying it out as rows of text, and the viewer that draws those rows and answers keys and clicks.

title: pane
text:
The snapshot
now_snapshot(agent) returns a plain dict that json.dumps can write. Its keys are:

root, the foreground turn: how many steps it has taken, how long it has run, its state, the call it is waiting on (current), and its status, the last line the model wrote before calling a tool.
plan, the agent’s checklist, with each item’s text and status.
subs, one row per sub-agent. A sub-agent is a second agent the turn starts to do part of the work. The list holds every delegation this turn started, and every background delegation that is running or has finished since the turn began. A row carries the sub-agent’s status, its last CALLS_KEPT calls with their results cut short, and its answer, cut to ANSWER_CHARS, once it has finished. A finished sub-agent stays listed until the next turn starts.
files, the files this turn wrote: path, lines added and removed, and the diff cut to DIFF_LINES lines.
notes, what the model wrote before each of this turn’s calls, in full and with a timestamp.
background, the work running behind the turn: background delegations, commands started with run_shell_bg, and folder watches. Each row has a kind, an id, a label, a state and the seconds it has been running. A finished shell command or a watch has no clock, so its elapsed is None.

The session writes a snapshot up to five times a second, so taking one has to be cheap when nothing has changed. The list of files is worked out again only after a call finishes. The state of a background shell command is asked of the host at most once every SHELL_EVERY seconds while it runs, and never again once it has ended.
Each recorded call (an Act) names the run whose model made it, so a sub-agent’s step count is the number of calls with its run id. A step of the main turn is counted the way the terminal counts it: a call whose parent_action_id does not name another call in the activity log. A sub-agent’s calls name the delegate call that started it, so they never count as steps of the main turn.


source

now_snapshot
def now_snapshot(
    agent
):
The foreground turn, its plan, sub-agents, writes and background work, as a JSON-able dict.


The example builds an agent with fake_agent and a scripted model, Root. The model reads a file, then asks a sub-agent one question with delegate_search, and the sub-agent reads the same file before it answers. The activity log’s on_change hook takes a snapshot when the sub-agent’s read starts, which is the moment the pane would show both agents working. The main turn has taken two steps and the one sub-agent is running with one step:

from ramabana.runtime import current_run
from ramabana.testing import ScriptedBackend, Step, fake_agent

READ = ('view_file', {'path': '/proj/a.py'})
a, _ = fake_agent()
seen = []
a.activity.on_change = lambda act: seen.append(now_snapshot(a)) if not act.done and current_run().kind != 'root' else None
class Root(ScriptedBackend):
    def spawn(self, sp='', tools=(), **kw):
        return ScriptedBackend(self.spec, steps=[Step(tool=READ), Step('a() is defined')], token_delay=0, tools=tools)
be = Root(steps=[Step(tool=READ), Step(tool=('delegate_search', {'questions': ['what does a.py define?']})), Step('done')],
          token_delay=0, tools=a.tools, sp=a.system_prompt())
a._be = a._be_or_none = lambda job='turn': be
list(a.stream('go'))
mid = seen[0]
test_eq((mid['busy'], mid['root']['steps'], [(s['state'], s['steps']) for s in mid['subs']]), (True, 2, [('running', 1)]))
mid

{'at': 1792474688.9890528,
 'busy': True,
 'root': {'turn_elapsed': 0.0,
  'steps': 2,
  'state': 'running',
  'status': '',
  'current': 'Delegate: what does a.py define?'},
 'plan': [],
 'subs': [{'id': 'run_5837d1bea07d',
   'question': 'what does a.py define?',
   'elapsed': 0.0,
   'state': 'running',
   'steps': 1,
   'status': '',
   'current': 'View /proj/a.py',
   'calls': [{'line': 'View /proj/a.py',
     'ok': True,
     'done': False,
     'out': ''}],
   'answer': ''}],
 'files': [],
 'background': [],
 'notes': []}


Once the turn ends, the sub-agent stays listed as completed. The next turn clears it:

test_eq([s['state'] for s in now_snapshot(a)['subs']], ['completed'])
be.steps = [Step('ok')]
list(a.stream('again'))
test_eq(now_snapshot(a)['subs'], [])

The plan and the files this turn wrote are part of the snapshot too, each file with its diff. Here the example sets a two-item plan and changes a.py by hand:

a.plan.set('ship', ['read a.py', 'fix it']); a.plan.update(a.plan.todos[0].id, status='active')
a.before['/proj/a.py'] = 'def a(): pass\n'; a.host.files['/proj/a.py'] = 'def a(): return 1\n'
snap = now_snapshot(a)
test_eq(snap['plan'], [{'text': 'read a.py', 'status': 'active'}, {'text': 'fix it', 'status': 'pending'}])
test_eq([(f['path'], f['added'], f['removed']) for f in snap['files']], [('a.py', 1, 1)])
print(snap['files'][0]['diff'])

write_snapshot writes the snapshot to a file and read_snapshot reads it back. The writer goes through a temporary file and renames it into place, so the pane never reads half a file. The reader returns None when the file is missing or does not yet hold valid JSON, and the pane then keeps showing what it had. The example checks both cases, and that the temporary file is gone afterwards:


source

read_snapshot
def read_snapshot(
    path
):
The snapshot at path, or None when it is missing or unreadable.




source

write_snapshot
def write_snapshot(
    agent, path
):
Write now_snapshot(agent) to path atomically.



import tempfile
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    p = Path(d)/'now.json'
    test_eq(read_snapshot(p), None)
    write_snapshot(a, p)
    test_eq((read_snapshot(p)['busy'], [f.name for f in Path(d).iterdir()]), (False, ['now.json']))
    p.write_text('{"busy": tr')
    test_eq(read_snapshot(p), None)

title: pane
text:
Drawing it
board(snap, width) lays a snapshot out as rows for a pane width cells wide, one row per screen line. Each row is a (key, Text) pair, where Text is a rich styled string. Long lines are cut at the width, not wrapped. Use board when you need the rows themselves, as the viewer does to know which row a click landed on. Use render when you only want something to print: it returns the same rows as one rich renderable.
From the top, the board shows:

A header with main, its step number, its clock and its status line. The chat already shows the call the main agent is waiting on, so the header leaves it out. An idle agent gets one line.
The plan as a checklist, with the active item highlighted.
The sub-agents, one row each: id, status line (or its question when it has none), clock, and a mark: ▶ running, ✓ completed, ✗ stopped or failed. An open row, marked ▾ in place of ▸, adds the question, each recent call with its result, and the answer once there is one.
The files this turn wrote, each with its lines added and removed. An open row shows the diff, drawn by hl.diff_rich with the code coloured for the file’s language and the added and removed lines tinted.
The background work: kind, label, state and clock. A row opens to a shell command’s last SHELL_LINES lines of output, a watch’s pattern and last review, or a background sub-agent’s detail.
The notes, newest first, for reading back what the model said along the way. Each is a ▸ row with its time and first line, and opens to the whole note wrapped to the pane. The newest note starts open.

Empty sections are left out. A row that can open carries a key: ('sub', id), ('file', path), ('bg', id) or ('note', at). The caller passes the keys of the open rows in open, so a row stays open when the next snapshot arrives. A running clock adds the time since the snapshot was written, so a long call does not look frozen between writes. The colours are the terminal session’s default github-dark palette, copied into PALETTE here because ramabana.cli imports this module and this module cannot import it back.


source

render
def render(
    snap, width:int=40, now:NoneType=None, open:tuple=()
):
The pane for snap as a rich renderable, width cells wide, with the rows keyed in open opened.




source

board
def board(
    snap, width:int=40, now:NoneType=None, open:tuple=(), err:str=''
):
The pane for snap as (key, row) pairs, one per screen line; a row with a key opens and closes.


A snapshot of a busy turn, written five seconds before now, with every row closed. The turn’s clock reads 47s, its 42 seconds plus the five since the write:

call = lambda line, ok=True, done=True, out='': {'line': line, 'ok': ok, 'done': done, 'out': out}
now = time.time()
busy = {'at': now - 5, 'busy': True,
        'root': {'turn_elapsed': 42, 'steps': 7, 'state': 'running', 'status': 'Checking the pane tests', 'current': 'Run shell: pytest'},
        'plan': [{'text': 'Read the viewer', 'status': 'done'}, {'text': 'Rewrite render', 'status': 'active'},
                 {'text': 'Wire the CLI', 'status': 'pending'}, {'text': 'Poll the file', 'status': 'cancelled'}],
        'subs': [{'id': 'run_aaa', 'question': 'which files import fastllm?', 'elapsed': 12, 'state': 'running', 'steps': 2,
                  'status': 'Searching for imports', 'current': 'Search code: fastllm',
                  'calls': [call('Search code: import fastllm', out='agent.py:12: import fastllm'), call('Search code: fastllm', None, False)],
                  'answer': ''},
                 {'id': 'run_bbb', 'question': 'is the pane tested?', 'elapsed': 8, 'state': 'completed', 'steps': 1, 'status': '',
                  'current': '', 'calls': [call('Read tests/test_pane.py')], 'answer': 'Yes, in tests/test_pane.py.'}],
        'files': [{'path': 'ramabana/pane.py', 'added': 1, 'removed': 1, 'diff': '@@ -1 +1 @@\n-from rich.live import Live\n+from teleprint.keys import Parser'}],
        'background': [{'kind': 'shell', 'id': 'cmd_1234abcd', 'label': 'pytest -x tests', 'state': 'running', 'elapsed': 30}]}
def show(snap, open=()):
    con = Console(record=True, width=40, color_system=None)
    con.print(render(snap, 40, now=now, open=open))
    return con.export_text()
out = show(busy)
assert '47s' in out and 'Run shell' not in out and '▸ run_aaa' in out and 'import fastllm' not in out
assert all(len(l) <= 40 for l in out.splitlines())
print(out)

Passing the keys of the running sub-agent and the file in open shows the sub-agent’s calls and the diff:

out = show(busy, {('sub', 'run_aaa'), ('file', 'ramabana/pane.py')})
assert '▾ run_aaa' in out and '✓ Search code: import fastllm' in out and '+from teleprint.keys import Parser' in out
print(out)

In an open file the diff is drawn by hl.diff_rich in the pane’s palette. The code in each hunk is coloured by the file’s language, and added and removed lines get a tinted background. The cell checks that an added line carries more than two styles, so the code is highlighted and not drawn in one colour:

py = {**busy, 'files': [{'path': 'a.py', 'added': 1, 'removed': 1, 'diff': diff_text('x = 1\n', 'def f(): return 2\n', 'a.py')}]}
rows = [t for _, t in board(py, 40, now=now, open={('file', 'a.py')})]
added = next(t for t in rows if 'def f' in t.plain)
test_eq(added.plain, '  +def f(): return 2')
assert len({str(s.style) for s in added.spans}) > 2, 'the code is highlighted, not one colour'
added

title: pane
text:
The viewer
Viewer(path, tty) is the program that runs in the pane. It reads the snapshot at path and draws the board on tty. A tty is any object with read(timeout), write, size and restore, as teleprint’s RealTty has. PaneTty is RealTty with a read that returns None at the end of input, so the viewer can tell that its terminal has gone.
The viewer switches the terminal to the alternate screen, the separate screen full-screen programs use so that the shell’s scrollback comes back unchanged when they exit, and asks the terminal to report mouse clicks. Each tick waits up to every seconds for input and acts on it. The controls are:

A click opens or closes the row under it, and the mouse wheel scrolls.
j and k, or the arrow keys, move the cursor over the rows that open. Past the first or last such row they scroll, so a board taller than the pane can be read to its end.
Page up and page down scroll by a page, and g and G jump to the top and the bottom.
Enter or space opens or closes the row under the cursor.
p on a background shell command opens a tmux pane below this one that follows the command’s log with less +F. q closes it.
q or ctrl+c quits.

The last line of the pane is always HINT, so the main keys stay on screen however far the board scrolls.
The viewer reads the snapshot again only when its file has changed. It lays out the board on every tick but writes only the lines that differ from what is on screen, so a clock that moves once a second rewrites one line a second and a board that is not changing writes nothing. When the terminal changes size, the viewer clears it and draws everything again.
The viewer must keep running whatever a single frame does. If drawing fails, it keeps the last good snapshot and shows the error as a row until a good snapshot arrives. However it exits, it gives the terminal back its normal screen and modes. When the user quits, it leaves a file named by quit_mark beside the snapshot, now.closed. The terminal session checks for it, so it can tell a pane the user closed, which it leaves closed, from one that crashed. A hangup (tmux closing the pane), SIGTERM and the end of input count as quitting too.


source

Viewer
def Viewer(
    path, tty
):
The board for the snapshot at path, drawn on tty: the last good snapshot, the open rows, the cursor and the scroll.




source

PaneTty
def PaneTty():
RealTty whose read returns None at the end of input, where RealTty.read would spin.




source

quit_mark
def quit_mark(
    path
):
The file a viewer the user quit leaves beside the snapshot at path, so the CLI keeps it closed.


The example drives a Viewer with a test terminal, Tty, that replays scripted input and keeps everything written to it. A click on the running sub-agent opens it and puts the cursor there. A tick with nothing new writes nothing. Then j moves the cursor down, space opens run_bbb, and q quits:

class Tty:
    "A terminal for tests: scripted input chunks, a size, and every write kept."
    def __init__(self, *input, size=(40, 30)): self.input, self.size, self.writes = list(input), size, []
    def read(self, timeout=0): return self.input.pop(0).encode() if self.input else b''
    def write(self, s): self.writes.append(s)
    def restore(self): pass
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    (p := Path(d)/'now.json').write_text(json.dumps(busy))
    v = Viewer(p, Tty()); v.tick(now=now)
    y = next(i for i, (k, _) in enumerate(v.rows) if k == ('sub', 'run_aaa'))
    v.tty.input.append(f'\x1b[<0;3;{y + 1}M'); v.tick(now=now)
    test_eq((v.open, v.cursor), ({('sub', 'run_aaa')}, ('sub', 'run_aaa')))
    n = len(v.tty.writes); v.tick(now=now)
    test_eq(len(v.tty.writes), n)
    v.tty.input += ['j', ' ', 'q']
    for _ in range(3): v.tick(now=now)
    test_eq((v.cursor, v.open, v.done), (('sub', 'run_bbb'), {('sub', 'run_aaa'), ('sub', 'run_bbb')}, True))

main is the viewer’s command line: ramabana-pane PATH runs the viewer on the terminal it was started in. The terminal session starts it in a tmux split when you type /pane, and prints the command when there is no tmux, so you can run it in another terminal yourself. --every sets how long each tick waits for input.


source

main
def main(
    path:str, # the snapshot file the CLI writes
    every:float=0.2, # seconds to wait for input between frames
):
Show the now snapshot at path as a board until q or ctrl+c.

title: Write docs
text:
This page is one of the five skills that ship with Ramabana. A skill is a piece of markdown that the agent reads when a task calls for it, so that the guidance costs nothing in turns that do not need it. The system prompt lists every skill the session found with a one-line description, the read_skill tool returns one in full, and /skill write_docs prints it in a terminal session.
The skill’s text is this module’s docstring. nbdev builds it from the description line above and the exported markdown cell below, and pyproject.toml registers the module under the pyskills entry point as write_docs, so any agent built on shalya can find it once Ramabana is installed. To change what the agent reads, edit the exported cell.
The agent reads this skill before it writes the prose that ships with code: docstrings, comments, READMEs, changelogs, commit messages and pull request descriptions. Its companion write_prose covers narrative writing.
Read this before writing the prose that ships with code: docstrings, code comments, READMEs, API and reference docs, changelogs, PR descriptions, commit messages, and messages to a colleague. The register is GOV.UK/GDS house style with ASD-STE100’s discipline. Very plain, very direct, no author’s voice. Narrative prose has an author on the page; reference prose has only the contract. For blog posts, essays and announcements read write_prose instead.
Here is a passage from a design doc, written in this register:
Write like that. Each sentence states one fact and stops. Each guarantee is its own sentence. The negative guarantee is stated too: what the gateway never does. Every status is named by its real identifier. Sentences this uniform would read as monotone in an essay. In reference prose they are correct. Readers scan, take the fact they came for, and leave.
Here is the same passage before editing:
Do NOT write like that. Nothing in it is false. In a blog post it might pass. As reference prose it fails. Each sentence carries several facts. The key guarantee is an aside. The final state gets a flourish instead of its name. The opener announces the section instead of starting it. A question delays a fact the reader came for.
The numbers refer to the [bracketed] markers in both passages. Where a number appears in each, the pair is the failing and the working version of the same thing.
Entries 7 to 12, 14, 17, 22 and 24 to 26 are tells the passage pair is too short to show.
Instructions address the reader as “you”, in the imperative: “Run the tests”, not “The tests should be run”. Prefer active voice everywhere. A passive that hides the actor usually hides part of the contract with it.

title: Write docs
text:
Banned words
Always use the plainest word that is still correct: use, not “utilize” or “leverage”; improve, not “enhance” or “optimize” unless something is literally being optimized; complete, not “comprehensive”; strong, not “robust”; help, not “facilitate”.
Kill on sight: seamless, streamline, empower, foster, pivotal, “a testament to”, realm, landscape (metaphorical), navigate (metaphorical), delve, myriad, plethora, paradigm, synergy, holistic, catalyze, juxtapose, tapestry, embark, endeavor, encompass, multifaceted, elucidate, nuanced (as filler), minted (metaphorical). For “land”/“landed” say what happened: merged, committed, released, appears. For metaphorical “shape”/“shaped” say structure, format, or the actual event. “Invariant” is usually “rule” or “guarantee”. Compounds in “-bearing”, such as load-bearing, have plainer forms.

title: Write docs
text:
Doc types

Docstrings: the first line states what the function does, and for most functions it is the whole docstring. Parameter detail goes in docments, never repeated in prose. State inputs, outputs, errors raised and guarantees. Never restate the signature.
Code comments: only a constraint the code cannot show, per coding_patterns. Almost never.
READMEs: read like docstrings, not like blogs. The first paragraph says what the package does and for whom. Then install, then a minimal example. No journey, no sales language.
API docs and changelogs: the contract or the change, one entry per behaviour. Rationale goes in design docs.
PR descriptions and commit messages: lead with the behaviour change, name who did what, and give reviewers what they need to judge the diff.
Messages to a colleague: the answer first, support after. No softening preamble, no closing offer of further help.

title: Write docs
text:
Summaries
A summary of a conversation, a diff, a review thread or a paper has to say what is now true. It does not shorten the source in the source’s own order. Write from the situation the source describes. Six failures cover nearly all bad summaries.

Walking the source: reporting turn by turn, file by file, section by section. Order by subject instead. The reader never needed to know when something was said.
Topics without content: “we discussed the migration”, “this PR refactors the auth module”. A sentence that could have been written before reading the source says nothing about it. Cash every topic out in specifics or drop it.
Pointers to nowhere: “the approach discussed earlier”, “the second reviewer’s concern”. Every reference has to resolve inside the summary itself.
Claims with no owner: the reader cannot tell a fact from someone’s position from your own inference. Give every claim its owner, name people rather than anonymizing them, and mark your inferences as yours.
No status and no why: a thread reported without its current state, or a conclusion kept while the reason that supports it is dropped. State means decided, dropped or still open; merged, blocked or awaiting review. Gathering the reasons scattered across a long source is most of the work of summarizing, which is why lazy summaries lose them first.
Space by bulk and buried lede: length tracks the size of the source material instead of how much it changed the situation, and the biggest change arrives last because that is where the source got to it. Weight by importance. Put the largest change first.

A summary has to still work a week later with the source gone. Naming what the source introduced is part of that; reciting background the reader already holds is not.
Never hard-wrap prose. Write each paragraph as one continuous line and let the display soft-wrap it. Put code symbols in backticks: function names, parameters, file paths, module and package names, and literal syntax.
To have a draft checked, send these rules and the draft to a subagent with delegate_search. Name the audience, so tell 12 can be judged. Ask for flagged spans rather than a rewrite. Only do this when the user asks for a docs check.

title: core
text:
Ramabana reports a failure in one of two ways. AgentError is a refusal: something the harness will not do, with a message the user can act on, such as a write outside the open folders or a model whose key is missing. It is shalya’s HostError under another name, so a refusal from a tool and a refusal from the agent are caught the same way. Any other exception is a bug, and is left to look like one.
BranchChanged is the refusal raised when a git branch moved while a person was deciding whether to approve a write to it. Nothing was written.

agent_err(FileNotFoundError('nbs/99_missing.ipynb'))

env reads one setting from the environment. os.environ['LEELA_MODEL'] = 'opus'

'opus'



os.environ['RAMABANA_MODEL'] = 'sonnet'
test_eq(env('MODEL'), 'sonnet')
del os.environ['RAMABANA_MODEL'], os.environ['LEELA_MODEL']
env('MODEL', 'gemma-e4b')

'gemma-e4b'

title: core
text:
The model tables
MODELS is the table of short model names you can type, such as sonnet or gemma-e4b. Each name maps to a pair: the runtime that serves it, and the id that runtime knows the model by. It is built from smaller tables. LOCAL holds the LiteRT models, MLX the models for Apple silicon, LLAMA the llama.cpp models, CLOUD the OpenAI and Codex models, and the Claude tables come from the catalog in models.
JOBS lists every job the policy can route on its own: the turn, one-shot prompts, inline edits, code completion, classification, summaries, and sub-agents. ONESHOT_JOBS are the jobs that send one prompt and read one answer back.
claude_ctx gives a Claude model’s context window, the number of tokens it can read at once. claude_wire gives the id to ask Claude Code for, which carries a [1m] suffix for the models that have a million-token window.


source

title: core
text:
Probing the machine
Some questions are about this machine: whether a runtime is installed, which models an API key can list, which models a Copilot plan reaches. Each answer takes too long for a model picker to wait on, and changes rarely enough that the last answer is usually still right. probed(key, fn) remembers these answers. Use it for any slow question whose last answer is good enough to show.

The first call runs fn() and returns its answer.
Later calls return the remembered answer at once. When it is older than ttl seconds, a background thread asks again, and a later call gets the new answer.
The answer is also saved to a file under ~/.config/ramabana/probes, so the next run of the program has a value on its first call. Pass disk=False to keep it in memory only.

forget_probes drops every remembered answer, for a refresh button. forget_probes(disk=True) deletes the files too. The hidden test below walks through each case.
