Extras
The core install is the agent, its hosts, and the file, code, shell and git tools. Each extra, such as ramabana[search], adds the packages for one more use. installed says whether a module would import, without importing it. need(extra, *mods) returns an empty string when the packages are present, and otherwise the sentence telling the user what to install, so a command that needs an extra can refuse with something useful. Azure OpenAI
Azure OpenAI needs AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT, the resource such as https://NAME.openai.azure.com, and AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY. config.toml’s [azure] table can hold the endpoint instead, as endpoint, and name another env var for the key with api_key_env; the key itself never goes in the file. for u in ('https://r.openai.azure.com', 'r.openai.azure.com/', 'https://r.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/', 'https://r.openai.azure.com/openai/deployments/x/chat/completions?api-version=2024-10-21'):

text:
Configurable models
register_model adds a short name of your own to the tables for the rest of this process. Use it for a model the tables do not list. A Hugging Face URL is enough, because rishi works out which runtime serves it. unregister_model removes it.

    name

Remove one process-local configurable model alias.

def register_model(
    name, model_id, runtime:NoneType=None, ctx:int=128000, note:str='custom model', **config
):
Add a model name that lasts until this process exits; save_model keeps one on disk.


A name added with register_model is gone after a restart. save_model keeps one in a file, and every application that offers its own names needs the same file, so the file is handled here:

save_model(row) checks a row, registers it, and writes it to the file.
load_models() reads the file at startup, registers every row that still resolves, and skips the rest.
delete_model(name) removes a name from the file and from this process.
saved_models() returns the rows on disk.

A row holds name, model_id, runtime and ctx. A row for the remote runtime may also name an endpoint with base_url, vendor_name and api_name, and the environment variable that holds its key with api_key_env. The file never holds a key. path names the application’s own file and defaults to ~/.config/ramabana/models.json.

Point every alias call that names no file at an application’s own, as use_env_prefix does for env vars.


config.toml can define a model as well as correct one. A [model."NAME"] table with model_id registers NAME for this process, for [jobs], --model and /model, with the same base_url, api_key_env, api_name, vendor_name and runtime a saved alias carries; ctx is another name for max_input_tokens. The runtime is remote when any of those API settings is given. On an Azure host, api_name defaults to openai, the Responses API, and api_key_env to AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY. A table that names a built-in model, a runtime nobody knows or a runtime that is missing here is ignored with one warning, which model_problems() and Agent.problems repeat. Nothing raises.
sync_models() registers the application’s saved aliases and then config.toml’s definitions, and does it again whenever either file changes. resolve, available_models and Routing call it, so the terminal session, ramabana-mcp, ramabana-acp, a headless run and an embedding app all see the same names without a call at startup. A name defined in both places is config.toml’s: load_models skips it and save_model refuses it. An application with its own alias file points the calls that name no file at it with use_aliases(path).

title: core
text:
Listing models
available_models builds the list a model picker shows. Each row names a model this process can actually run. The on-device models appear when their runtime is installed, ollama’s models when its daemon answers, and a vendor’s models only when the credential for it exists. The hosted lists come from provider_models in models. copilot_catalog is the model list for your Copilot plan, which the Copilot server reports and probed remembers for five minutes. A model config.toml defines appears with source config.toml once it can run.


source

    include_legacy:bool=False
):
Models selectable here, with older generations only when include_legacy.




source

def copilot_catalog(
    ttl:int=300
):
Copilot’s catalogue for this account, cached: {id: entry}, or {} when it cannot be reached.


Each row has a value to pass to resolve, a label to show, its provider, and the source that made it available, which the picker shows beside it. This check stands in a fake Copilot plan with one chat model:

_orig_avail, _orig_cat = _copilot_available, copilot_catalog
_copilot_available = lambda: True
copilot_catalog = lambda ttl=300: {'test-chat': {'capabilities': {'type': 'chat'}}}
try:
    rows = available_models()
    test_eq([r['value'] for r in rows if r['provider'] == 'litert'], list(LOCAL))
    test_eq([r['value'] for r in rows if r['provider'] == 'copilot'], ['copilot/test-chat'])

Older model generations, such as gpt-4.1, are left out unless you ask for them with include_legacy=True:

names = {r['value'] for r in available_models()}
legacy = {r['value'] for r in available_models(include_legacy=True)}
test_eq(names - legacy, set())
sorted(legacy - names)

['openai/gpt-4.1', 'openai/gpt-4.1-mini', 'openai/gpt-4.1-nano']

title: core
text:
Defaults and context windows
Every default route is a hosted model:



job
default model
through




turn
claude-opus-5-5
Claude Code


subagent
claude-sonnet-5-5
Claude Code


oneshot, inline, summary
gpt-6-luna
a Codex login


completion, classify
claude-haiku-5-5
Claude Code



DEFAULT_POLICY leaves turn empty, so that $RAMABANA_MODEL or DFLT_TURN fills it, and leaves inline empty, so that it follows oneshot. A model on this machine runs the turn only when you name it with --model, /model or $RAMABANA_MODEL. Once you do, the other jobs follow the turn onto the machine. DFLT_LOCAL, qwen-4b, is the local model to suggest; it is never a route unless named.
When none of the hosted models for a job can run here, the job moves to DFLT_FALLBACK, Gemma 4 E4B on LiteRT, rather than failing. The turn never moves. Changing models in the middle of a conversation is your decision, not a default.
A local model’s context window is the size Ramabana uses, which can be smaller than the size it was trained with, because a larger window costs memory and time. local_ctx gives that size: $RAMABANA_LOCAL_CTX first, then config.toml’s max_input_tokens for that model and its window.local_ctx, then the table. The engine still caps it at the size the model was trained with. local_window reads the trained size from the model’s own config, for the runtimes that publish it.


source

local_ctx
def local_ctx(
    name, dflt:int=32768

The context window to use for local model name: $RAMABANA_LOCAL_CTX if it sets one, then config.toml’s [model."NAME"] and window.local_ctx, else the table.

A local model’s trained context window from its own config, else 0.


Every job has an entry in the default policy, so a new job cannot be added without deciding where it runs:

test_eq(set(JOBS) - set(DEFAULT_POLICY), set())

local_ctx('gemma-e4b'), local_ctx('gemma-12b'), local_ctx('a-model-nobody-tabled')

(16384, 16384, 32768)



os.environ['RAMABANA_LOCAL_CTX'] = 'gemma-e4b:4096'

test_eq(local_ctx('gemma-12b'), 16_384)
del os.environ['RAMABANA_LOCAL_CTX']
local_ctx('gemma-e4b')

16384

title: core
text:
Resolving a model
resolve(name) turns a model name into a ModelSpec: the runtime, the model id, the context window, any runtime options, and a note for the user. Every place that needs to run a model calls it, and code further down accepts the ModelSpec rather than resolving the name again. A runtime that is not installed here does not raise: the spec comes back with missing saying which binary or package is absent and how to get it, the same way a missing API key is left for Agent.start to report. missing_runtime(spec) asks the same question live, and Agent.start turns the answer into a failed turn that names a model that does run here, from available_models. resolve raises KeyError with the closest known names for a name it cannot place.
azure/DEPLOYMENT names an Azure OpenAI deployment on the v1 API of azure_endpoint(), with the key in azure_key_env(), through the Responses API. It resolves whether or not the deployment is listed. A deployment named for a model fastllm knows, such as gpt-5.4, gets that model’s window and briefing; any other name gets 128k and a note saying which [model."azure/NAME"] entry corrects it.
A hosted model’s window comes from fastllm’s table, which can be out of date. A [model."NAME"] table in config.toml corrects it on this machine: max_input_tokens replaces the window, max_output_tokens becomes the reply cap the chat is started with, and supports_images answers accepts(spec, 'image'). The route name you chose the model by wins over its model id.
spec_caps and accepts say what a resolved model can be sent, such as images or audio. A model rishi knows nothing about counts as accepting everything. model_note describes a spec in one line for a status bar.


source

ModelSpec

    name:str, runtime:str, model_id:str, ctx:int=128000, note:str='', opts:dict=<factory>, missing:str=''

urai’s ModelSpec, with backend and config as views of runtime and opts.

resolve('gemma-e4b')

spec = resolve('claude/claude-sonnet-5')
test_eq(spec.backend, 'claude')
test_eq(spec.local, False)
assert isinstance(spec, urai.ModelSpec) and spec.runtime == spec.backend and spec.opts is spec.config
test_eq(set(RUNTIME_NAMES), set(urai.RUNTIMES)); assert 'ollama' in RUNTIME_NAMES
test_eq({r for r in RUNTIME_NAMES if ModelSpec('x', r, 'x').local}, {k for k, v in urai.RUNTIMES.items() if v.local})
assert ModelSpec('fake', 'fake', 'fake/model').local
model_note(spec)

if runtime_available('mlx'):
    spec = resolve('mlx-community/a-model-nobody-tabled')
    test_eq((spec.backend, spec.model_id), ('mlx', 'mlx-community/a-model-nobody-tabled'))
else:
    assert 'mlx runtime is unavailable (mlx_lm is not installed)' in resolve('mlx-community/a-model-nobody-tabled').missing
test_eq(resolve('somevendor/some-model').backend, 'remote')
test_fail(lambda: resolve('gpt-image-2'), contains='unknown model')

The tables list what the picker offers, not everything that runs. A Claude id the tables have moved past, such as claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-4-6 or opus-5, still resolves to the Claude Code runtime with the id passed through. A saved session or a pinned setting keeps working, and Claude Code decides whether it still serves that id. Any other unknown name is taken as a typo, and fails where it was typed rather than in the middle of a turn.

_orig_ra = runtime_available
runtime_available = lambda rt: rt == 'claude' or _orig_ra(rt)
try:
    for old in ('claude-opus-5', 'claude-sonnet-4-6', 'claude-haiku-4-5', 'claude-opus-4-8', 'claude-sonnet-5', 'claude-fable-5-1'):
        spec = resolve(old)
        test_eq((spec.backend, spec.model_id), ('claude', old))
    test_eq(resolve('opus-5').model_id, 'claude-opus-5')
    for full in ('claude/claude-opus-5', 'claude/claude-opus-4-8', 'claude/claude-haiku-4-5', 'claude/opus-5', 'claude/sonnet', 'claude/haiku', 'claude/claude-fable-5-1'):
        bare = full.split('/', 1)[1]
        test_eq(resolve(full).model_id, CLAUDE_ALIASES.get(bare, bare))
    test_eq(resolve('opus').model_id, CLAUDE_ALIASES['opus'])
    test_eq([r['label'] for r in available_models() if r['provider'] == 'claude'], list(CATALOG['claude']))
finally: runtime_available = _orig_ra
test_fail(lambda: resolve('gpt-9'), contains='unknown model')

Copilot needs its own runtime. If copilot/gpt-5.5 were handed to remote, rishi would read copilot as a prefix it knows and drop it, and send the bare gpt-5.5 to OpenAI on your OpenAI key. The turn would work, and the charge would land on the wrong account. So resolve handles the copilot/ prefix itself. The Copilot model list is asked for rather than written into a table, because it depends on the plan and changes often, and each entry carries the context window Copilot allows:

_cat = {'gpt-5.5': {'capabilities': {'type': 'chat', 'limits': {'max_prompt_tokens': 272000}}},
        'claude-opus-4.7': {'capabilities': {'type': 'chat', 'limits': {'max_context_window_tokens': 264000}}},
        'text-embedding-3-small': {'capabilities': {'type': 'embeddings'}}}
_orig_avail, _orig_cat = _copilot_available, copilot_catalog
_copilot_available, copilot_catalog = (lambda: True), (lambda ttl=300: _cat)
try:
    test_eq(runtime_available('copilot'), True)
    test_eq(auth_status()['copilot']['available'], True)

    spec = resolve('copilot/gpt-5.5')
    test_eq(spec.runtime, 'copilot')
    test_eq(spec.model_id, 'gpt-5.5')
    test_eq(spec.local, False)
    test_eq(spec.ctx, 272000)
    test_eq(resolve('copilot/claude-opus-4.7').ctx, 264000)

    assert resolve('copilot/gpt-6-unreleased').ctx > 0

    rows = [r for r in available_models() if r['provider'] == 'copilot']
    test_eq({r['value'] for r in rows}, {'copilot/gpt-5.5', 'copilot/claude-opus-4.7'})
    assert all(r['label'] and r['source'] for r in rows)

finally: _copilot_available, copilot_catalog = _orig_avail, _orig_cat

_copilot_available = lambda: False
try: assert 'sign in to Copilot' in resolve('copilot/gpt-5.5').missing
finally: _copilot_available = _orig_avail

title: core
text:
What a model can afford
Before a turn, the agent sends the model a briefing: the system prompt with the project’s rules, the tool schemas, and sometimes the full text of a skill. On a small context window this fills most of the space before any work starts. On a full host the tool schemas cost about 4.7k tokens, an inlined skill 3k more, and the briefing 1.4k, which leaves a 16k model room for about one tool result.
budget_for(spec, tool_max) sizes the briefing to the model’s window and returns a Budget. For a window above 24k tokens the budget changes nothing except the cap on each tool result. For a smaller window it drops the memory and web tool groups, stops inlining skill text, and clips each tool result harder. It only holds things back: a skill it does not inline is still one read_skill call away. With channel='tags' it first subtracts the tokens the tool schemas will take inside the prompt (see below).


source

budget_for
def budget_for(
    spec, tool_max, channel:str='native'
):
A window-sized budget; tool_max=None selects an automatic cap up to 32000 characters.




source

Budget
def Budget(
    drop:tuple=(), inline:bool=True, tool_max:int=0, note:str=''
)->None:
What a model can afford to be told, and to be sent back.


The window decides what a model has room for. It does not decide what a model can follow. Given thirty-six tool schemas and a five-thousand-token briefing, a 4B model picks the wrong tool or none, however large its window. The profile makes that second choice:

small offers the fourteen tools in SMALL_TOOLS, which cover a coding turn, and a one-screen briefing.
full offers everything.
auto picks small for a model on this machine or a window of 32k tokens or less, and full otherwise. A model whose window is unknown counts as full.

profile_for(spec, profile) makes the choice, and the budget above still sizes the tool results. The first cell below checks the profile, the next two the budget:


source

profile_for
def profile_for(
    spec, profile:str='auto'
):
Resolve profile for spec: auto is small for a local or small-window model.

title: core
text:
Where the tool schemas travel
A tool schema tells the model what a tool is called and what arguments it takes. There are two ways to send them. The native channel uses the model API’s own tool field: the API checks the schemas, and tool calls come back as structured data. The tags channel, rishi’s tool_mode='tags', writes the schemas into the system prompt and reads tool calls back out of the reply text, written as Hermes-style tags. The local engines have always worked this way, which is why parse_tool_tags exists.
Native is better wherever it is open, but it is not always open. Claude Code receives tools as an in-process MCP server, and a company-managed Claude Code configuration can forbid every MCP server it did not approve. Without the tags channel, that policy would leave the agent unable to read a file. Rishi uses the native channel for Claude Code where its SDK can, and tags in the CLI or wherever the server is refused.
tool_channel(spec, chat) returns 'native' or 'tags'. It is the one place that picks. $RAMABANA_TOOL_CHANNEL overrides everything. Otherwise it asks the open chat, which knows which channel it ended up on, and without a chat it predicts from the spec: tags for Claude Code, and tags for a model that force_tags marked because a request refused its schemas. forget_forced_tags clears those marks so the native channel is tried again. budget_for takes the channel as an argument because the schemas cost prompt tokens on the tags channel.

The channel (‘native’ or ‘tags’) a model’s tool schemas travel on.

title: core
text:
Routing
Routing decides which model runs each job. It is the only place that does. Build one with the turn model you want, or leave it out to use $RAMABANA_MODEL, then turn in config.toml’s [jobs], then DFLT_TURN. name_for(job) gives the model name for a job, and spec(job) resolves it to a ModelSpec ready to run. To give one job a model of its own, set $RAMABANA_MODEL_<JOB>, name it in config.toml’s [jobs] (the env var wins), call set(name, job), or type /model JOB NAME in a session. A job with no entry in the policy uses the turn’s model, so adding a job to JOBS never leaves a caller with nothing.
When the turn runs on this machine, every job without a model of its own stays on it too, sub-agents included, so nothing leaves the machine.
When a job’s model cannot run here, spec moves the job to another hosted route it already knows, and never to a local model nobody named. When claude-haiku-5-5 cannot run, it tries claude-sonnet-5-5 first. alternatives(job) lists the routes in the order they are tried, ending with DFLT_FALLBACK. A hosted model whose key is missing counts as one that cannot run, for every job but the turn; the turn’s missing key is reported by Agent.start. A model whose answer failed or came back empty is set aside for DOWN_TTL, five minutes. Each move is written to notes, keyed by job, and news holds one line per model that fell, for the chat to show once. When no route is left, the error names the job, the model, and the key or command it needs. missing_key and needs build that part of the message.
A machine with no Claude Code and no Codex login cannot run the defaults, and nothing is chosen in their place: Ramabana asks for a provider instead. PROVIDERS lists the ones it can use and what each needs, provider_ready says which are set up here, and needs_setup(routing) says why the turn’s model cannot run, a missing runtime or a missing key, or nothing. setup_guide puts it together for a person: the providers, then each job, the model it runs on, where that was chosen (job_source: an env var, config.toml, the turn it follows, or the default) and whether it can run. The terminal prints it before a session whose turn cannot run, and ramabana setup adds a provider.
AWS Bedrock is reached through its OpenAI-compatible Mantle endpoint, https://bedrock-mantle.<region>.api.aws/v1, with a Bedrock API key in AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK sent as a bearer token; such keys are often short-lived, so renew them as AWS says. Model ids are Bedrock’s own, such as openai.gpt-5.4, and their windows come from fastllm’s bedrock_mantle table. Bedrock’s native Converse and InvokeModel APIs, and with them Claude on Bedrock, are not supported: fastllm has no SigV4 signing, no AWS credential chain or profile, and no Converse wire format.
image_route is the image job, which generate_image draws with: $RAMABANA_MODEL_IMAGE, config.toml’s [jobs] image, or DFLT_IMAGE, OpenAI’s gpt-image-1. It gives the endpoint, key and model of an OpenAI-shaped images API, such as an Azure deployment of gpt-image-1, or a sentence saying what to set up; Bedrock’s Mantle endpoint and OpenRouter have no images endpoint.
video_route is the video job in the same way: $RAMABANA_MODEL_VIDEO, config.toml’s [jobs] video, or DFLT_VIDEO, Google’s Veo 3. It gives api, gemini for Gemini’s long-running predictLongRunning API or openai for an OpenAI-shaped /videos API such as sora-2 on OpenAI or Azure, with the endpoint, key and model id. A model fastllm knows to return no video is refused, as is a local model or a host with no video endpoint, and each refusal says what to set up. video_route(name) resolves one named model, so a job started earlier is polled with the key it was started with.

With a hosted turn, completion and classification go to claude-haiku-5-5, one-shot prompts and summaries to gpt-6-luna, and sub-agents to claude-sonnet-5-5. With a local turn, every job stays on the turn’s model:

r.name_for('turn'), r.name_for('summary'), r.name_for('completion')

('sonnet', 'gpt-6-luna', 'claude-haiku-5-5')

test_eq(Routing().alternatives('classify')[0], DFLT_SUBAGENT)
test_eq(Routing().alternatives('classify')[-1], DFLT_FALLBACK)
test_eq(missing_key(ModelSpec('g', 'remote', 'gemini/x', 1)), '' if os.environ.get('GEMINI_API_KEY') else 'GEMINI_API_KEY')

set resolves the name before storing it, so a misspelled model fails at the /model command instead of during the next turn:

title: models
text:
CATALOG maps each provider to the model ids a picker offers before anything is asked over the network, in display order.

claude is what Claude Code’s --model accepts: the tier names fable, opus, sonnet and haiku, which follow the newest model of each family, then the full ids.
anthropic is the same models through the Anthropic API.
openai and gemini are the models offered through those APIs.
codex is what Codex’s own picker lists.

claude_ids returns the full Claude ids without the tier names. claude_aliases maps each tier name to the id it means here, which is the last id of that family in CATALOG. Adding a newer Opus to the end of the list moves opus to it.

title: models
text:
Live discovery
Each provider that can be asked for its models has one function in LIVE. The function returns the ids the provider lists, or [] when it cannot ask: no key, no file, no network, or an answer it cannot read. It never raises.

openai_ids asks OpenAI’s /v1/models with $OPENAI_API_KEY.
anthropic_ids asks Anthropic’s /v1/models with $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. It serves both anthropic and claude, since Claude Code runs the same models.
codex_ids asks no server. Codex keeps its picker list in models_cache.json under $CODEX_HOME, which defaults to ~/.codex, and the entries marked visibility: 'list' are the ones it offers. The test below writes a small cache file and reads it back.

title: models
section: What a live listing may add
text:
What a live listing may add
A provider’s listing holds everything it serves: dated snapshots, fine-tunes, realtime and audio models, embeddings, moderation, image and search models. A picker wants none of these. _current decides which listed ids a picker may show. It hides an id by what kind of model it is, not by which generation it belongs to, so a new generation shows up the day the provider lists it. Older chat generations (gpt-4*, gpt-3.5*, claude-2-* and claude-3-*) appear only with legacy=True. The cell below lists ids it keeps, ids it always hides, and ids it shows only with legacy.

for ok in ('gpt-6-astra', 'gpt-7', 'o5-mini', 'claude-fable-5-1', 'claude-haiku-4-5-20251001', 'gemini-3.5-flash'): assert _current('openai', ok), ok
for hidden in ('gpt-6-astra-2026-09-01', 'gpt-3.5-turbo-0125', 'ft:gpt-3.5-turbo-0125:org::abc', 'ada:ft-org-2023-04-06-20-44-19', 'gpt-realtime', 'gpt-6-audio', 'gpt-image-2', 'gpt-6-transcribe', 'tts-1', 'gpt-live-1', 'gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct', 'text-embedding-4', 'omni-moderation-latest', 'dall-e-3', 'whisper-1', 'davinci-002', 'babbage-002', 'sora-2', 'computer-use-preview', 'gpt-5-search-api', 'gpt-4o-search-preview', 'o3-deep-research', 'chat-latest', ''):
    assert not _current('openai', hidden), hidden
    assert not _current('openai', hidden, legacy=True), hidden
for old in ('gpt-4.1', 'gpt-4o', 'gpt-3.5-turbo', 'claude-3-5-haiku-latest'):
    assert not _current('openai', old) and _current('openai', old, legacy=True), old

title: models
text:
What a picker offers
provider_models(p) is the list a picker shows for provider p. It starts with the CATALOG ids in their order, then adds the ids from the live listing that _current admits and that are not dated snapshots, newest first by version number, with nothing repeated. The live answer is remembered for five minutes with ramabana.core.probed. If the listing fails, the result is the catalog alone. A provider that is neither in CATALOG nor in LIVE gives [].
The first cell below stands in a fake OpenAI listing. The second makes every listing fail. The third fakes Anthropic’s endpoint and shows that claude and anthropic share one request.


source

provider_models
def provider_models(
    p, legacy:bool=False, ttl:int=300
):
Ids a picker offers for provider p: the curated ones in their order, then what live discovery adds.



from ramabana.core import forget_probes
_orig = dict(LIVE)
forget_probes()
LIVE['openai'] = lambda: ['gpt-6-astra', 'gpt-6-nova', 'gpt-6-nova-2026-09-01', 'gpt-6-audio', 'gpt-4.1']
try:
    got = provider_models('openai')
    test_eq(got[:len(CATALOG['openai'])], list(CATALOG['openai']))
    test_eq(got[len(CATALOG['openai']):], ['gpt-6-nova'])
    test_eq(got.count('gpt-6-astra'), 1)
    assert 'gpt-4.1' in provider_models('openai', legacy=True)
    # newest first, by the numbers: alphabetical put gpt-6.1 after every gpt-5
    forget_probes(); LIVE['openai'] = lambda: ['gpt-5.1', 'gpt-6.1-nova', 'gpt-5.10']
    test_eq(provider_models('openai')[len(CATALOG['openai']):], ['gpt-6.1-nova', 'gpt-5.10', 'gpt-5.1'])
finally: LIVE.clear(); LIVE.update(_orig); forget_probes()


def _boom(): raise OSError('no network')
forget_probes()
LIVE.update({p: _boom for p in LIVE})
try:
    for p in CATALOG: test_eq(provider_models(p)[:len(CATALOG[p])], list(CATALOG[p]))
finally: LIVE.clear(); LIVE.update(_orig); forget_probes()
test_eq(provider_models('nobody'), [])


_n, _key, _lst = [], os.environ.get('ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'), _listed
def _fake(*a, **kw): _n.append(1); return ['claude-sonnet-6', 'claude-sonnet-6-20270101', 'claude-sonnet-5-5']
forget_probes(); os.environ['ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'] = 'k'; _listed = _fake
try:
    got = provider_models('claude')
    test_eq(got[:len(CATALOG['claude'])], list(CATALOG['claude']))
    test_eq(got[len(CATALOG['claude']):], ['claude-sonnet-6'])
    assert 'claude-sonnet-6' in provider_models('anthropic') and len(_n) == 1
    forget_probes(); del os.environ['ANTHROPIC_API_KEY']
    test_eq(provider_models('claude'), list(CATALOG['claude']))
finally:
    _listed = _lst; forget_probes()
    if _key is None: os.environ.pop('ANTHROPIC_API_KEY', None)
    else: os.environ['ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'] = _key

title: models
text:
Through available_models
ramabana.core.available_models builds its hosted rows from provider_models, and includes a provider only when runtime_available and auth_status say it can be used here. Each row has a value, label, provider and source. With a fake OpenAI key and listing, the OpenAI rows are the catalog followed by the one new model:

import ramabana.models as _m
from ramabana.core import available_models, CLAUDE, CLAUDE_ALIASES, CLAUDE_MODELS
_orig_live, _key = dict(_m.LIVE), os.environ.get('OPENAI_API_KEY')
forget_probes()
_m.LIVE.update({'openai': lambda: ['gpt-6-astra', 'gpt-6-nova', 'gpt-6-nova-2026-09-01', 'gpt-6-audio'], 'anthropic': lambda: [], 'codex': lambda: []})
os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY'] = 'sk-not-a-real-key'
try:
    rows = available_models()
    test_eq({tuple(sorted(r)) for r in rows}, {('label', 'provider', 'source', 'value')})
    openai = [r['label'] for r in rows if r['provider'] == 'openai']
    test_eq(openai, [*CATALOG['openai'], 'gpt-6-nova'])
    test_eq([r['value'] for r in rows if r['provider'] == 'openai'][0], 'openai/gpt-6-astra')
finally:
    _m.LIVE.clear(); _m.LIVE.update(_orig_live); forget_probes()
    if _key is None: del os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY']
    else: os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY'] = _key
test_eq(CLAUDE_MODELS, claude_ids())
assert {'claude-fable-5-1', 'claude-opus-5-5'} <= set(CLAUDE_MODELS)
test_eq(CLAUDE_ALIASES['fable'], 'claude-fable-5-1')
test_eq(CLAUDE['claude/opus'], 'claude-opus-5-5')

title: mcp
text:
server builds the MCP server. Pass a host to serve its tools. Pass an agent as well and the server mounts the agent’s own tools, the same objects a turn gets, so a client’s calls appear in the same activity feed and changes() report as a turn’s. Agent._record wraps each tool with functools.wraps, which keeps its signature and docstring, and FastMCP builds each tool’s schema from those. A tool is therefore described in one place, and the description a client sees cannot drift from the one a model sees. Without an agent, the server builds the tools from the host with tools_for.
readonly defaults to True because the client is another agent, and this server cannot put an approval prompt in front of the client’s user. Read-only leaves out every write tool. The read tools stay, and so do acting tools such as inspect_python and generate_image. readonly=False mounts the write tools too, and then the client’s own approval settings are what stands in front of them. delegate=False leaves out ask even when an agent is given, and any other keyword goes to FastMCP.
INSTRUCTIONS is the text the server sends a client when it connects. It tells the client’s model how to read and edit through these tools.


source


def server(
    host:NoneType=None, agent:NoneType=None, name:str='ramabana', readonly:bool=True, delegate:bool=True, **kw
):
An MCP server over one host’s tools, and optionally over Ramabana’s own agent.


Below is a server over FullHost, a test host from testing that declares the code, file, git, memory, notebook, session, shell and web groups. The server is read-only by default, so replace_text and create_file are absent. Without an agent it also mounts shalya’s legacy group (list_files, list_vars and others) for one release, so that a client written against version 0.1 keeps working. edit_file belongs to the opt-in exhash group and is not mounted.

host = FullHost(files={'pkg/sizes.py': 'RESERVE = 16_384\n\ndef threshold(ctx):\n    return ctx - RESERVE\n'})
mcp = server(host)
tools = await mcp.list_tools()
[t.name for t in tools]


test_eq(set(t.name for t in tools) & WRITE_TOOLS, set())
test_eq('view_file' in [t.name for t in tools], True)
assert 'list_files' in [t.name for t in tools] and 'edit_file' not in [t.name for t in tools]
len(tools)

Each tool arrives with the schema FastMCP derived from the function itself. The description is the docstring a model reads in a turn, and the parameters come from the type annotations.

t = next(t for t in tools if t.name == 'view_file')
t.description.splitlines()[0], t.inputSchema['properties'], t.annotations.readOnlyHint

MCP tool annotations tell a client which calls only read, which are destructive, and which reach the open world, meaning the web and API tools. _annotate sets them from the same catalog entry that approvals and the activity feed use. A client can use them to decide which calls to ask its user about. This server is built with readonly=False, so replace_text is there to compare.

mcp_w = server(host, readonly=False)
{t.name: (t.annotations.readOnlyHint, t.annotations.destructiveHint, t.annotations.openWorldHint)
 for t in await mcp_w.list_tools() if t.name in ('view_file', 'replace_text', 'web_search')}

Calling a tool goes through the same code path as a turn, and the client gets back exactly the text the model would get. view_file returns one lineno|hash|content line per line of the file.

out = await mcp.call_tool('view_file', {'path': 'pkg/sizes.py'})
print(out[0][0].text if isinstance(out, tuple) else out)

A write tool left out of a read-only server is absent from the MCP surface, and calling its name returns an error. The last line lists the write tools that readonly=False mounts.

with expect_fail(contains='Unknown tool'): await mcp.call_tool('replace_text', {'path': 'pkg/sizes.py', 'edits': []})
with expect_fail(contains='Unknown tool'): await mcp.call_tool('edit_file', {'path': 'pkg/sizes.py', 'commands': []})
[t.name for t in await mcp_w.list_tools() if t.name in WRITE_TOOLS]

title: mcp
text:
Skills as resources
Skills are offered as resources, not tools. A resource is text a client can read, where a tool is a call that may have an effect. The server publishes three kinds:

ramabana://skills, an index of every skill with its one-line description of when it applies
skill://{name}, one skill in full, the same text read_skill returns in a turn
ramabana://status, a JSON summary of the open folders, the mounted tools, the skills and, with an agent, the agent’s status

A client reads the index and fetches only the skill it needs, the same saving read_skill gives a model in a turn. Without an agent, the server finds skills in the served folders and in ~/.agents/skills.

[str(r.uriTemplate) for r in await mcp.list_resource_templates()] + [str(r.uri) for r in await mcp.list_resources()]


print((await mcp.read_resource('ramabana://status'))[0].content[:200])

title: mcp
text:
The agent as one tool
With an agent passed in, the server also offers ask, which runs a whole Ramabana turn behind one call. The client sends one task and gets back one answer. The tool loop, the tool results and any compaction of the history happen on this side, and the client never sees them. Below, fake_agent from testing supplies an agent with a scripted reply, so the example needs no model.

agent, be = fake_agent(replies=['`threshold` is defined in pkg/sizes.py, and subtracts the reserve.'])
full = server(agent.host, agent)
[t.name for t in await full.list_tools() if t.name == 'ask']


out = await full.call_tool('ask', {'task': 'where is the threshold defined?'})
out[0][0].text if isinstance(out, tuple) else out

ask runs the turn on a worker thread, because a turn blocks and an MCP server is asynchronous. The client’s one call sent the agent’s backend one message.

test_eq(len(be.sent), 1)
(await full.read_resource('ramabana://status'))[0].content[:60]

title: mcp
text:
Running it
ramabana-mcp is the command-line entry point, main. It splits --root into folders and serves them over --transport, which is stdio by default. --model builds a full agent on that model and turns on the ask tool. Without it there is nothing to hand a task to, so the server offers tools only. --write mounts the write tools, and the other options build the host the way the terminal does.
The agent behind ask is built with approve='none', which means no approval gate at all, so the turn ask runs may use the agent’s write tools without asking anyone. --write decides only which tools the client may call directly.


source

main
def main(
    root:str='.', # comma-separated folders to serve
    model:str=None, # model for `ask`; omit to serve tools only
    write:bool=False, # mount the write tools too
    web:bool=True, # let web tools reach the network via fossick
    read_outside:bool=False, # reads may name any path; writes stay inside
    vault:bool=False, # keep reads in a vishalakshi vault
    pii:str='off', # off | redact | refuse PII from the vault
    pii_ner:bool=False, # --pii also gates titled names, not only patterns
    transport:str='stdio', # stdio | sse | streamable-http
    cfg:str=None, # config dir, for skills and extensions
):
Serve Ramabana tools over MCP.


A client that launches its own servers takes the command and its arguments. Over a repository, with ask running on a local model, that is:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ramabana": {
      "command": "ramabana-mcp",
      "args": ["--root", "/path/to/repo", "--model", "qwen-4b"]
    }
  }
}
Start with the default, read-only tools and no model:
ramabana-mcp --root .

title: testing
text:
A ModelSpec describes one model: its name, the runtime that serves it, the model id and the context window in tokens (ctx). The two specs here differ mainly in that window. SPEC has 1,000 tokens, small enough that compaction arithmetic can be checked by hand. Compaction is how the agent keeps a long conversation inside the window: it replaces older messages with a summary. SCRIPTED has 8,000 tokens, so compaction never fires in the middle of a recorded demo.

SPEC, SCRIPTED.ctx

title: testing
text:
A host in memory
MemHost keeps the project’s files in a dict keyed by absolute path, and the file and search tools read and write that dict instead of the disk.
A host says what it can do by the classes it inherits. Each capability class, such as CodeHost for code search or ShellHost for running commands, names a capability group, and tools_for(host) builds the tools of every group the host declares. MemHost starts from NullHost, which declares only the file group and offers a lone view_file, and adds CodeHost and ShellHost. Every other group, the live Python session among them, contributes no tools. Checking that a missing group really removes its tools is one of the main uses of this class.
commands scripts the shell. It maps a command string to (exit_code, output). A command not in the dict exits 0 with no output, and every command that runs is appended to host.cmds. The cell below builds a host with two files.


source

MemHost
def MemHost(
    files:NoneType=None, root:str='/proj', commands:NoneType=None
):
A host whose folders live in a dict, so the file tools never touch disk.



host = MemHost({'/proj/a.py': 'def a(): return 1\n', '/proj/b.py': 'def b(): return a() + 1\n'})
host.roots, host.walk()

search is a plain substring scan, but it returns Hit objects, the same type a real code index returns, so code that formats search results sees the usual shape.

host.search('return a'), host.search_note

write stores text in the dict and text_at reads it back, with an empty string for a file that does not exist. That is all Agent.changes() needs to report which files a turn edited, so it can be tested against this host.

host.write('/proj/c.py', 'def c(): pass\n')
host.text_at('/proj/c.py'), host.text_at('/proj/never.py')

run_python records the code instead of running it, so a test can check what the agent tried to run without starting a kernel. A test has to call the method directly. MemHost does not declare the session group, so tools_for gives the model no run_python tool for it, as the second cell checks. host.provides lists the groups the host does declare.

host.run_python('df2 = df.dropna()'), host.ran


test_eq(host.can('session'), False)
test_eq(names(tools_for(host)) & {'run_python', 'list_vars', 'inspect_python'}, set())
sorted(host.provides)

title: testing
text:
A host with everything
LocalHost is the host the terminal session runs on: real folders on disk, a real shell and a real Python kernel. Some of its groups are switched off because they need something it lacks. Memory and watches need a vault, the web tools need the network, and its inspect_python has only the isolated scope. Tests for those tools find nothing to test on a LocalHost.
FullHost is a LocalHost that fills each gap with a small working implementation over in-process state. Its web is a dict of pages you pass in. Its memory really stores and searches the pages it has read. Its terminal is a transcript you supply. Nothing reaches the network. It works in a fresh temporary folder unless you pass root, so a test or a docs page can write files freely. Three groups stay off because they need a model, an API specification or a vault: ask, api and watch.


source

FullHost
def FullHost(
    files:NoneType=None, pages:NoneType=None, root:NoneType=None, terminal:str='', **kw
):
Every host capability in process over a temporary folder, never the network.


Here it is seeded with one file, one web page and a terminal that has already printed a test run. The cell lists every tool tools_for builds for it, and the next cell checks that this is a strict superset of what NullHost gets.

host = FullHost(
    files={'pkg/sizes.py': 'RESERVE = 16_384\n\ndef threshold(ctx):\n    return max(1, ctx - min(RESERVE, ctx // 4))\n'},
    pages={'https://nbdev.fast.ai/api/export.html': (
        '# Exporting a notebook to a library\n\n'
        '## nb_export\n\n'
        'Named exports append to a module another notebook owns, so a second run duplicates them.\n\n'
        '## default_exp\n\n'
        'One module per notebook, named by the default_exp directive.\n')},
    terminal='$ pytest -q\n3 failed, 66 passed')
[t.__name__ for t in tools_for(host)]


names = {t.__name__ for t in tools_for(host)}
assert 'run_shell' in names
test_eq({t.__name__ for t in tools_for(NullHost())} < names, True)
host.kernel_kind, host.concurrent, host.scopes

Underneath it is a real LocalHost. The sandbox that keeps every path inside the open folders, the file tools and the Python namespace are the production code. The next cells view a file through the real view_file tool, show a path outside the folder being refused, and run Python in the live namespace.

view_file, replace_text, create_file, add_root = file_tools(host)
print(view_file('pkg/sizes.py'))


test_fail(lambda: host.check('/etc/passwd'), contains='outside the open folders')
host.run_python('total = threshold_calls = 0\ntotal'), host.list_vars().splitlines()

The web is the dict of pages passed in. web_search matches the query against each page’s url and text, and read_url returns a page. Reading a page also stores it in memory, which gives the memory tools below something to find.

web_search, read_url = web_tools(host)
print(web_search('nbdev'))
print(read_url('https://nbdev.fast.ai/api/export.html')[:80])

Memory is where the agent keeps pages and notes beyond the current conversation. A memory search returns sections of a stored document, each with a breadcrumb naming the document and heading it came from, rather than loose snippets. FullHost makes those sections by splitting a page at its headings, and memory_tree lists the headings of each stored document.

memory_search, memory_read, remember, memory_forget = memory_tools(host)
host.memory_search('duplicates')


test_eq(len(host.remembered), 1)
host.memory_tree()[0]['headings']

memory_forget deletes a stored document and its sections. The same search then finds nothing.

doc_id = next(iter(host.remembered))
memory_forget(doc_id), host.memory_search('duplicates')

research searches the web, reads every page that matches and returns them as one digest, with a source line under each page. It belongs to an opt-in tool group: tools_for(host) leaves it out and tools_for(host, optin='research') includes it. This cell builds the tool directly with shalya.research_tools.

from shalya import research_tools


research, = research_tools(host)
print(research('export')[:220])

inspect_python lets the agent look at the user’s live Python namespace. It has two scopes. The isolated scope runs the code against a copy of the namespace. The overlay scope runs it against the real namespace, so it sees every object as it is, and afterwards puts back every name that existed before. An IDE host enforces the same rule by checking the code’s syntax tree before running it; FullHost restores the bindings after.
Restoring bindings undoes an assignment such as kept = None, but it does not undo a change made inside an existing object. The cell below appends to kept in the overlay scope, and the list stays one item longer.

host.run_python('kept = [1, 2, 3]')
host.inspect_python('kept.append(99)\nlen(kept)', scope='overlay'), host.run_python('len(kept)')

The isolated scope copies the namespace dict, not the objects in it. A new name defined there disappears, but kept is the same list in both, so this append also lands on the real list, as the output shows.

host.inspect_python('kept.append(4)\nlen(kept)', scope='isolated'), host.run_python('len(kept)')

read_terminal is the tool that reads the terminal beside the agent. On FullHost it returns the transcript passed as terminal. note is how a host leaves a message for the agent, such as a report that compaction ran, and FullHost also keeps every note in host.notes so a test can check it.

read_terminal = {t.__name__: t for t in session_tools(host)}['read_terminal']
print(read_terminal())


host.note('compacted 12 messages')
host.notes

title: testing
text:
A backend with no model
FakeBackend replies from a list of strings, in order, and says (done) once the list runs out. It subclasses the real Backend, so these parts are production code:

the lock that serialises calls
the usage accounting
the list of problems shown to the user
the history replacement that compaction uses

Only the replies are made up. Every message sent is kept in sent, and every sub-agent backend made by spawn in spawned. Its one-shot calls, used for short jobs such as summaries, return ONESHOT: followed by the start of the prompt.


source

FakeBackend
def FakeBackend(
    spec:ramabana.core.ModelSpec=ModelSpec(name='fake', runtime='fake', model_id='fake/model', ctx=1000, note='', opts={}, missing=''),
    replies:tuple=(), **kw
):
A backend over a scripted list of replies, for turns with no model.



be = FakeBackend(replies=['the first answer', 'the second'])
be.send('a question'), be.send('another'), be.send('one more than were scripted')

The history holds both the user and the assistant messages, so compaction has a real conversation to shorten.

be.hist[:2]

stream yields the same reply one word at a time. That is enough to test a frontend that draws text as it arrives.

''.join(FakeBackend(replies=['streamed one word at a time']).stream('go'))

use is a Usage record of tokens in and out, the same type a live backend reports, and two of them add up.

be.use, be.use + be.use

fake_agent builds a real Agent and points all of its jobs at one FakeBackend. A job is one kind of model call the agent makes: the turn itself, a summary, a classification, a sub-agent. Normally each job can be routed to a different model. Routing every one to the fake means no call can reach a real model.
The host is a MemHost with one file unless you pass host, and other keyword arguments go to Agent. It returns (agent, backend), so a test can script the replies and then read what was sent. Use it whenever a test needs a whole turn, and FakeBackend alone when it only needs a backend.


source

fake_agent
def fake_agent(
    host:NoneType=None, replies:tuple=(), **kw
):
Build an Agent whose every job runs on one FakeBackend, and return (agent, backend).



agent, backend = fake_agent(replies=['`threshold` lives in `ramabana/runtime.py`.'])
agent.ask('where is the compaction threshold?')

The turn ran through the real agent: it built the tools, recorded the activity lines a frontend shows, and counted the tokens.

len(agent.tools), agent.turn_lines(), repr(agent.use)

title: testing
text:
A real model, recorded
The doubles above show the control flow with no model at all. A docs page that shows what a real model does is harder. Running a multi-gigabyte model in CI is too slow, and pasting a transcript means nobody checks it still holds. recorded sits between the two. Inside with recorded(): every chat the agent opens is urai’s CachedChat, which stores what the model said the first time, keyed by the model, the briefing, the tools and the conversation so far. Later runs replay the stored answer and start no model. Every runtime counts as available inside it, so a page replays Claude’s answers on a machine without Claude Code.
Answers live in CHATS, the chatcache folder beside the package, unless you pass path. record=False only replays. record=True lets a miss reach the real model and stores the answer. With record=None the URAI_RECORD_CHAT environment variable decides. The example uses an empty cache with record=False: the one-shot call gets an empty answer, and the backend’s problems say no recording was found.


source

recorded
def recorded(
    path:NoneType=None, record:NoneType=None
):
Replay recorded model answers for the duration, instead of calling a model; every runtime counts as available.



import tempfile
from ramabana.core import ModelSpec
from ramabana.runtime import make_backend

with recorded(Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'chats', record=False) as p:
    be = make_backend(ModelSpec('unrecorded', 'remote', 'openai/gpt-x', 8000))
    test_eq(be.oneshot('nothing was ever recorded for this'), '')
    assert 'no recording' in ' '.join(be.problems)
p.name

'chats'



from ramabana.core import resolve


with patch('ramabana.core._claude_available', lambda: False):
    with recorded(Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'chats', record=False): test_eq(resolve('claude/claude-sonnet-4-5').backend, 'claude')
    assert 'unavailable' in resolve('claude/claude-sonnet-4-5').missing

VaultHost, the host with durable memory from the vault notebook, rebuilds its memory graph in a background thread with a chat called graph_chat. no_model returns a stand-in chat that answers {} to every prompt, so that thread starts no model. It also works as mk_chat. This matters under nbdev’s test runner, which runs several notebooks in each worker process: two of them loading a model onto the GPU at once can crash the worker.


source

no_model
def no_model(
    model:NoneType=None, **kw
):
Return a stand-in chat that answers {} to everything, for use as graph_chat or mk_chat in tests.



test_eq(no_model('any/model', sp='x').oneshot('extract the entities'), '{}')
test_eq(no_model()('hello')['content'], '{}')

title: testing
text:
Compaction, end to end
Compaction replaces the older part of a conversation with a summary followed by the most recent messages. The agent compacts on its own when the history nears the window, and agent.compact() does it on demand. After six more questions the fake_agent history is still well under its 1,000-token threshold, so compactor.due is False. The second cell compacts anyway, with the summary written by the fake’s one-shot answer.

for i in range(6): agent.ask(f'question {i} about the exporter')
len(backend.hist), agent.compactor.due(backend)


summary = agent.compact()
agent.compactor.note

The history now begins with the summary. The text after it tells the model what happened: its conversation was rewritten, but the Python kernel was not, so the user’s variables are still there.

print(backend.hist[0]['content'][:200])


test_eq(backend.hist[0]['content'].startswith('Previous conversation summary:'), True)
test_eq(agent.compactor.count, 1)
agent.compactor.last[:60]

title: testing
text:
A backend that mutters
Local model engines sometimes fail without raising. The engine prints its error to its own output stream, returns an empty string, and the caller sees an empty reply with no reason. Ramabana’s local backend keeps what the engine printed and adds it to the backend’s problems. MutteringBackend reproduces the failure so tests can check that handling. GEMMA is a real error line from the LiteRT engine, kept exactly as printed, so the test sees the real shape of it.


source

MutteringBackend
def MutteringBackend(
    spec:NoneType=None, mode:str='empty', **kw
):
A backend that fails the way litert does: it prints, returns nothing, and raises nothing.



mute = MutteringBackend()
mute.send('anything'), mute.problems

That is the contract. send returns a sentence saying the model returned nothing and why, instead of an empty string, and last_native keeps the engine’s own words for the status line. Sending again does not add the same problem twice.

test_eq(mute.last_native, GEMMA.strip())
mute.send('again')


test_eq(len(mute.problems), 1)
mute.spec.ctx

title: testing
text:
A backend that performs
ScriptedBackend plays a list of Steps. A step can call a tool, say some text, or both, and can pause first. The text streams out one word at a time, token_delay seconds apart. The delay exists for screenshots: at zero the turn finishes before the screen repaints, and every capture shows a finished answer where it should show one in progress.
A tool step looks the tool up by name in the backend’s tool list, which refresh sets, and calls it. With the agent’s own tools in that list, the activity feed, the approval gate and the file snapshots all run as they do in production. A step naming a tool the list lacks is skipped. Use FakeBackend to test logic, and ScriptedBackend for demos where the tool calls have to happen.


source

ScriptedBackend
def ScriptedBackend(
    spec:ramabana.core.ModelSpec=ModelSpec(name='scripted', runtime='scripted', model_id='scripted/model', ctx=8000, note='', opts={}, missing=''),
    steps:tuple=(), token_delay:float=0.02, **kw
):
Play a list of Steps, streaming words one at a time every token_delay.




source

Step
def Step(
    text:str='', tool:NoneType=None, pause:float=0.0
):
One scripted model action: call a tool through the real tool list, or say something.



script = [Step('Looking at the file.', tool=('view_file', {'path': '/proj/a.py'})),
          Step('It returns 1, so the caller gets an int.')]
play = ScriptedBackend(steps=script, token_delay=0)
play.refresh('', [t for t in agent.tools if t.__name__ == 'view_file'])
play.send('what does a() return?')

The tool really ran. Its result is in the history as a tool message, where compaction or a UI would find it.

[m['role'] for m in play.hist], play.hist[2]['content'][:40]

spawn returns the backend for a sub-agent, and its answer depends on the question: it looks for a keyword from SUB_ANSWERS in it. When a demo fans out three sub-agents, three different answers show that they are separate calls. Its usage is fixed, as the last cell shows.

sub = play.spawn()
''.join(sub._run('which files import fastllm?')), ''.join(sub._run('what shape is df?'))


test_eq(play.use.total, 1936)
play.use

title: testing
section: A real model with every tool
text:
A real model with every tool
The doubles above check control flow. This last section checks the assembled product: a FullHost, an Agent over it on a made-up remote model, and every tool the host supports handed to the model’s conversation.
Everything runs inside recorded(), so it starts no model and makes no network call. The two cells that would talk to the model are marked #| eval: false, so the test suite skips them. Run by hand, they check that the model compiled every tool schema and that it can answer.

from contextlib import ExitStack

replay = ExitStack()
replay.enter_context(recorded())

# `remote`: `resolve` refuses a runtime that is not installed
register_model('release-model', 'openai/release-model', 'remote', 32_768)
real_host = FullHost(
    files={'pkg/sizes.py': 'RESERVE = 16_384\n\ndef threshold(ctx):\n    return ctx - RESERVE\n'},
    pages={'https://example.test/nbdev': '# nbdev export\n\nOne module belongs to one notebook.'},
    terminal='$ pytest -q\n69 passed')
real_agent = Agent(real_host, model='release-model', extensions=False)
for job in ('classify', 'summary', 'completion', 'subagent'):
    real_agent.routing.set('release-model', job)
real_agent.start() is not None, real_agent.note

(False,
 'turn job: release-model needs OPENAI_API_KEY; set it in the environment. `ramabana setup` lists the providers and adds one')


Agent.tools is the complete tool list: code, files, notebooks, web, memory, the live session, the shell, skills, delegation, the plan and git, plus image generation when a key for it is set. None of them is a stub that always fails. The next cell checks the list group by group.

real_tool_names = [tool.__name__ for tool in real_agent.tools]
real_tool_names


FILES = {'search_code', 'outline', 'grep', 'ls',
         'view_file', 'replace_text', 'create_file', 'add_root'}
NOTEBOOK = {'notebook_cells', 'view_cell', 'edit_cell', 'add_cell'}
WEB = {'web_search', 'read_url'}
MEMORY = {'memory_search', 'memory_read', 'remember', 'memory_forget'}
SESSION = {'run_python', 'inspect_python', 'restart_kernel', 'read_terminal'}
SHELL = {'run_shell', 'run_shell_bg', 'shell_output', 'shell_stop'}
SKILLS = {'read_skill'}                      # `create_skill` is the `author` opt-in
DELEGATION = {'delegate_search', 'delegate_async', 'delegate_result', 'delegate_cancel'}
PLAN = {'set_plan', 'update_todo'}
# only with a key for the endpoint
IMAGE = {'generate_image'} if image_available() else set()
GIT = {'git_status', 'git_divergence', 'git_remote', 'git_checkout',
       'git_commit', 'git_diff', 'git_log', 'git_stash'}
expected = (FILES | NOTEBOOK | WEB | MEMORY | SESSION | SHELL | SKILLS | DELEGATION | PLAN | IMAGE
            | GIT)
test_eq(set(real_tool_names), expected)
len(real_tool_names)

Attaching the tools to Agent does not prove the model accepts them. The backend’s live chat compiles a schema for each tool, so comparing the number of compiled schemas with the number of tools catches a missing type annotation, a lost functools.wraps, or a tool shape the runtime rejects.

real_backend = real_agent.backend
test_eq(real_backend.ready, True)
test_eq(len(real_backend.chat.toolspecs), len(real_agent.tools))
test_eq(len(real_backend.chat.toolspecs), len(expected))
(real_backend.spec.model_id, len(real_backend.chat.toolspecs))

Then the model is asked for a one-word reply on the classify job, which is routed to the same model. A non-empty reply shows the model really generates text, which accepting the tool schemas alone would not show.

real_reply = real_agent.oneshot(
    'Reply with exactly READY and nothing else.',
    'Return only the requested answer.', job='classify', max_tokens=192)
assert real_reply.strip()
real_reply


real_agent.close()
replay.close()
real_agent.status()['model'], real_agent.use.total

title: hl
text:
hl_text(code, lang, theme) colours a piece of code for the terminal. theme is a Lumis theme name, and HL_THEMES gives the Lumis theme for each palette name the terminal accepts, so --theme nord colours code with nord. scope_style looks up the style a theme gives one scope. A scope the theme does not name uses its longest dotted prefix that it does name, so function.builtin falls back to function.


source


def hl_text(
    code, lang, theme:str='github_dark'
):
code as a rich Text, coloured by fastpylight with Lumis theme.




source


def scope_style(
    scope, theme:str='github_dark'
):
The rich style Lumis theme gives token scope; the longest dotted prefix it names wins.


fastpylight counts positions in UTF-8 bytes and rich counts characters, and hl_text converts between them, so each coloured span starts on the character its token starts on. A line ending that rich rewrites, such as \r\n, leaves the spans in place:

t = hl_text('a\r\nb = 1  # one', 'python')
test_eq(t.plain, 'a\nb = 1  # one')
assert any(t.plain[s.start:s.end] == '1' for s in t.spans)
t

hl_toks(code, lang) returns the tokens as data instead: one list per line, each token a (start, end, scope) tuple in characters. Use it when you draw the code yourself. A token that runs across a line break, such as a triple-quoted string, is cut at the break and appears on both lines:


source


def hl_toks(
    code, lang
):
Per line of code, its tokens as (start, end, scope) in characters; a token crossing a line break is cut at it.



t = hl_toks('é = """a\nb"""', 'python')
test_eq(t[0][0], (0, 1, 'variable'))
test_eq([k for *_, k in t[1]], ['string'])

title: hl
text:
Diffs
diff_rich(s, palette, theme) colours a unified diff for the terminal. It also colours a diffstat, the file | 3 ++- summary git prints, and returns any other text in gray. palette maps fg1, gray, red, green, aqua and bg0 to colours. File headers are bold, hunk headers are aqua, and added and removed lines get a background tinted 15% toward green or red. The code inside each hunk is coloured with theme in its own language. The old side and the new side of a hunk are each tokenized whole, so a string that spans several lines keeps its colour on every one. is_diff says whether a text holds a unified diff at all.
The same split is available as data. diff_toks returns one entry per line of a diff: the line’s tokens, or None for a line outside a hunk body, such as a header. hunk_toks does the same for one hunk body. diff_html renders each code line as HTML through toks_html, which wraps each token in a span whose classes are its scope and every prefix of it, as in hl-function hl-function-builtin, so a stylesheet that styles only function still colours it.
diff_lang picks the language of a hunk from the path on its --- or +++ line. A notebook’s diff holds the source of its cells, so a path ending in .ipynb reads as Python. So does a single cell, written nb.ipynb#id the way edit_cell writes it. Any other path takes fastpylight’s guess from the file name. The cells below check diff_lang, then diff_html on a small diff.


source

diff_rich
def diff_rich(
    s, palette, theme:str='github_dark'
):
s coloured in palette when it holds a unified diff, its code by the file’s language, or a diffstat; else gray.




source

diff_html

    s, lang:NoneType=None
):
Per line of unified diff s, the HTML of its code after the prefix, or None outside a hunk body.




source

toks_html
def toks_html(
    code, toks
):
code escaped, each token a span whose classes are its scope and every dotted prefix of it, as fastpylight.theme_css names them.




source

diff_toks
def diff_toks(
    s, lang:NoneType=None
):
Tokens per line of unified diff s, relative to the line after its prefix; None for every line outside a hunk body. lang overrides the ---/+++ paths.




source

diff_lang
def diff_lang(
    path
):
fastpylight’s language for a diffed path; a notebook, or one cell of it as nb.ipynb#id, is Python.




source

is_diff
def is_diff(
    s
):
Whether s holds a unified diff: at least one hunk header.




source

hunk_toks
def hunk_toks(
    ls, lang
):
Tokens per hunk body line, relative to the line after its prefix; each side is tokenized whole, so a string spanning lines keeps its scope. None for a \ line.



test_eq([diff_lang(p) for p in ('a/x.py', 'b/nbs/05_cli.ipynb', 'b/nbs/05_cli.ipynb#2874a64d', 'a/README.md')],
        ['python', 'python', 'python', 'markdown'])


d = '--- a/x.py\n+++ b/x.py\n@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@\n import os\n-x = "a<b"\n+s = """one\n+two"""\n é = 1  # ü\n\\ No newline at end of file'
h = diff_html(d)
test_eq(len(h), len(d.split('\n')))
test_eq(h[:3] + h[-1:], [None] * 4)
assert '<' in h[4] and 'hl-string' in h[6]
assert '# ü' in h[7] and h[7].startswith('<span class="hl-variable">é</span>')
test_eq(diff_html('@@ -1 +1 @@\n-a<\n+b', 'plaintext'), [None, 'a<', 'b'])
test_eq(toks_html('len(x)', [(0, 3, 'function.builtin')]), '<span class="hl-function hl-function-builtin">len</span>(x)')

Here is a notebook cell’s diff, as edit_cell reports it, in the default github-dark colours. The added line carries the colour of its + mark, the green tint, and the code’s own colours:

dark = {'fg1': '#c9d1d9', 'gray': '#8b949e', 'red': '#ff7b72', 'green': '#3fb950', 'aqua': '#39c5cf', 'bg0': '#0a0c10'}
nb_diff = diff_rich('--- a/nbs/x.ipynb#c1\n+++ b/nbs/x.ipynb#c1\n@@ -1 +1 @@\n-x = 1\n+def f(): return 2', dark)
added = nb_diff.split('\n')[-1]
test_eq(added.plain, '+def f(): return 2')
assert len({str(s.style) for s in added.spans}) > 2
test_eq(diff_rich('3 passed', dark).spans, [])
nb_diff

title: spec
text:
An agent that has to call an HTTP API with no client library can fetch pages and run commands, but neither tells it what the API accepts. Without a description it has to guess paths and field names, and a wrong guess can come back as a plausible 200 or an unhelpful 400.
Most public APIs publish a specification: a machine-readable document that lists every operation, its HTTP verb and path, and its parameters and their types. This module reads two families of them: OpenAPI, including Swagger 2.0 and Azure’s variant, and Google Discovery documents. fastspec parses a document into OpSpec records, one per operation, each holding the verb, path, parameters, types, defaults and documentation. fastcore.apisurface turns each record into a Python signature such as list_repo_issues(owner, repo, state='open').
The result is the api tool group, which Ramabana offers when it runs with --spec. It has three tools. api_load reads a specification, api_ops lists its operations with their signatures, and api_call calls one of them by name.

title: spec
text:
When to use a specification
A maintained client library is the better choice when one exists. A specification helps with internal services, clients that have fallen behind their API, and one-off endpoints. The web tools find one: web_search for where a service publishes its document, and read_url for its documentation pages.

title: spec
section: Why the host holds the specifications
text:
Why the host holds the specifications
A loaded specification stays on the host for the rest of the session, so the agent can browse its operations again without fetching the document again. Because this state lives on the host, the terminal and the editor server share one implementation.

title: spec
text:
Reading a document
load_spec takes a URL, a file path, or a dict that is already parsed, and returns the document as a dict. It reads JSON or YAML. A URL is fetched with fossick, which comes with the [search] extra. A link to a file’s page on GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket is first turned by raw_url into the link to the raw file, since the page itself is HTML. parse_spec does the parsing, and when it is handed a web page instead of a document it says so and explains how to get the raw link.
parse_ops builds the fastspec parser for a document, choosing the Discovery or the OpenAPI reader by the document’s shape, and spec_ops returns the operations, at most MAX_OPS of them. norm_paths first merges Azure’s x-ms-paths into paths. op_row turns one operation into the dict that api_ops returns: group, name, verb, path, summary, signature, required parameters and a documentation link. Every failure raises SpecError with a message that says what went wrong.

    op
):
One operation as a readable row, signed by fastcore.apisurface.

    spec
):
Every operation in spec as OpSpec records, whatever its flavour.

    spec
):
spec with x-ms-paths folded into paths.

    src, timeout:int=30
):
Load a JSON or YAML spec from a URL, a path, or a parsed dict.

The raw file behind a code-host page url.

A spec document as a dict, from JSON or YAML.

SpecError

    *args, **kwargs
):
A specification could not be read, or an operation could not be called.




source

parse_ops
def parse_ops(
    spec
):
A fastspec.SpecParser for an OpenAPI/Azure or Google Discovery document.


Azure Blob Storage shows why norm_paths exists. Its Swagger 2.0 document leaves paths empty and declares its operations under x-ms-paths, because Swagger 2.0 cannot list operations that differ only in their query string, such as /?comp=list and /?restype=service&comp=properties, under paths. A parser that reads only paths finds no operations at all.
nbs/fixtures/azure-blob-excerpt.json holds three of the original entries, so the example runs without the network. It finds six operations, and when a path appears in both places the entry under paths wins. The cell after it checks raw_url on code-host links and the refusal of a web page.

azure = load_spec(Path('fixtures/azure-blob-excerpt.json'))
assert azure['swagger'] == '2.0' and not azure['paths'], 'the whole point: paths is empty'
assert len(azure['x-ms-paths']) == 3

ops = spec_ops(azure)
rows = [op_row(o) for o in ops]
assert len(rows) == 6, 'three paths, six operations, none of them under `paths`'
assert {r['verb'] for r in rows} == {'GET', 'PUT', 'DELETE'}
assert any(r['path'] == '/?comp=list' for r in rows), 'a query-only path survived'
assert all(r['signature'].startswith(r['name']) for r in rows)

# `paths` wins a collision
clash = dict(azure, paths={'/?comp=list': {'get': {'operationId': 'mine'}}})
assert norm_paths(clash)['paths']['/?comp=list'] == {'get': {'operationId': 'mine'}}

for r in rows[:3]: print(f"{r['verb']:6} {r['path'][:38]:40} {r['name']}")

PUT    /?restype=service&comp=properties        service__set_properties
GET    /?restype=service&comp=properties        service__get_properties
GET    /?comp=list                              service__list_containers_segment



test_eq(raw_url('https://github.com/stripe/openapi/blob/master/openapi/spec3.json'),
        'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stripe/openapi/master/openapi/spec3.json')
test_eq(raw_url('https://github.com/o/r/blob/main/a/b.yaml?plain=1#L4'),
        'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/o/r/main/a/b.yaml')
test_eq(raw_url('https://gitlab.com/o/r/-/blob/main/api.yaml'), 'https://gitlab.com/o/r/-/raw/main/api.yaml')
for u in ('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/o/r/main/s.json', 'https://api.example.com/openapi.json',
          'https://github.com/o/r', 'specs/local.yaml'):
    test_eq(raw_url(u), u)

test_fail(lambda: parse_spec('<!DOCTYPE html><html><body>hi</body></html>', 'that address'),
          contains='served a web page')

title: spec
text:
The host
SpecHost is a LocalHost that also holds specifications, by name, and it is what makes the api tool group available. api_load(src, name) reads a document and keeps it under name, or under its title when no name is given. It returns a short summary: the operation count, the groups, and a note when the list is longer than one page. api_names lists what is loaded.
api_ops lists the operations, narrowed by group or by match, a piece of text to look for in the name or summary, and paged with limit and offset. api_count says how many operations a narrowing matches in all. api_call(operation, **params) calls one operation by its name, with the parameter names its signature shows. When more than one specification is loaded, each of these needs name to say which one.
headers go with every call to every specification. api_creds sets headers, such as an API key, for one specification only, as the last example shows.


source

SpecHost
def SpecHost(
    roots:tuple=('.',), # the folders the agent is confined to
    specs:NoneType=None, # name -> parsed spec, preloaded
    headers:NoneType=None, # sent with every API call
    creds:NoneType=None, # name -> headers, sent only to that spec
    timeout:float=60.0, # per-call timeout, in seconds
    max_ops:int=400, # rows per `api_ops` page; 0 for all
    *, ns:NoneType=None, # live namespace; fresh dict when None
    approvals:NoneType=None, # write approval handler
    note:NoneType=None, # status callback
    web:bool=True, # use fossick when installed
    index:bool=True, # start a Kosha sync for every open root
    graph:bool=False, # build Kosha's call graph during sync
    rerank:bool=True, # rerank Kosha hits with flashrank
    rerank_model:NoneType=None, # flashrank model; None uses its default
    memory:NoneType=None, # memory, ask and watch backend
    apis:NoneType=None, # API specification backend
    kernel:NoneType=None, # live kernel; None runs in process
    read_outside:bool=False, # let read-only tools name any path on this machine
    deny:tuple=('*/.ssh/*', '*/.aws/*', '*/.gnupg/*', '*/.config/gcloud/*', '*/.netrc', '*/.git-credentials', '*/.codex/auth.json', '*/.claude/.credentials.json', '*/.env', '*/.env.*', '*/id_rsa*', '*/id_ed25519*', '*.pem', '*.key', '*.p12'), # what `read_outside` still refuses to open
    read_roots:tuple=(), # folders the read tools search and no write may touch
    tmux:NoneType=None, # None detects `$TMUX`; False off; True on; or this host's own pane (target or `Pane`)
    read_guard:NoneType=None, # `(ReadCheck) -> None | str | Refusal`: what the read tools may send
