title: spec
text:
Examples
The examples build small specifications in the notebook, so none of them needs the network. The first loads a two-operation OpenAPI document, lists its operations with the signature api_ops gives each one, and shows the errors when name is missing or names nothing loaded.

SPEC = {'openapi': '3.0.0', 'info': {'title': 'Widgets', 'version': '1.2.0'},
        'paths': {'/widgets': {'get': {'operationId': 'listWidgets', 'tags': ['widgets'],
                                       'summary': 'Every widget',
                                       'parameters': [{'name': 'limit', 'in': 'query',
                                                       'schema': {'type': 'integer'}}]}},
                  '/widgets/{id}': {'get': {'operationId': 'getWidget', 'tags': ['widgets'],
                                            'summary': 'One widget',
                                            'parameters': [{'name': 'id', 'in': 'path',
                                                            'required': True,
                                                            'schema': {'type': 'string'}}]}}}}

h = SpecHost(roots=['.'])
loaded = h.api_load(SPEC, 'widgets')
test_eq(loaded['operations'], 2)
test_eq(loaded['title'], 'Widgets')

rows = {r['name']: r for r in h.api_ops(name='widgets')}
test_eq(sorted(rows), ['get_widget', 'list_widgets'])
assert 'id' in rows['get_widget']['signature'], rows['get_widget']['signature']
assert 'limit' in rows['list_widgets']['signature'], rows['list_widgets']['signature']
test_eq(rows['get_widget']['verb'], 'GET')
test_eq(rows['get_widget']['required'], ['id'])

test_eq([r['name'] for r in h.api_ops(match='one widget', name='widgets')], ['get_widget'])
test_eq(h.api_ops(group='nothing', name='widgets'), [])

h.api_load(SPEC, 'other')
test_fail(lambda: h.api_ops(), contains='name which api')
test_fail(lambda: h.api_ops(name='nope'), contains='no api')
print(rows['get_widget']['signature'])

get_widget(id: str)



A specification as a document
A real specification can hold hundreds of operations, too many to read as a list of rows. spec_markdown(host, name) renders a loaded one as a reference page in markdown and returns (title, markdown). Each group gets a ## heading and each operation a ### heading, followed by what the operation does, how to call it and which parameters it requires. It uses the same rows as api_ops, all of them rather than one page. op_markdown renders one operation and op_heading writes its heading.
Operation names are often lowercase, and some markdown readers handle lowercase headings badly, so group headings start with a capital letter. Each operation is headed by its verb and path, which stays unique when several operations share a path. The parsed document keeps only its base URL and its operations, so api_load saves the title, version and source in spec_info for this page to use.
The first cell below loads a 25-operation document into a host that shows ten per page, and checks the paging and narrowing. The second renders a document with two groups.

BIG = {'openapi': '3.0.0', 'info': {'title': 'Big', 'version': '1'},
       'paths': {f'/g{i//10}/thing{i}': {'get': {'operationId': f'getThing{i}',
                                                 'summary': 'the last one' if i == 24 else f'thing {i}'}}
                 for i in range(25)}}
small = SpecHost(roots=['.'], max_ops=10)
info = small.api_load(BIG, 'big')
test_eq(info['operations'], 25)
test_eq(info['shown'], 10)
assert info['truncated'] and 'limit' in info['more'], info
test_eq(len(small.api_ops(name='big')), 10)
test_eq(len(small.api_ops(name='big', limit=0)), 25)
test_eq(len(small.api_ops(name='big', limit=5, offset=22)), 3)
test_eq(small.api_count(name='big'), 25)
test_eq(info['groups'], ['g0', 'g1', 'g2'])

test_eq([r['name'] for r in small.api_ops(name='big', match='the last one')], ['get_thing24'])
test_eq(small.api_count(name='big', group='g2'), 5)

whole = SpecHost(roots=['.'], max_ops=0)
assert 'truncated' not in whole.api_load(BIG, 'big')
test_eq(len(whole.api_ops(name='big')), 25)


ADMIN = {'openapi': '3.0.0', 'info': {'title': 'Widgets', 'version': '1.2.0'},
         'paths': {**SPEC['paths'],
                   '/admin/flush': {'post': {'operationId': 'flush', 'tags': ['widgets'],
                                             'summary': 'Empty the cache'}}}}
d = SpecHost(roots=['.'])
d.api_load(ADMIN, 'widgets')

assert not getattr(d.specs['widgets'], 'title', None)
test_eq(d.spec_info['widgets']['title'], 'Widgets')
test_eq(d.spec_info['widgets']['version'], '1.2.0')
test_eq(d.spec_info['widgets']['url'], '')
test_eq(SpecHost(roots=['.']).spec_info, {})

title, doc = spec_markdown(d, 'widgets')
test_eq(title, 'Widgets')
assert doc.startswith('3 operations in version 1.2.0'), doc[:60]
assert '## Admin' in doc and '## Widgets' in doc
assert doc.index('## Admin') < doc.index('## Widgets')
assert '### GET /widgets/{id}' in doc and '### POST /admin/flush' in doc
assert 'Call it as `get_widget(' in doc and 'Required: id' in doc
assert not doc.startswith('#') and '\n# ' not in doc

heads = [l for l in doc.splitlines() if l.startswith('#')]
assert heads and all(l.lstrip('#').strip()[0].isupper() for l in heads), heads

d.spec_info.clear()
test_eq(spec_markdown(d, 'widgets')[0], 'Widgets')

test_eq(op_heading({'verb': 'delete', 'path': '/widgets/{id}'}), 'DELETE /widgets/{id}')
bare = op_markdown({'verb': 'get', 'path': '/x', 'name': 'x'})
assert bare.startswith('### GET /x') and 'Required' not in bare and 'Docs' not in bare


d.api_load(ADMIN, 'second')
test_fail(lambda: spec_markdown(d, ''), contains='name which api')
print(doc)

paged = SpecHost(roots=['.'], max_ops=1)
paged.api_load(ADMIN, 'widgets')
assert spec_markdown(paged, 'widgets')[1].count('###') == 3

A SpecHost offers the three api tools, and a plain LocalHost offers none of them:

from ramabana.tools import tools_for
names = {t.__name__ for t in tools_for(SpecHost(roots=['.']))}
assert {'api_load', 'api_ops', 'api_call'} <= names, sorted(names)
assert not {'api_load', 'api_ops', 'api_call'} & {t.__name__ for t in tools_for(LocalHost(roots=['.']))}
print(sorted(n for n in names if n.startswith('api_')))

['api_call', 'api_load', 'api_ops']


A Google Discovery document loads the same way. Its operations are grouped by resource, here buckets, and its base URL comes from baseUrl:

GCP = {
    'kind': 'discovery#restDescription', 'discoveryVersion': 'v1', 'name': 'storage', 'version': 'v1',
    'title': 'Cloud Storage JSON API', 'baseUrl': 'https://storage.googleapis.com/storage/v1/',
    'resources': {'buckets': {'methods': {'get': {
        'id': 'storage.buckets.get', 'path': 'b/{bucket}', 'httpMethod': 'GET',
        'parameters': {'bucket': {'location': 'path', 'required': True, 'type': 'string'},
                       'projection': {'location': 'query', 'type': 'string'}},
        'description': 'Returns metadata for the specified bucket.'
    }}}}
}
gcp = SpecHost(roots=['.'])
loaded_gcp = gcp.api_load(GCP, 'gcp')
test_eq(loaded_gcp['title'], 'Cloud Storage JSON API')
test_eq(loaded_gcp['operations'], 1)
gcp_row = gcp.api_ops(name='gcp')[0]
test_eq((gcp_row['group'], gcp_row['name'], gcp_row['path'], gcp_row['required']),
        ('buckets', 'get', 'b/{bucket}', ['bucket']))
test_eq(gcp.specs['gcp'].base_url, 'https://storage.googleapis.com/storage/v1/')
from fastspec.oapi import OpenAPIClient
assert isinstance(OpenAPIClient(gcp.specs['gcp'], sync=True), OpenAPIClient)



A key for one specification
Headers passed as headers go with every call. Credentials should not: one host can hold several specifications, and an Authorization header meant for one service would then reach all the others. api_creds(name, headers) stores headers for one specification only, and calling it with headers=None removes them. api_keyed shows which specifications carry credentials and the names of their headers, never the values. In the example only the client for rates sends the API key.

RATES = {'openapi': '3.0.0', 'info': {'title': 'Rates', 'version': '1'},
         'servers': [{'url': 'https://api.example.com'}],
         'paths': {'/v1/latest': {'get': {'operationId': 'latest', 'summary': 'Latest rates'}}}}

k = SpecHost(roots=['.'], headers={'User-Agent': 'ramabana'})
k.api_load(RATES, 'rates'); k.api_load(SPEC, 'widgets')
k.api_creds('rates', {'X-Api-Key': 'secret'})
test_eq(k.api_keyed(), {'rates': ['X-Api-Key']})

test_eq(k._client('rates', k.specs['rates']).transport.base_headers,
        {'User-Agent': 'ramabana', 'X-Api-Key': 'secret'})
test_eq(k._client('widgets', k.specs['widgets']).transport.base_headers, {'User-Agent': 'ramabana'})

assert not callable(getattr(k._client('rates', k.specs['rates']), 'latest'))
test_fail(lambda: k.api_call('nope', name='rates'), contains='no operation')

title: shop
shop
shop
text:
The real one
FossickCart drives a logged-in Chrome tab through fossick.shop. It starts the browser session on first use, on the debugging port port, and reuses it after that.
fossick.shop does the hard part:

it injects its helper scripts into the page
it finds the page’s add-to-cart control
on Shopify stores, it posts to /cart/add.js directly
it watches the cart for a sign that the add worked

FossickCart is a thin adapter from the Cart methods to those calls. stores() lists the stores fossick knows the search and trolley pages of, from its SITES table. Both stores in the example are in that table, so their urls are known rather than guessed. Coles blocks bots that come from datacentre addresses and Ceres is a members’ shop, so the cart drives a browser you have logged into instead of fetching pages.


source

FossickCart
def FossickCart(
    port:int=9223, tout:int=180, headless:NoneType=None
):
Real Chrome trolley via fossick.shop, opened on first use and reused.

title: shop
text:
The double
FakeCart is a shop with a fixed catalogue, CATALOGUE unless you pass one, and a list for a trolley. It picks the store from the catalogue by matching the current url. It matches products the way fossick does. A number means that row of the last search. A title is matched exactly first, then as a substring, against the last search and then the whole store, and the shortest matching title wins. When nothing matches it raises CartError listing what the store stocks, rather than guess. A model can recover from “no product matching ‘caviar’” followed by a list of titles. It cannot recover from a silent wrong add.
The cells below search for milk, add two of it and a loaf of sourdough, and read the total.


source

FakeCart
def FakeCart(
    catalogue:NoneType=None, url:str='https://www.coles.com.au'
):
A browserless cart with a fixed catalogue, for tests and docs.



cart = FakeCart()
cart.find('milk')


cart.add('milk', qty=2)
cart.add('Sourdough Loaf 680g')
cart.total()

A failed match names the options instead of guessing, so the model can try again instead of buying the wrong thing.

test_fail(lambda: cart.add('caviar'), contains='no product matching')
test_fail(lambda: cart.add(99), contains='no product #99')

title: shop
text:
The tools
cart_tools(cart) turns any Cart into six tools for the model: cart_stores, cart_open, cart_find, cart_add, cart_show and cart_remove. cart_add reports added only when the trolley changed, DID NOT ADD when it did not, and UNVERIFIED when the cart could not tell.


source

cart_tools
def cart_tools(
    cart
):
Return the six tools that let a model shop with cart.


Registering them takes one extension file in the config folder. Nothing in the harness changes:
# ~/.config/ramabana/extensions/shopping.py
from ramabana.shop import FossickCart, cart_tools

def setup(reg):
    for t in cart_tools(FossickCart()): reg.tool(t)
The cell below does the same with a Registry and a FakeCart.

from ramabana.tools import Registry, WRITE_TOOLS
reg = Registry()
for t in cart_tools(FakeCart()): reg.tool(t)
[t.__name__ for t in reg.tools]

['cart_stores',
 'cart_open',
 'cart_find',
 'cart_add',
 'cart_show',
 'cart_remove']


cart_add and cart_remove are in WRITE_TOOLS, the set of tools the approval gate guards, so an Approvals gate asks before either runs, as it would before a file write. Spending money deserves a confirmation at least as much.

test_eq({'cart_add', 'cart_remove'} <= WRITE_TOOLS, True)

title: shop
text:
The weekly shop
This is the whole job end to end: a reminder set once, noticed later, and acted on.
Only the model’s decisions and the trolley are fakes. The vault, the watch and the poll are real, and every tool call below runs the actual tool. ScriptedBackend, from the testing notebook, chooses which tool to call and streams the words, and the harness does everything else. The host is a VaultHost over a temporary vault, with no_model as its graph chat so no model loads.

import time
from ramabana import Agent
from ramabana.vault import VaultHost
from ramabana.testing import ScriptedBackend, Step, no_model

tmp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
host = VaultHost(roots=[tmp], vault=tmp/'vault.db', index=False, web=False, graph_chat=no_model())
host.open_vault(wait=True)

Warning: You are sending unauthenticated requests to the HF Hub. Please set a HF_TOKEN to enable higher rate limits and faster downloads.


<ramabana.vault.VaultHost at 0x7f31a5cf6270>


Once, weeks ago. Store the shopping list as a note and set a weekly reminder against it. start is when the reminder first comes due. Setting it a second in the past makes the rest of the page the morning the reminder fires, with no fake clock.

host.remember('Weekly Coles order: milk, sourdough, eggs, baby spinach, olive oil. '
              'Plus a seasonal fruit box from Ceres Fair Food.',
              title='the weekly shop', tags=['groceries'])

due = host.watch('Put the weekly groceries in the Coles trolley, and add a Ceres fruit box.',
                 action='remind', every='1w', note='weekly shop', start=time.time() - 1)
int(due['every'])

No one has polled yet, so the vault shows the reminder as due.

test_eq(len(host.watches(due_only=True)), 1)

The morning it fires. The agent gets the host’s own tools plus the cart’s. gpt-mini resolves to openai/gpt-5.6-luna, fast and cheap, which suits a run of many small steps that each can be checked. The script never calls it: the steps below are played by ScriptedBackend.

shop = FakeCart()
agent = Agent(host, model='gpt-mini', extensions=False)
tools = {t.__name__: t for t in agent.tools} | {t.__name__: t for t in cart_tools(shop)}
agent.routing.turn


script = [
    Step('There is a weekly shop. Pulling the list.',
         tool=('memory_search', {'query': 'weekly Coles order list', 'limit': 2})),
    Step('Opening Coles.', tool=('cart_open', {'url': 'https://www.coles.com.au'})),
    *[s for item in ['milk', 'sourdough', 'eggs', 'baby spinach', 'olive oil']
      for s in (Step(f'Looking for {item}.', tool=('cart_find', {'query': item})),
                Step(f'Adding {item}.', tool=('cart_add', {'item': item})))],
    Step('Now the fruit box.', tool=('cart_open', {'url': 'https://members.ceresfairfood.org.au'})),
    Step('', tool=('cart_find', {'query': 'fruit box'})),
    Step('', tool=('cart_add', {'item': 'Seasonal Fruit Box - Medium'})),
    Step('Reading the trolley back.', tool=('cart_show', {})),
    Step('Done: five staples in the Coles trolley and a medium seasonal fruit box from Ceres.'),
]

be = ScriptedBackend(steps=script, token_delay=0)
be.refresh('', list(tools.values()))
agent.poll_watches(force=True).join()
print(be.send('anything outstanding this week?'))

The harness polls, not the model: there is no poll_watches tool. In a session Agent.poll_watches runs at the start of each turn. Here the script is sent to the backend directly, so the cell calls it by hand first. The reminder that fired became a vault note, and the first memory_search finds it:

[h['content'] for h in be.hist if h['role'] == 'tool'][0]

Check the trolley, not the transcript. cart_add compares the trolley before and after each add, so a reported add is one the cart confirmed.

shop.total()

The reminder has rescheduled itself for next week, so the job repeats with no new setup.

w = host.watches()[0]
test_eq(w['runs'], 1)
test_eq(w['last_status'], 'ok')
test_eq(w['next_run'] > due['next_run'], True)


Against the real shops
The same run on a browser you are already logged into. The cart is FossickCart, and the agent asks before every write:
from ramabana import Agent
from ramabana.agent import Approvals
from ramabana.shop import FossickCart, cart_tools
from ramabana.tools import WRITE_TOOLS
from ramabana.vault import VaultHost

host  = VaultHost(roots=['~/notes'])              # the shared ~/.vishalakshi/vault.db
agent = Agent(host, model='gpt-mini', approvals=Approvals(WRITE_TOOLS, mode='ask'))
for t in cart_tools(FossickCart()): agent.add_tool(t)

agent.ask('anything outstanding this week?')
Two rules for a real trolley. Keep the approval gate on: cart_add is in WRITE_TOOLS, so you see every add before it happens. And leave the checkout alone. fossick.shop has shop_fill for the payment form, and this module does not wrap it. A trolley can be emptied again. A placed order cannot.

title: control
text:
A program that hosts agent jobs, such as a web app, often runs each job in a process of its own, so that restarting the web server does not kill a turn halfway through. The page that started the job then needs a way to reach it: to send a prompt, steer the running turn, stop it, and answer the approval requests it raises. Control gives it that way in. It opens a Unix socket, an address in the file system that only processes on this machine can connect to, in the session’s run folder, and only the current user may connect.
The protocol is one JSON object per line in each direction. A request is {"id", "method", "params"}. The reply is {"id", "result"} on success and {"id", "error"} on failure. METHODS lists the methods:

prompt(text) starts a turn on a worker thread. If a turn is already running, text is queued to run after it.
steer(text) hands text to the running turn along with its next tool result, which redirects the model without stopping it.
cancel() stops the running turn and drops the prompts queued behind it.
asks() lists the approval requests waiting for an answer, oldest first. answer(id, ok, note) answers one of them.
status() says whether a turn is running, how many prompts are queued, and how the last turn ended.
events(offset) returns the records in the session’s event file from byte offset on, and the offset to pass next time. It works only after the runner has called agent.events_to(path).

control_call(path, method, **params) is the other end. It connects, sends one request, and returns the result, or raises RuntimeError with the error’s message. The page uses it, and so can any script that needs to reach a running job.
start refuses a path where another runner is already listening, and a path that holds something other than a socket. It removes a socket left behind by a runner that crashed. A Unix socket path may be at most about a hundred bytes long (SOCKET_MAX), so when the session’s run folder is deeper than that, the socket goes in the temporary folder as ramabana-<session>.sock.


source


def control_call(
    path, method, timeout:int=30, **params
):
Send one request to the Control socket at path and return its result; an error reply raises RuntimeError.




source


def Control(
    agent, path:NoneType=None, # the socket; None puts it in the session's run folder as `CONTROL`
):
A Unix socket through which another process prompts, steers, stops and answers an agent running in this one.


The example plays both sides in one process. fake_agent from ramabana.testing supplies an agent whose model replies with a scripted line. The first cell sends a prompt through the socket, waits for the turn to finish, checks how it ended, and reads the turn’s events.
The second cell raises an approval request for edit_file from another thread, as a tool would, finds it through asks, and approves it through the socket. The agent was built with no_listener='wait', which keeps the request waiting for an answer rather than refusing it because no terminal is attached. An unknown method comes back as an error, which control_call raises as RuntimeError.

import tempfile, time
from ramabana import agent
from ramabana.testing import fake_agent

d = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp(dir='/tmp'))   # a Unix socket path must stay short
a, be = fake_agent(cfg=d, replies=['the first reply'], approvals=agent.Approvals(tools={'edit_file'}, timeout=5, no_listener='wait'))
a.events_to(d/'job.events')
ctl = Control(a).start()
call = lambda method, **kw: control_call(ctl.path, method, **kw)

test_eq(call('prompt', text='hello'), {'started': True})
for _ in range(200):
    if not call('status')['running']: break
    time.sleep(.01)
st = call('status')
test_eq((st['running'], st['last']['state'], st['last']['reply']), (False, 'complete', 'the first reply'))
ev = call('events')
assert {'turn_start', 'turn_end'} <= {e['kind'] for e in ev['events']} and ev['offset'] > 0
test_eq(call('events', offset=ev['offset'])['events'], [])


out = {}
threading.Thread(target=lambda: out.setdefault('r', a.approvals.request('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'})), daemon=True).start()
for _ in range(200):
    if (waiting := call('asks')): break
    time.sleep(.01)
test_eq(waiting[0]['tool'], 'edit_file')
assert call('answer', id=waiting[0]['id'], ok=True)
for _ in range(200):
    if 'r' in out: break
    time.sleep(.01)
assert out['r'], 'answered through the socket'
try: call('fly')
except RuntimeError as e: assert 'no method' in str(e)
ctl.close(); a.close()

title: racp
text: The Agent Client Protocol (ACP) lets an editor, such as Zed, run a coding agent as a child process and talk to it in JSON-RPC over stdin and stdout. The editor opens a session for a folder, sends prompts, shows the agent’s messages and tool calls as they happen, and asks the person to allow or refuse each action the agent wants to take. This module is the ramabana-acp command: it puts a Ramabana agent behind that protocol.

title: racp
text:
What maps onto what
Each part of the protocol already has a counterpart in Ramabana, so this module translates between them and adds no behaviour of its own.

session/prompt, the editor sending a prompt, is one turn.
The session/update messages that stream the reply carry the chunks of Agent.stream.
The tool calls the editor shows are Ramabana’s Activity rows, one per tool call.
session/request_permission, the editor’s allow-or-refuse prompt, is the approval gate, Approvals. The gate waits for the editor’s answer. If the editor fails to answer, the action is refused, so losing the editor never lets a write through.
session/load, reopening an earlier conversation, is resume_session, so a conversation started in the terminal can continue in the editor.

Two requests go the other way, from the agent to the editor. A client that offers fs/read_text_file can hand over the text of a file as it stands in an open buffer, including changes not yet saved to disk. A client that offers terminal/* can run a command in a terminal the person can watch. When the editor offers these, Ramabana reads and runs through it, so the agent works on what the person sees.

title: racp
text:
The bridge
Ramabana runs every tool and every host method on the turn’s worker thread, a plain thread that blocks while it waits. The ACP library runs on an asyncio event loop. A tool that needs the editor, for example to read a buffer, has to hand a coroutine to that loop and wait for the result. Bridge is the one place that does this. call sends a request and blocks until the editor replies or timeout passes, and post sends an update without waiting.


source

Bridge
def Bridge(
    conn, # the connected ACP `Client`
    sid, # the session every call is about
    loop, # the loop serving the connection
    timeout:int=300, # seconds to wait on a person or editor
):
The one crossing between the turn’s thread and the client’s event loop.

title: racp
section: The host the editor answers for
text:
The host the editor answers for
EditorHost is the ordinary WorkspaceHost from ramabana.vault, with four methods sent to the editor when the editor says it can serve them: read, text_at, write and run_cmd. attach records what the editor offered.
The four differ in what happens when the editor fails. A read falls back to the file on disk, because a read the editor declined should not cost the turn. A write does not fall back: if the editor refused the write, that refusal is the answer, and writing to disk anyway would defeat the reason for asking the editor. A command does not fall back once the editor’s terminal has opened, because by then the command has run and a second run on this side would run it twice.
read matters most. view_file reads through Host.read, so the text the model sees, and against which it writes its edits, is the same text those edits are applied to. If the two came from different places, the edits would be addressed to text that is not there.

title: racp
text:
The prompt
An ACP prompt is a list of content blocks. blocks turns that list into the text and media that Agent takes. Text blocks join into one string, separated by blank lines. An embedded file becomes a <file> element holding its text, and a link to a resource becomes @uri. Image and audio blocks are decoded to bytes and passed to the model when its capabilities accept that kind of media, or when its capabilities are unknown. Otherwise the block is dropped and a line saying so is added to the text. The examples under Tests show a text prompt and an image.

title: racp
text:
The session
Session holds one editor session: one agent, its host, and the bridge to the editor. Everything the editor shows comes from hooks the agent already has. on_activity reports each tool call, on_plan reports the agent’s checklist, and Approvals.listen is told about each approval request. Session turns each of these into the matching ACP update. For an edit it also works out the file’s text before and after, without writing anything, so the editor can show a diff in its permission prompt.


source

Session
def Session(
    roots, conn, loop, sid:NoneType=None, model:NoneType=None, mk:NoneType=None, timeout:int=300, **kw
):
One ACP session: an agent, and the editor it reports to.


The editor’s permission prompt offers three choices. The second reads “Allow every write this session”, so choosing it answers the request with scope='edits': file and notebook edits stop asking for the rest of the session, while shell commands and add_root still ask. Only the terminal’s own approve-all key switches the gate to auto. The example below stands in an editor that always picks that option, and checks what the gate decides afterwards.

class _Editor:
    "A bridge whose editor always picks `allow_always`."
    def call(self, coro): coro.close(); return True, 'allow_always in the editor', True
    def post(self, coro): coro.close()
s = Session.__new__(Session)
s.agent, s.host = mk_agent([tempfile.mkdtemp()], web=False)
s.conn, s.br, s.gated, s.seen = None, _Editor(), {}, set()
ap = s.agent.approvals
s.unhook = ap.listen(s._ask)
test_eq(bool(ap.request('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'}, force=True)), True)
test_eq(ap.mode, 'edits')
test_eq(ap.decide('run_shell', {'command': 'ls'}, force=True), None)
test_eq(ap.decide('add_root', {'path': tempfile.mkdtemp()}, force=True), None)
test_eq(ap.decide('create_file', {'path': 'b.py', 'text': ''}, force=True).answer, True)
s.unhook()

title: racp
text:
The agent
AcpAgent is the object the ACP library drives. It answers initialize, opens a Session for each session/new, resumes one for session/load and replays its turns to the editor, runs session/prompt, and handles cancel and close. A prompt that starts with / runs as a Ramabana slash command instead of a turn.
initialize records the capabilities the editor declares, and EditorHost.attach turns on only those. A client that declares none gets a host that reads, writes and runs on this machine, as a plain WorkspaceHost would.
serve speaks the protocol on stdin and stdout until the editor closes the connection, and main is the ramabana-acp command around it. Its options are listed on the index page.

title: Debugging
text:
This page is one of the five skills that ship with Ramabana, built the way theory is: the exported markdown cell below is the module’s docstring, and pyproject.toml registers ramabana.debugging under the pyskills entry point as debugging.
It exists because of one comparison. An agent on Ramabana and Claude Code, on the same model, worked through the same failed Dhrona night and the same set of harness faults. Ramabana’s agent found the launchd PATH cause about as fast, but it then said two things about code it had not read, one of which another commit had already fixed that day, and it did not know where its own launcher, plist and source live. Earlier it had taken a grep that returned “no matches” for text it had just read as the tool working as designed, and a sub-agent that noticed the same fault mentioned it only in passing. The briefing already says not to work around a broken tool. What was missing was how to tell that a tool is broken, how to check a claim before making it, and a map of Ramabana’s own files. Those cost nothing in a turn that is not debugging, so they live here rather than in the system prompt.
Read this before explaining why something failed: a test, a command, a scheduled job, a sub-agent, one of your own tools, or Ramabana itself.

title: Debugging
text:
Find the root cause

Read the raw error first. Open the failing component’s own record (its log, summary file or transcript) and quote the line that names the failure. A count such as “3 failed” points to that record. It is not the cause.
Reproduce the failure in the environment it ran in. A scheduled job does not run in your shell, so rerun the failing step with the scheduler’s environment before blaming or clearing it.
Check a claim about code in that code before making it. “X has no timeout” and “Y already writes Z” are both claims; read or grep the code first. Check the version that ran as well as the checkout, because an installed package can predate a fix in its repository.
Name the cause and the evidence for it before changing anything. A fix that cannot be tied to the quoted error is a guess, and a workaround leaves the cause in place for the next run.
When an earlier claim turns out to be wrong, say so in the reply.

title: Debugging
text:
A tool that misbehaves
A result that contradicts what you have already seen is a tool fault until shown otherwise. Examples:

grep or search_code reports no matches for text you have just read.
ls lists nothing in a folder that exists.
A schema reaches a model without the fields you declared.
The user refers to a message you never received.
A tool reports success and the file or state is unchanged.

Confirm the fault once by a second route, such as rg through run_shell, or view_file. Do not explain it away as how the tool is meant to work unless its description says so. Then:

record it with remember, with component='tool' and the call and its result as evidence
say in the reply, beside the work it affected, which tool failed and how
carry on by the second route

The fault belongs to the harness and is fixed there. The second route keeps this turn going and nothing more.
A sub-agent whose answer says its tool-call budget ran out has returned part of an answer, and its saved answer names what it did not read. Delegate that remainder as narrower questions, or read it yourself, before relying on anything in the gap.

title: Debugging
section: Where Ramabana keeps its own state
text:
Where Ramabana keeps its own state
The running code is the installed package. With the interpreter that “On this machine” lists as this process, python -c 'import ramabana; print(ramabana.__file__, ramabana.__version__)' names it, and uv tool list shows the installed tool’s version. A source checkout, if the user has one, is an nbdev repository whose notebooks under nbs/ are the source. A fix goes there, and the running copy changes only once a release is installed. An editable install runs the checkout’s code, but its entry points (pyskills, ramabana.ticks, scripts) change only on reinstall.
The config folder is ~/.config/ramabana unless --cfg names another:

config.toml holds models, jobs and settings, and models.json the saved model aliases.
agent-history.jsonl has one line per finished turn, with its model, usage, error and the lines the user sent while it ran (steered).
runs/<session>/ has one folder per session. run_<id>.log is one run’s transcript, the turn’s or a sub-agent’s. answer_<id>.txt is a sub-agent’s whole answer. stderr.log is the process’s error output, where a backend crash can appear and nowhere else. start.json records each open folder’s repository state at the first turn.
learned/ is a git repository of the rules, skills and extensions that learning keeps.

A turn on a Claude model runs through Claude Code. Its transcripts are under ~/.claude/projects/, in the folder named after ~/.rishi-claude, one .jsonl per conversation, sub-agents included. Each holds the system prompt, model, effort and every tool result exactly as the model received them.
The beat runs scheduled jobs while no session is open:

ramabana-tick runs one beat, and ramabana-tick --install --every 300 schedules it and prints the PATH each beat runs on.
~/.pobblebonk/ramabana.sh is the launcher the scheduler starts, ~/.pobblebonk/ramabana.log holds its output, and ~/.pobblebonk/pob.db holds the schedules, their fires and the notes a session shows inside <beat>.
The scheduler entry is ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ramabana.plist on macOS, a line in the user crontab on Linux, and a Task Scheduler task named ramabana on Windows.
Dhrona’s nightly batch writes ~/.cache/dhrona/nightly/<time>/summary.json, one row per round with its error, beside one folder per round.

title: Debugging
text:
A scheduled job that fails
launchd and cron start a job with PATH=/usr/bin:/bin and none of the exports in a shell profile. When a beat fails with “not found”, “not on PATH” or a missing key:

Read the launcher with cat ~/.pobblebonk/ramabana.sh. Since Ramabana 0.2.52 it starts with /usr/bin/env PATH=…, the PATH of the shell that installed it.
Read what the scheduler gives it: launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/ramabana on macOS shows its environment, and crontab -l on Linux.
Reproduce it: env -i HOME="$HOME" PATH='<that PATH>' /bin/sh -c 'command -v claude git-lfs uv'.
Running ramabana-tick --install again from a shell that finds the tools rewrites the launcher with that shell’s PATH. A key exported in a shell profile still does not reach the beat.

The skill names files that other modules decide. The test below finds the skill the way an agent does, through shalya’s discovery of installed entry points, and checks that every such name in it still matches the code that writes it, so the map cannot drift from the files. The skill is only found once the package is installed, so after adding the entry point an editable install needs reinstalling.

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from shalya.skills import discover
from pobblebonk.heartbeat import LaunchdBeat
from rishi.claude import CLAUDE_WORK_DIR
from ramabana.monitor import BEAT_TAG, POB_HOME, pob_path
from ramabana.agent import Agent
from ramabana.testing import MemHost

s = next(s for s in discover() if s.name == 'debugging')
text, home = s.text(), Path.home()
assert s.where == 'ramabana.debugging' and len(s.description) <= 70, s.description
def tilde(p): return '~/' + str(Path(p).expanduser().relative_to(home))
a = Agent(MemHost(), cfg=Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()), extensions=False, profile='full')
for p in (tilde(Path(POB_HOME)/f'{BEAT_TAG}.sh'), tilde(Path(POB_HOME)/f'{BEAT_TAG}.log'), tilde(pob_path()),
          tilde(LaunchdBeat()._p(BEAT_TAG)), tilde(CLAUDE_WORK_DIR), a.history_path.name,
          f'{a.runs_dir.parent.name}/<session>/'):
    assert p in text, p
try:
    from dhrona.improve import NIGHTLY
    assert NIGHTLY in text, NIGHTLY
except ImportError: pass

text:
The activity feed is the list of tool calls a turn has made, one row per call. A frontend draws each row as a short human line, such as View a.py:4-, rather than a raw view_file(path='a.py', start=4). Each tool carries its own summary function for that line, and summarise from tools calls it. The cell below shows the line for five common tools.

tool = {t.__name__: t for t in tools_for(FullHost())}
[summarise(tool[t], a) for t, a in [
    ('search_code', {'query': 'where is compaction triggered'}),
    ('view_file', {'path': 'nbs/01_runtime.ipynb', 'start': 40, 'end': 80}),
    ('edit_cell', {'path': 'nbs/00_core.ipynb', 'cell_id': '451586c0'}),
    ('inspect_python', {'code': 'list(df.columns)', 'scope': 'overlay'}),
    ('git_status', {}),
]]

A tool without a summary function, such as one an extension added, still gets a line: its name and arguments, as the last example shows. Every tool the toolset ships has a summary, which the bare check asserts.

test_eq(summarise(tool['view_file'], {'path': 'a.py', 'start': 4}), 'View a.py:4-')
test_eq(summarise(tool['view_file'], {'path': 'a.py', 'end': 8}), 'View a.py:-8')
test_eq(summarise('view_file', {'path': 'a.py'}), 'View a.py')
bare = sorted(t.__name__ for t in tools_for(FullHost()) if getattr(t, 'summary', None) is None)
test_eq(bare, [])
summarise('word_count', {'path': '/proj/a.py'})

Act is one row of the feed: one tool call, from the moment it starts. The row exists before the call returns, so a frontend can show ⏳ Web fetch: ... while the fetch is still running. kind comes from the tool’s group and picks the icon, and line gives the one-line text.


source


def Act(
    tool:str, args:dict=<factory>, summary:str='', detail:str='', ok:bool=True, done:bool=False, secs:float=0.0,
    started:float=<factory>, id:str=<factory>, turn_id:str='', revision:int=0, branch_id:str='main',
    parent_action_id:str='', run_id:str='', state:str='running', kind:str='', ask_id:str=''
)->None:
One tool call, from the moment it starts to whatever it returned.



a = Act('read_url', {'url': 'https://nbdev.fast.ai/api/export.html'},
        summarise(tool['read_url'], {'url': 'https://nbdev.fast.ai/api/export.html'}))
a.kind, a.icon, a.line()

finish records the outcome, the time taken and the result. state becomes complete or failed, which a frontend can colour on. A failed call’s line starts with a warning sign, as the second example below shows.

a.finish('# Exporting a notebook to a library\n\nnb_export(...)')
a.line(), a.state

md renders the row as markdown, with the result folded under a <details> tag. A notebook cell that saves an answer then keeps the tool work one click away, instead of printing thirty results above the answer.

print(a.md())


bad = Act('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'}, 'Edit a.py').finish('edit failed: stale address', ok=False)
test_eq(bad.state, 'failed')
bad.line()

Activity is the whole feed for a session. on_change is called whenever a row starts or finishes, so twice per call, and a frontend redraws from it. rows returns the feed as dicts, lines as one string per call, and md as folded markdown.


source


def Activity(
    on_change:NoneType=None, max_acts:int=500
):
The stream of calls for a session, and the hook a frontend hangs a redraw on.



seen = []
feed = Activity(on_change=lambda act: seen.append((act.tool, act.done)))
act = feed.start('search_code', {'query': 'compaction'})
feed.finish(act, 'nbs/01_runtime.ipynb:88  threshold')
seen

Activity calls on_change outside its lock and swallows any exception the callback raises, so a broken frontend cannot stop the model’s turn. The callback below divides by zero, and the row is still recorded.

noisy = Activity(on_change=lambda act: 1/0)
noisy.finish(noisy.start('outline', {'path': 'a.py'}), 'ok')
len(noisy)

mark remembers where the current turn began and tags every new row with the turn’s id. Passing mark= to rows, lines or md then limits them to that turn, so one feed serves both a whole-session view and a one-turn summary.

feed.mark('turn_000002')
feed.finish(feed.start('view_file', {'path': 'a.py'}), 'def a(): return 1')
feed.lines(), feed.lines(mark=feed._mark)


test_eq(len(feed.rows()), 2)
test_eq(len(feed.rows(mark=feed._mark)), 1)
feed.rows(mark=feed._mark)[0]['turn_id']

title: agent
text:
Approvals
A write tool is one that changes something: it edits a file, runs a command, or commits to git. The approval gate stands between the model and those tools. Before a write runs, the gate raises an Ask, a request a person answers yes or no, shows a preview of what the call would do, and waits. A refusal goes back to the model as the tool’s result, with the person’s reason, so the model can change its approach.
The gate’s mode decides who answers:



mode
what happens




ask
every write waits for a person


edits
file and notebook edits run; other writes wait


auto
every write runs


off
every write is refused



edits never covers the ALWAYS_ASK tools (add_root, restart_kernel, page_eval); they still wait for a person. A session built with approve='none' has no gate at all.


source

preview_for
def preview_for(
    name, args, host:NoneType=None
):
What this call would actually do, as text a person can read in a couple of seconds.


A backend hands the approver each tool call as a dict in the OpenAI shape, {'function': {'name': ..., 'arguments': ...}}, where the arguments may be a JSON string. _tc returns the name and the parsed arguments.

_tc({'function': {'name': 'edit_file', 'arguments': '{"path": "a.py", "commands": "[]"}'}})

preview_for turns one call into the text a person reads before approving it. The useful preview depends on the tool: the edit commands for edit_file, a diff for replace_text and edit_cell when the host can read the file, the head of the new file for create_file (and whether it overwrites one), and the command line for run_shell.

print(preview_for('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py', 'commands': [['2|ab12|', 's', 'return 1', 'return 2']]}))


h = MemHost({'/proj/a.py': 'x = 1\n'})
p = preview_for('replace_text', {'path': '/proj/a.py', 'edits': [{'oldText': 'x = 1', 'newText': 'x = 2'}]}, h)
assert '-x = 1' in p and '+x = 2' in p, p
assert 'old' in preview_for('edit_cell', {'path': '/proj/n.ipynb', 'cell_id': 'c1', 'edits': [{'oldText': 'old', 'newText': 'new'}]})
assert '12|ab| s' in preview_for('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py', 'commands': [['12|ab|', 's', 'old', 'new']]})
assert 'a.py' in preview_for('replace_text', {'path': '/proj/a.py', 'edits': 'not json'}, h)


print(preview_for('create_file', {'path': 'new.py', 'text': 'def f(): pass\n'}, host=NullHost(['/proj'])))

A tool preview_for does not know falls back to its arguments as JSON.

print(preview_for('word_count', {'path': '/proj/a.py'}))

An Ask is one approval request and the person’s answer to it. answer is None while it waits. The object is truthy only when approved, so a backend’s if not approve(tool_call) check works on it directly, and reply gives the text the model sees.


source

Ask

A refusal can carry a reason. The model receives it, so it can change its approach instead of sending the same edit again.

ask.resolve(False, 'keep the docstring')

An approval can carry a note too, such as “yes, but keep the docstring”, which the model needs while it makes the edit. A plain approval tells the model nothing extra, so its reply is None.

answer_md(ask)

Approvals is the gate itself. It holds every request still waiting (waiting lists them oldest first, and pending is the oldest), tells the frontends that listen, and blocks the model’s thread until each request is answered, refused or timed out. Each call gets its own decision, so a model that asks for four writes gets four requests. Its main parameters are:

tools, the names that need approval; an agent adds every write tool it builds;
mode, one of the four modes above;
timeout, the seconds a request waits (DFLT_TIMEOUT, 300), or None to wait forever;
policy, a host’s function fn(name, args) returning 'allow', 'deny', 'ask' or None, consulted before saved rules and the mode;
rules_path, a JSON file of saved allow and deny rules, which always adds to;
no_listener and on_timeout, what happens when no frontend listens or nobody answers in time.

The examples below walk through each case.


source

Approvals
def Approvals(
    tools:tuple=(), # tool names that need approval
    mode:str='ask', # 'ask', 'edits', 'auto' or 'off'
    timeout:int=300, # seconds to wait; None waits forever
    host:NoneType=None, # for previews that read disk
    on_ask:NoneType=None, # called with the `Ask` when one is raised
    on_answer:NoneType=None, # called with the `Ask` when it is answered
    rules_path:NoneType=None, # saved allow/deny rules, `<cfg>/approvals.json`
    no_listener:str='refuse', # with nobody listening: 'refuse', or 'wait' for a listener
    on_timeout:str='refuse', # an ask nobody answers in time: 'refuse' or 'allow'
    policy:NoneType=None, # `fn(name, args)` -> a `VERDICTS` entry or None, consulted before rules and modes
):
Every request waiting for an answer, and the thread handshake behind each.

What a saved rule is matched against: the command, else the path, else the summary.


Some tools write only for certain arguments. generate_image with a path saves the picture where the model says, so it is gated like a write. Without a path it only adds a file under media/, and runs without asking. path_write encodes that rule. The cell also shows a saved rule, made with always, refusing a path under .git/ even in auto mode.

ap = Approvals(tools=WRITE_TOOLS)
assert path_write('generate_image', {'path': 'main.py'}) and not path_write('generate_image', {'path': ''}) and not path_write('create_file', {})
test_eq(ap.request('generate_image', {'prompt': 'x'}).answer, True)
probe = ap.request('generate_image', {'prompt': 'x', 'path': 'main.py'})
test_eq(probe.answer, False); assert 'nothing is listening' in probe.reply(), probe.reply()
ap.mode = 'auto'; test_eq(ap.request('generate_image', {'prompt': 'x', 'path': 'refs/a.png'}).answer, True)
ap.always('generate_image', '.git/*', 'deny', glob=True)
test_eq(ap.request('generate_image', {'prompt': 'x', 'path': '.git/config'}).answer, False)

A request raised inside a run records which run raised it (run_id), so a frontend can tell a sub-agent’s ask from the main turn’s. close refuses everything still waiting and every request after it, which is what happens when a session ends.

gate = Approvals(tools={'edit_file'}, mode='ask', timeout=1)
test_eq(gate.request('edit_file', {'path': '/proj/a.py'}).note,
        'nothing is listening for approvals, so this could not be asked')

from ramabana.runtime import Run, run_context
auto = Approvals(tools={'edit_file'}, mode='auto')
with run_context(Run('run_bg', 'background', 'q')):
    test_eq(auto.request('edit_file', {}).run_id, 'run_bg')
test_eq(auto.request('edit_file', {}).run_id, '')

test_eq(gate.closed, False)
test_eq(gate.close(), [])
test_eq(gate.closed, True)
test_eq(gate.request('edit_file', {}).note, 'the session is closing')

A request with no frontend listening is refused at once, and the reason says so. Waiting would hold the model’s thread for the whole timeout, for an answer that cannot come. no_listener='wait' holds the request until a frontend calls listen instead.

gate = Approvals(tools=WRITE_TOOLS)
gate.listeners, gate.request('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'}).reply()

listen registers a frontend. Its on_ask callback receives each new Ask, and the frontend answers with answer(ask.id, ok, note). Here the callback answers at once; a real interface shows the preview and answers when the person decides. listen returns a function that unregisters the frontend.

stop = gate.listen(on_ask=lambda a: gate.answer(a.id, False, 'rewrite it as a patch instead'))
decision = gate.request('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py', 'commands': '[]'})
bool(decision), decision.reply()

A tool outside tools is approved on the spot, with no request shown to anyone. It is still recorded in history.

test_eq(bool(gate.request('search_code', {'query': 'x'})), True)
test_eq(gate.pending, None)
len(gate.history)

In auto mode every write is approved without asking, and a plain approval has no note, so its reply is None. In off mode every write is refused, with a reason that names the mode.

Approvals(tools=WRITE_TOOLS, mode='auto').request('edit_file', {}).reply(), Approvals(tools=WRITE_TOOLS, mode='off').request('edit_file', {}).reply()

answer(..., session=True) approves the request and switches the gate’s mode for the rest of the session, to auto unless scope says otherwise. The approval’s note records the change.

stop()
gate.listen(on_ask=lambda a: gate.answer(a.id, True, session=True))
first = gate.request('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'})
gate.mode, first.note
test_eq(gate.mode, 'auto')

scope='edits' makes that switch to edits mode instead, so approving every file edit does not also unlock the shell. edits mode never covers add_root: widening the folders the agent may touch always asks.

scoped = Approvals(tools=WRITE_TOOLS | {'run_shell', 'add_root'}, timeout=1)
scoped.listen(on_ask=lambda a: scoped.answer(a.id, True, session=True, scope='edits'))
first = scoped.request('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'})
test_eq((bool(first), scoped.mode), (True, 'edits'))
test_eq(first.note, 'writes approved for the rest of this session (edits)')
test_eq(scoped.decide('edit_cell', {'path': 'n.ipynb'}, force=True).answer, True)
test_eq(scoped.decide('run_shell', {'command': 'ls'}, force=True), None)
test_eq(scoped.decide('add_root', {'path': '/elsewhere'}, force=True), None)
test_eq(Approvals(mode='edits').decide('add_root', {'path': '/elsewhere'}, force=True), None)
test_eq(Approvals(mode='auto').decide('add_root', {'path': '/elsewhere'}, force=True).answer, True)
test_eq(Approvals.edits_cover('edit_file'), True)
test_eq([Approvals.edits_cover(n) for n in ('add_root', 'run_shell')], [False, False])

A model that makes the same gated call three times in a row is stuck. The same call means the same tool with the same arguments, with no other gated call in between. auto mode would let it carry on, and ask mode would put the same question a third time. Instead the DOOM_LOOPth repeat, the third, goes to a person as a forced ask, whatever the mode.

It takes the ordinary request path, so the terminal waits and a frontend is asked again.
With nobody listening, it is refused, and the reason names the loop.
off mode and a saved deny rule still answer first.
A different call starts the count again.


spin = Approvals(tools={'edit_file'}, mode='auto', timeout=1)
asked = []
spin.listen(on_ask=lambda a: (asked.append(a), spin.answer(a.id, False, 'stop looping')))
call = {'function': {'name': 'edit_file', 'arguments': {'path': 'a.py'}}}
test_eq([bool(spin.gate(call)) for _ in range(3)], [True, True, False])
test_eq(len(asked), 1)
assert asked[0].preview.startswith('the same call three times running')
test_eq(bool(spin.gate({'function': {'name': 'edit_file', 'arguments': {'path': 'b.py'}}})), True)
alone = Approvals(tools={'edit_file'}, mode='auto')
[alone.gate(call) for _ in range(2)]
alone.gate(call).reply()

A request nobody answers within timeout is refused, and the reason gives the wait. on_timeout='allow' lets it through instead, except for a request the policy or the loop guard put to a person. When a turn is cancelled, cancel_all refuses what is waiting, so no worker thread is left blocked.

slow = Approvals(tools=WRITE_TOOLS, timeout=0.01)
slow.listen(on_ask=lambda a: None)
slow.request('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'}).reply()

timeout=None waits as long as it takes. mk_agent passes None by default, which suits the terminal, where a person sits at the screen. Approvals itself, and the ACP server, keep DFLT_TIMEOUT.

patient = Approvals(tools=WRITE_TOOLS, timeout=None)
patient.listen(on_ask=lambda a: threading.Timer(0.05, patient.answer, (a.id, True)).start())
test_eq(bool(patient.request('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'})), True)
test_eq(Approvals().timeout, DFLT_TIMEOUT)
test_eq(DFLT_TIMEOUT, 300)

gate is the function a backend calls before running a tool: it takes the tool-call dict, raises a request and blocks until it is decided. Every backend takes the same approve(tool_call) shape, and the gate works without the local engine installed. always and never are the two fixed approvers, for code that needs one without a gate.

Tools the user names
The model chooses its own tools during a turn. A person can also name one in the prompt: /search_code compaction threshold asks for search_code with that query. prompt_directives finds such names, and the turn adds them to its plan. A named search tool (search_code, web_search, research or memory_search) runs before the model is called, and its result goes into the message as evidence. Nothing else runs ahead of the model.

title: agent
text:
The briefing
The briefing is the system prompt: the standing instructions the model reads with every turn. system_prompt builds it from these parts, in order:

what the agent is, and the folders it may work in;
a description of this machine, when the host gives one;
the working rules (work_rules), keeping only those whose tool is offered;
the skill catalogue, each skill’s name and the first sentence of its description;
any skill inlined whole;
lessons kept in <cfg>/learned/AGENTS.md;
the project’s own instructions (project_context);
extra, text the caller adds last.

A skill is a markdown document that tells the model how to do one kind of work. The catalogue lists names only, and the model calls read_skill for a body when it needs one, because a dozen full skills would crowd out the code the model has to read. The one exception is INLINE_SKILLS: exhash is inlined, and inline_for keeps it only when edit_file, the tool it teaches, is offered.
small_system_prompt is the short briefing for small local models: the folders, one line about the machine, SMALL_RULES, and clipped project instructions.

work_rules
def work_rules(
    names:tuple=(),
    rules:tuple=((None, 'Act on the user’s verb. “Create”, “run”, “fix”, “add” and “as NAME” request a\n  result, not a plan: use the tool that produces it, verify it, then report what exists.\n  Never stop at “I will…”.'), (None, 'Before each tool call, write one short line in the -ing form saying what you are doing, so the\n  user can follow the work: “Reading the config loader.” End with the result, conclusion, or what\n  is needed.'), (None, 'Never claim a file changed, a command passed, or a test went green unless a tool\n  result in this conversation says so. If you did not run it, say you did not run it.'), (None, 'A tool result starting with ERROR: is a failure. Read it, fix the cause, and try a\n  different approach. Calling the same tool again unchanged is never the fix.'), (None, 'Keep a plan small enough that every step has one independently verifiable outcome, and verify\n  a step before building on it. If verification would widen the scope, split the step or report\n  the blocker.'), ('search_code', 'Use `search_code` for project behaviour, unfamiliar APIs, or uncertainty about an\n  installed library -- the index covers this repo *and* every installed package. Do not\n  search for routine Python you already know.'), ('grep', 'Use `grep` when you know the exact string: a symbol you are renaming, an error\n  message, an import. `search_code` finds what is *like* the query; `grep` finds every\n  place it literally occurs, which is what a rename or an audit needs.'), ('view_file', 'Prefer `view_file` over guessing. Copy paths exactly from the workspace, notebook\n  context, or search results; never shorten, repair, or reconstruct a path.'), ('replace_text', 'To change a file: read it, then `replace_text` with `oldText` copied exactly from\n  what you read. Send every change to one file as one call.'), ('edit_file', '`edit_file` addresses lines by the hashes `view_file` returns, so a stale read fails\n  instead of damaging the wrong line; read the `exhash` skill before your first one.'), ('notebook_cells', 'Never use `view_file` or `replace_text` on an `.ipynb` file. Call `notebook_cells` on\n  its exact path, choose the returned cell id, then `view_cell` and `edit_cell`.'), (None, 'A `<notebook path="…">` block is the open notebook and its exact path. Its cells are\n  already visible; use that path with the notebook tools and never reconstruct it.'), ('run_shell', 'Check your work with `run_shell`: after an edit run the project’s tests, after a\n  signature change run its linter or type checker. Use the commands the project itself\n  documents (README, pyproject, Makefile). Only commands that exit on their own: a server,\n  watcher or slow suite goes to `run_shell_bg`, read with `shell_output`.'), ('run_python', 'Code cells inside `<notebook>` have already executed. Their printed `<output>` is not\n  Python and must never be copied into `run_python`. For a request about `df`, call\n  `inspect_python()` with no code first, then run only the transformation the user asked for.'), ('run_python', '`run_python` shares the user’s kernel namespace. Read anything; bind results to NEW\n  names. You cannot rebind or delete the user’s variables, so do not try.'), ('web_search', '`web_search` and `read_url` reach what is outside this machine: current documentation,\n  releases, news. The repository and its installed packages are answered locally.'), ('memory_search', 'When prior context could change what you do -- a project you have worked on before, a\n  preference, an earlier decision -- search Vishalakshi durable memory with `memory_search`.'), ('read_skill', 'Before writing prose that ships with the work -- a docstring, a comment, a README, a\n  commit message, a PR description, a message to a colleague -- read the `write_docs`\n  skill. For narrative writing read `write_prose`, and for the design a codebase is\n  derived from, `theory`.'), (None, 'Before bulk work on an uncertain task, state the question, the smallest experiment that answers\n  it, and what counts as success; run one pilot first, and report “it ran” apart from “the output is right”.'), ('git_status', 'Git goes through its tools: `git_status`, `git_diff`, `git_log`, `git_divergence` to look;\n  `git_commit`, `git_checkout`, `git_stash`, `git_remote` to act, each returning an `undo` token.\n  `run_shell` refuses `git commit|push|pull|fetch|stash|switch|checkout`.'), ('run_shell', 'This kernel, the project venv and bare `python` can be three interpreters; "On this\n  machine" above lists them, and `run_shell` needs the one you mean.'), ('delegate_search', 'A sub-agent’s report is a hypothesis until a tool result of your own confirms the facts your\n  next step rests on. Verify those and only those.'), ('delegate_search', 'When two or more questions are independent and each would take several tool calls,\n  pass them together as `questions` rather than working through them yourself.'), ('screenshot', {True: 'A picture a tool returns (`screenshot`, `view_file` on an image) arrives as an image right after\n  the tool results; look at it directly. A resumed conversation replays its path, not the picture,\n  so call the tool again to see it.', False: 'This model cannot see pictures, so `screenshot` and `view_file` on an image give a path. To look at\n  one, call `delegate_search(questions, images=[path])`. If that is refused because the sub-agent\n  model cannot see pictures either, say so and read the page with `page_text` instead.'}), ('watch', "`watch(target, kind='folder', instructions=…)` is for work happening beside this conversation:\n  another agent editing the repo, a build writing output. `instructions` are the whole brief the\n  reviewer gets, so write them self-contained; `pattern` narrows the files. Reviews arrive at the\n  start of a later turn; `list_watches` shows what is watched."), (None, 'Make the change the user asked for and no other. Do not reformat, reorganise, or\n  “improve” code you were not asked to touch, and never discard their edits.'), (None, 'Writes may be put to the user for approval. A refusal comes back with their reason --\n  read it and change the approach, do not retry the same call.'), (None, 'Write, edit and run only inside the folders above. Anything else is refused.'), (None, 'Report what you did, what you found and what it cost, and cut what the reader does not need.'), (None, 'Answer in plain sentences. Headings, bullet lists and bold belong in a document the\n  user asked for, not in a reply, and a code fence holds code rather than prose.')),
    pictures:bool=True
):

title: agent
text:
The session plan
The session plan is the checklist the model keeps of what it is doing: a title and a list of todos, each pending, active, done or cancelled, with at most one active. It is saved beside the history, so it survives a stopped turn and a restart. While it has steps it appears in every briefing, so after a stop the model continues from the active item. It lives on the Agent rather than the host, so the terminal, the MCP server and Leela all read the same object.
Plan holds the list and Todo is one step. Plan.update changes a step found by id, unique id prefix or unique text, and marking one step active moves any other active step back to pending.

A model sends a list of steps as a JSON array, as one step per line, or as a real list. parse_plan_items accepts all three. It lives in ramabana.tools, because delegate_search reads its questions argument the same way.

parse_plan_items('["Cut shalya", "Rewire ramabana"]'), parse_plan_items('one\ntwo')


test_eq(parse_plan_items('["a", "b"]'), ['a', 'b'])
test_eq(parse_plan_items('one\ntwo'), ['one', 'two'])
test_eq(parse_plan_items(['a', 'b']), ['a', 'b'])
test_eq(parse_plan_items(''), [])
test_eq(parse_plan_items('  spaced  '), ['spaced'])

plan_tools gives the model two tools over the plan:

set_plan(items) replaces the steps and keeps any title the person set with /plan. An empty list clears the plan.
update_todo changes one step’s status or text by id or unique prefix, or appends a step when no id is given.

There is no tool to read the plan: it is in the briefing, and both tools return it. plan_tools takes a function that returns the plan and an optional save function, so the caller decides where the plan lives. save takes no arguments, and an error inside it is ignored, so a failed write never ends a turn.

held = Plan('Ship the split', ['Cut shalya', 'Rewire ramabana'])
saves = []
pt = {t.__name__: t for t in plan_tools(lambda: held, save=lambda: saves.append(held.md()))}
sorted(pt)


test_eq(sorted(pt), ['set_plan', 'update_todo'])
assert 'added' in pt['update_todo'](text='Migrate leela')
test_eq(len(held.todos), 3)
pt['update_todo'](held.todos[0].id, 'done')
test_eq(held.todos[0].status, 'done')
assert failed(pt['update_todo']('no-such-id', 'done'))
assert failed(pt['update_todo']())
assert saves, 'every change is handed to the saver'
assert pt['set_plan'](['only step']).startswith('**Ship the split**')
test_eq([t.text for t in held.todos], ['only step'])
test_eq(pt['set_plan']([]), 'plan cleared')
test_eq(pt['set_plan'](['fresh']).splitlines()[0], '**Plan**  ·  0/1 done')
test_eq(get_schema(pt['set_plan'])['input_schema']['properties']['items']['type'], 'array')

broken = {t.__name__: t for t in plan_tools(lambda: held, save=lambda: 1/0)}
assert 'still works' in broken['set_plan'](['still works'])

title: agent
text:
The agent
One Agent holds one continuous model conversation. Building one is cheap: no model loads until the first turn. Attached to it are:

routing, which model each job runs on (see core);
tools, skills and extensions;
the approval gate and compaction;
the activity feed, the plan and the history on disk.

A job is one kind of model work. turn is the main conversation; oneshot, inline, completion, classify, summary and subagent are short jobs that can run on other, cheaper models. A missing model is reported, never raised. The model may be a download of several gigabytes or need an API key, and an editor should still open without either; ready and note say whether the turn model is up, and why not.
The main constructor options:

approvals, an Approvals gate, or None for no gate;
cfg, the config folder for history, plans, skills and extensions; None keeps nothing on disk;
subagent_writes, on by default: sub-agents get write tools, behind the same gate;
readonly, which withholds every tool that acts;
max_cost, max_tokens, session_max_cost and session_max_tokens, budgets that stop a turn;
keep_conversation, which saves the whole conversation each turn for a full resume;
profile, auto, small or full, described below.



source

Agent
def Agent(
    host, model:NoneType=None, # turn model; None takes the routing default
    routing:NoneType=None, sp:NoneType=None, # override the whole briefing
    extra_sp:str='', # text added after the briefing, which stays
    global_skills:bool=True, # read skills from `~/.agents/skills` too
    approvals:NoneType=None, # an `Approvals`; None gates nothing
    cfg:NoneType=None, # config dir, for skills and extensions
    compact:NoneType=None, # compact automatically at the threshold; None reads config.toml's `compaction.auto`, else True
    compact_strategy:NoneType=None, # 'summary' or deterministic 'surgical'; None reads `compaction.strategy`, else 'summary'
    kernel_alive:bool=True, # what the post-compaction note may promise
    extensions:bool=True, project_extensions:bool=False, # project extensions execute repo code: opt in
    ext_paths:tuple=(), inline_skills:tuple=('exhash',), subagents:bool=True,
    subagent_writes:bool=True, # sub-agents get write tools, behind the same approvals
    subagent_steps:int=60, # steps a sub-agent may take; caps a delegation's `max_steps`
    subagent_timeout:int=1800, # seconds before a delegation is stopped; 0 never
    subagent_depth:int=2, # levels of sub-agents that may delegate again, at most `SUB_DEPTH_MAX`
    readonly:bool=False, # withhold every tool that acts
    readonly_calls:NoneType=None, # hard cap on read-only calls, when set
    max_cost:NoneType=None, # dollars the turn model may spend in one turn; None has no limit, and a local model reports none
    max_tokens:NoneType=None, # tokens the turn model may spend in one turn; None has no limit
    session_max_cost:NoneType=None, # dollars the whole session may spend, earlier turns included
    session_max_tokens:NoneType=None, # tokens the whole session may spend, earlier turns included
    local_multimodal:bool=False, # load LiteRT vision/audio encoders for local models
    tool_max_len:NoneType=None, # None scales the result cap to the model window
    on_compact:NoneType=None, on_activity:NoneType=None,
    history_name:str='agent', # names this durable conversation in the config dir
    session_id:NoneType=None, # this session's id, for a host that keeps its own; None makes a new one
    keep_conversation:bool=False, # save the turn model's whole conversation each turn, for `resume_session(full=True)`
    poll_every:int=900, # seconds between automatic watch polls; 0 never polls
    verify:str='', # the project's check; empty reads `[tool.ramabana] verify`
    instruction_style:str='ramabana', # 'ramabana' | 'aai' compatibility profile
    optin:tuple=(), # shalya's opt-in tool groups, see `OPTIN`
    profile:str='auto', # 'auto', 'small' or 'full'; see `profile_for`
    warm:NoneType=None, # seed with dhrona's examples; None: off
    learned:bool=True, # brief from `<cfg>/learned`; False runs without it
    fresh_hint:NoneType=None, # what a turn too large for any window tells the user to do, `{session}` its id; None suits any host
):
One model conversation on a host, with its tools, approvals, activity feed, plan and history.


__init__ calls these properties, directly or through each other, so they are patched in before any agent is built. Their examples come later, after the harness that builds a demo agent. The rest of the class follows in reading order rather than definition order.

def profile():
small or full: how the turn model is briefed. See core.profile_for.


profile decides how much the turn model is told. With profile='auto', a local model, or one whose window is 32k tokens or less, gets the small briefing and tool set, and a cloud model with a larger window gets full. Passing small or full overrides that. budget says how many characters of tool schemas and results the model can afford and which tool groups to drop; see budget_for in core. fake_agent fixes the profile at full, because its fake model has a 1k window and every test below exercises the full path.

from ramabana.core import ModelSpec, SMALL_TOOLS
from ramabana.agent import Agent as _Agent   # the installed class; this page's `Agent` is unfinished
_local, _big = ModelSpec('gemma-e4b', 'litert', 'litert-community/x', 16_384), ModelSpec('sonnet', 'remote', 'claude-sonnet-4-5', 200_000)
def _on(spec, **kw):
    a = _Agent(MemHost({'/proj/a.py': 'x = 1\n'}), extensions=False, **kw)
    a.routing.spec = lambda job='turn', fallback=True: spec
    return a
test_eq((_on(_local).profile, _on(_big).profile, _on(_local, profile='full').profile, _on(_big, profile='small').profile), ('small', 'full', 'full', 'small'))
test_eq(fake_agent()[0].profile, 'full')
test_fail(lambda: _Agent(MemHost(), profile='tiny'), contains='profile')
_h = MemHost({'/proj/a.py': 'x = 1\n'})
test_eq((_on(_local).warm, _on(_big).warm, _on(_local, warm=True).warm, _on(_big, warm=True).warm), (False, False, True, True))

Git writes go through git tools, never the shell. When the session offers the git tool, run_shell refuses the seven subcommands that have one (commit, push, pull, fetch, stash, switch, checkout) and names the tool to use. git_shell_denial finds them wherever they appear:

anywhere in a &&, ; or | chain, split after quoting, so a quoted git commit inside an echo is only text;
after any NAME=value prefix, or a git option such as -C;
behind one env, xargs, nohup, time, command, exec or nice wrapper, or inside a sh -c "..." line.

gheasy’s classify decides what counts as a read, so git stash list runs and git stash is refused. A git tool returns an undo token, and the agent keeps it so /rewind can undo the write.
_guard applies this rule and two more before any call runs. A shell line may not hide its own output with | head, | tail or 2>&1 (shell_denial), and a write may not hand-edit a module nbdev generated from a notebook (generated_denial).

Why run_shell refuses this git write, or ’’ when it may run or tools lacks the tool.

shell_denial

    command
):
Why a shell line hides its own output, or ’’. Quoted text never matches; a sh -c line is read too.



for cmd, tool in [('git commit -m x', 'git_commit'), ('git -C /p commit -am y', 'git_commit'), ('git status && git commit -m x', 'git_commit'),
                  ('git push origin main', 'git_remote'), ('GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 git pull', 'git_remote'), ('git stash', 'git_stash'),
                  ('git switch -c f', 'git_checkout'), ('/usr/bin/git checkout -- a.py', 'git_checkout'), ('ls | git fetch --all', 'git_remote'),
                  ('bash -c "git commit -m x"', 'git_commit'), ("sh -c 'cd /p && git push'", 'git_remote'), ('env GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 git pull', 'git_remote'),
                  ('git diff --name-only | xargs git commit -m x', 'git_commit'), ('nohup git fetch', 'git_remote'), ('bash -lc "git switch main"', 'git_checkout')]:
    assert f'`{tool}`' in git_shell_denial(cmd), cmd
for cmd in ['git log --grep=commit', 'git stash list', 'git status', 'git diff HEAD~1', 'echo "git commit" > notes.txt', 'ls', 'git rebase -i main', '', 'git -c core.pager=cat log',
            'echo "a; git commit -m y"', "echo 'git push' | tee notes.txt", 'bash -c "git log"', 'env | grep GIT']:
    test_eq(git_shell_denial(cmd), '')
import subprocess, tempfile
from shalya.host import LocalHost
repo = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'repo'; repo.mkdir()
subprocess.run(['git', 'init', '-q', str(repo)], check=True)
denied_agent, _ = fake_agent(host=LocalHost([str(repo)], index=False))
shell = next(t for t in denied_agent.tools if t.__name__ == 'run_shell')
out = shell('git commit -m x'); assert failed(out) and '`git_commit`' in out
test_eq(denied_agent.activity.rows()[-1]['ok'], False)
plain_agent, _ = fake_agent()
test_eq(plain_agent._deny_git_shell('run_shell', {'command': 'git commit -m x'}), '')
assert '`run_shell` refuses `git commit|push|pull|fetch|stash|switch|checkout`' in work_rules({'git_status'}) and '`run_shell` is never the way' in CLAUDE_NOTES

An approval request is not a tool call, so the tool wrapper never sees it; the agent hooks its Approvals instead. An ask put to a person adds one activity row the moment it is raised, with kind ask, state awaiting and its ask_id. The answer finishes that row. A refusal leaves ok False, with the reason the model was told as detail, and writes a line to the run’s transcript. An approval leaves ok True, and the call that follows gets its own row as usual. A refusal nobody was asked about, from a saved rule or the mode, still gets a row.

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from ramabana.runtime import Run, run_context

gated, _ = fake_agent()
gated.approvals = Approvals(tools=WRITE_TOOLS)
stop = gated.approvals.listen(on_ask=lambda a: threading.Timer(0.02, gated.approvals.answer, (a.id, False, 'not that file')).start())
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    with run_context(Run('run_t', question='q', log=Path(d)/'run_t.log')):
        refused = gated.approvals.request('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'})
    log = (Path(d)/'run_t.log').read_text()
rows = gated.activity.rows()
test_eq(len(rows), 1)
test_eq({k: rows[0][k] for k in ('tool', 'args', 'ok', 'kind', 'detail')},
        {'tool': 'edit_file', 'args': {'path': 'a.py'}, 'ok': False, 'kind': 'ask', 'detail': refused.reply()})
test_eq(refused.reply(), 'Denied by human operator. Reason given: not that file')
assert refused.reply() in log

stop()
gated.approvals.listen(on_ask=lambda a: gated.approvals.answer(a.id, True))
assert gated.approvals.request('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'})
rows = gated.activity.rows()
test_eq(len(rows), 2)
test_eq((rows[-1]['kind'], rows[-1]['ok'], bool(rows[-1]['ask_id'])), ('ask', True, True))

A before_tool extension hook may rewrite a call’s arguments. A rewritten write goes back through the gate with its new arguments, and a refusal there is still one row.

hooked, _ = fake_agent()
hooked.approvals = Approvals(tools=WRITE_TOOLS)
hooked.approvals.listen(on_ask=lambda a: hooked.approvals.answer(a.id, False, 'not b.py either'))
hooked.registry.on('before_tool', lambda agent, name, args: dict(args, path='b.py'))
edit = next(t for t in hooked.tools if t.__name__ == 'replace_text')
out = edit(path='a.py', edits=[])
assert 'not b.py either' in out
test_eq(len(hooked.activity.rows()), 1)
test_eq(hooked.approvals.history[0].args, {'path': 'b.py', 'edits': []})
test_eq(hooked.activity.rows()[0]['args']['path'], 'b.py')

Through urai’s real tool loop, the model receives exactly Ask.reply() as the tool result, and the refused tool never runs. This cell guards the uraiyadal>=0.0.8 pin, the first version that passes on the reply() of a refused approval.

from urai import Chat, ToolCall
from urai.opts import ChatOpts
from urai.core import Resp
from urai.loop import ToolLoopMixin

class _ScriptChat(ToolLoopMixin, Chat):
    "urai's loop over a fixed list of replies, and no model."
    _runtime, ctx_limit, token_count = 'script', 8192, 0
    def __init__(self, model=None, *, script=(), **kw):
        self.script, self.steps = list(script), 0
        self._setup(model, ChatOpts.create(kw.pop('opts', None), **kw)); self._set_tools(self.tools)
    def _model_step(self, **kw):
        r = self.script[min(self.steps, len(self.script) - 1)]; self.steps += 1
        return Resp({'role': 'assistant', 'usage': {'total_tokens': 10}, **r})

loop_gate = Approvals(tools=WRITE_TOOLS)
loop_gate.listen(on_ask=lambda a: loop_gate.answer(a.id, False, 'no answer after 300s'))
called = []
def edit_file(path: str) -> str:
    "Edit a file."
    called.append(path); return 'edited'
c = _ScriptChat('script-1', script=[{'content': '', 'tool_calls': [dict(ToolCall('edit_file', {'path': 'a.py'}))]}, {'content': 'ok'}],
                tools=[edit_file], approve=loop_gate.gate)
c('go')
test_eq([m['content'] for m in c.hist if m['role'] == 'tool'], ['Denied by human operator. Reason given: no answer after 300s'])
test_eq(called, [])

A sub-agent is a second model conversation the agent starts to work on one question, with its own tools and step limit; its answer comes back as a tool result. delegate_search waits for the answer. delegate_async starts the sub-agent in the background and returns at once, and delegate_result collects the answer later. background is where those background runs live. Each agent builds one on first use and closes it with the session, so nothing keeps running after the last turn. A finished answer waits for the next turn, and background_notice adds it to that prompt.

Each is wrapped by _record, so its calls reach the activity feed, the change tracking and the guards above. In read-only or plan mode it is the read-only view. system_prompt builds this agent’s briefing from the module-level system_prompt, adding the plan, remembered notes, the model family’s notes and the note about steering.

An application with a vault (see vault) overrides memory_context, which is why the agent calls the method instead of reading the file.

From here on the examples run a real Agent against a real model’s answers, recorded once into chatcache/ and replayed. A question nobody recorded raises instead of reaching a model, so this page never calls one. To add a question, record it on purpose:

Before a message goes out, _fit makes it fit the turn model’s window, cheapest step first, and stops at the first that fits:

A message, or a newest exchange, larger than half the room the briefing leaves is cut to an excerpt first, so a short conversation is not compacted to make room for one paste. A prompt holding a <notebook> is left to the notebook step.
The oldest tool results, then the oldest pictures, are trimmed (Backend.trim).
The conversation is compacted, whether or not compaction.auto is on.
The notebook’s discard and then auto cells are left out (compact_notebook_context).
The newest two messages are cut (Backend.shrink_recent).
The message itself is cut to the room left (fit_content): the newest pictures that fit stay, and text becomes its head and its end around a note naming the file that holds it whole. The reminders _prepare added to its end are kept whole.

Whatever is cut is written whole under <runs_dir>/full, readable by this user alone, and the note says how to read it with the tools the model has: view_file(path, start=N) in pieces, or grep. When the read tools cannot reach that folder, it is opened to them for reading only. The log keeps the prompt as it was typed.
ContextFull is left for a briefing and tools that alone overflow the window. Its message ends with fresh_hint, the host’s advice, {session} standing for the session id. The terminal session passes CLI_FRESH, which says to quit and ramabana --resume; an app that embeds the agent passes its own, and without one the advice is FRESH_HINT, which names no command.
